It must satisfy completeness (honest proofs succeed), soundness (false proofs fail), and zero-knowledge (the verifier learns nothing beyond the truth of the statement). ZK proofs are used in blockchain and privacy-preserving systems.
standard.deepDive: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) allow verification without disclosure. The classic analogy: proving you know the secret path through a cave without revealing the path. ZKPs must satisfy three properties: completeness (an honest prover can convince the verifier), soundness (a dishonest prover cannot fool the verifier), and zero-knowledge (the verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the statement). Modern applications include privacy-preserving cryptocurrencies (Zcash uses zk-SNARKs), identity verification, voting systems, and blockchain scaling solutions (zk-rollups). The development of efficient ZKP systems like Groth16, PLONK, and STARKs has made practical applications feasible.

standard.question: What is 'multi-head attention' in transformers?
options: Using multiple transformer models simultaneously
Running multiple attention operations in parallel with different learned projections, then concatenating the results
Attention applied to multiple input sequences at once
A technique where each layer attends to a different head of data
standard.explanation: Multi-head attention runs h parallel attention functions, each with independently learned linear projections for Q, K, and V. The outputs are concatenated and linearly transformed. This allows the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously — one head might capture syntax while another captures semantics.
standard.deepDive: Multi-head attention allows the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously. Each 'head' applies its own learned linear transformations to create its own Q, K, V matrices, computes attention independently, and the results are concatenated and linearly projected. With h=8 heads and d_model=512, each head works in d_model/h = 64 dimensions. Different heads learn to focus on different types of relationships: some attend to syntactic structure, others to semantic similarity, others to positional proximity. The concatenation of multiple perspectives provides richer representations than a single attention function with the same total dimensionality.

standard.question: What is 'Goodhart's Law' and how does it relate to AI alignment?
options: A law about the optimal size of datasets for training
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — in AI, optimizing a proxy reward can lead to behaviors that game the metric rather than achieve the intended goal
A law governing the rate of improvement in AI capabilities
A legal framework for governing AI development
standard.explanation: Goodhart's Law states that once a metric becomes a target for optimization, it is no longer a reliable metric. In AI alignment, this manifests as reward hacking — a model optimizing a proxy reward signal in ways that satisfy the metric but violate the designer's intent. This is a fundamental challenge in specifying objectives for AI systems.
standard.deepDive: Goodhart's Law is a central concern in AI alignment. When we train AI systems with reward models (proxies for human preferences), the system may optimise the proxy in ways that diverge from the true objective. Examples in RL: a game agent discovers exploits to maximise score rather than playing as intended; a recommendation system maximises engagement metrics by promoting addictive or polarising content rather than genuinely useful content. The problem intensifies with more capable optimisers: a superintelligent AI optimising a flawed reward signal could take extreme actions that score well on the metric while being catastrophic by human standards. Approaches to mitigate this include reward modelling, debate, and iterated amplification.

standard.question: Who founded information theory, and in what year was the seminal paper published?
options: Alan Turing, 1936
Claude Shannon, 1948
John von Neumann, 1945
Norbert Wiener, 1950
standard.explanation: Claude Shannon published 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' in 1948, founding the field of information theory. The paper introduced the concept of entropy as a measure of information, established the theoretical limits of data compression and reliable communication over noisy channels, and laid the mathematical groundwork for the digital age.
standard.deepDive: Shannon's 1948 paper introduced the concept of entropy as a measure of information, proved the fundamental limits of data compression (source coding theorem) and reliable communication over noisy channels (channel coding theorem), and established the mathematical framework used by all modern communication systems. Before Shannon, engineers had no way to determine whether their communication systems were close to optimal. Shannon showed that the channel capacity C = B × log₂(1 + S/N) gives the maximum data rate for reliable communication, and that any rate below capacity is achievable with sufficiently clever coding. His work enables everything from mobile phones to deep-space communication.

standard.question: What is 'formal verification' in software engineering?
options: Writing formal documentation for code
Using mathematical proofs to rigorously verify that a system satisfies specified properties, guaranteeing correctness
Formal code review by senior engineers
Testing software with formal test cases
standard.explanation: Formal verification uses mathematical methods (like model checking, theorem proving, and abstract interpretation) to prove that a program satisfies its specification for all possible inputs. Unlike testing (which checks some inputs), formal verification provides mathematical guarantees. It's used in safety-critical domains like aerospace, hardware design, and increasingly in AI safety research.
standard.deepDive: Formal verification provides mathematical guarantees of correctness, unlike testing which can only find bugs, not prove their absence. Methods include model checking (exhaustively exploring all possible states — used to verify hardware circuits and communication protocols), theorem proving (constructing mathematical proofs of correctness using tools like Coq, Isabelle, or Lean), and abstract interpretation (analysing programs by computing over abstract domains). Formal verification is standard in safety-critical domains: the Paris Métro Line 14 was the first fully automatic metro to use formally verified control software, and Intel uses formal methods extensively after the Pentium FDIV bug (1994) cost $475 million.

standard.question: What is the 'scaling laws' phenomenon in large language models?
options: Rules for scaling server infrastructure
Empirical findings that model performance improves predictably as a power law with increases in model size, dataset size, and compute
Guidelines for scaling development teams
Laws governing how fast models can be trained
standard.explanation: Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022, 'Chinchilla') found that LLM loss decreases as a smooth power law with model parameters, dataset size, and training compute. These scaling laws allow predicting performance before training and determine optimal resource allocation. They have been a key driver of the trend toward ever-larger models.
standard.deepDive: Scaling laws show that LLM cross-entropy loss L follows power laws: L ∝ N^(-α) for model size N, L ∝ D^(-β) for dataset size D, and L ∝ C^(-γ) for compute C. The Chinchilla paper (2022) showed that previous models (like GPT-3) were 'over-parameterised and under-trained' — for a given compute budget, using a smaller model trained on more data is more efficient. Chinchilla, with 70B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens, matched the performance of the 280B-parameter Gopher trained on 300B tokens. These findings shifted the field toward training smaller models on more data. However, inference costs depend on model size, so deployment considerations may favour larger models trained with less data.

standard.question: What is 'speculative execution' and why was it in the news?
options: A stock market prediction algorithm
A CPU optimization that pre-executes likely instruction paths — it was exploited by the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities
A speculative scheduling algorithm for cloud computing
An AI technique for predicting user behavior
standard.explanation: Speculative execution is a CPU optimization where the processor guesses which instruction path a branch will take and executes it ahead of time. If wrong, it rolls back. In 2018, the Spectre and Meltdown attacks showed that speculative execution leaves measurable traces in CPU caches, enabling attackers to read protected memory through timing side-channel attacks.
standard.deepDive: Modern CPUs predict which branch of a conditional statement will be taken and begin executing instructions along the predicted path before the condition is resolved. If the prediction is correct (which it is 95%+ of the time), this significantly speeds up execution. The Spectre vulnerability (discovered 2017, published 2018) exploited speculative execution by tricking the CPU into speculatively accessing memory it shouldn't, then measuring cache timing to infer the accessed data — a 'side-channel' attack. Meltdown specifically targeted Intel CPUs by exploiting speculative reads of kernel memory. These vulnerabilities affected virtually every modern CPU and required both hardware and software mitigations.

standard.question: What is the 'lottery ticket hypothesis'?
options: A theory about random weight initialization
The hypothesis that dense neural networks contain sparse subnetworks ('winning tickets') that, when trained in isolation from their original initialization, can match the full network's performance
A theory about random sampling in training data
A hypothesis about the randomness in gradient descent
standard.explanation: Proposed by Frankle and Carlin (2019), the lottery ticket hypothesis suggests that randomly-initialized dense networks contain small subnetworks that, when trained alone from their initial weights, achieve comparable accuracy. This implies most parameters are unnecessary, which has implications for model compression and our understanding of why overparameterized networks generalize well.
standard.deepDive: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis suggests that sparse subnetworks within randomly initialised dense networks are responsible for learning, and these 'winning tickets' can achieve comparable accuracy with a fraction of the parameters (often 90%+ pruning). Finding winning tickets requires training the full network, pruning weights with the smallest magnitudes, and rewinding remaining weights to their original random initialisation before retraining. This has practical implications for deploying models on resource-constrained devices. The hypothesis also raises theoretical questions about why overparameterised networks train well — the excess parameters may serve as a 'search space' that makes finding good solutions easier during training.

standard.question: What is 'Byzantine fault tolerance'?
options: A method for recovering from physical hardware damage
The ability of a distributed system to reach consensus and function correctly even when some nodes behave arbitrarily or maliciously
A type of error correction for data transmission
A backup strategy named after Byzantine architecture
standard.explanation: Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) means a distributed system can function correctly even if some nodes send conflicting, false, or arbitrary messages. The Byzantine Generals Problem (Lamport et al., 1982) proved that consensus requires more than 2/3 of nodes to be honest. BFT is crucial for blockchain consensus mechanisms and safety-critical distributed systems.
standard.deepDive: Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is named after the 'Byzantine Generals Problem' (Lamport, Shoustari, Pease, 1982): generals besieging a city must coordinate an attack, but some generals may be traitors sending contradictory messages. The key result is that BFT requires at least 3f+1 total nodes to tolerate f Byzantine (arbitrarily malicious) faults. This is stronger than crash fault tolerance (which only needs 2f+1 nodes). Practical BFT algorithms (PBFT by Castro and Liskov, 1999) enabled Byzantine fault tolerance in real systems but with high communication overhead. Blockchain networks use BFT variants: Bitcoin's proof-of-work provides BFT through economic incentives rather than traditional consensus.

standard.question: What is the 'knowledge distillation' technique?
options: Extracting knowledge from databases
Training a smaller 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model, often using the teacher's soft output probabilities
Compressing knowledge graphs
Removing unnecessary knowledge from a model
standard.explanation: Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) trains a compact 'student' model to mimic a large 'teacher' model by learning from the teacher's soft probability distributions rather than hard labels. The soft outputs contain richer information about inter-class similarities. This enables deploying smaller, faster models that retain much of the teacher's performance.
standard.deepDive: Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a large 'teacher' to a small 'student' by training the student on the teacher's soft output probabilities (logits) rather than just the hard labels. The soft outputs contain information about relationships between classes — a digit classifier's output might assign 7% probability to '7' being a '1' (due to visual similarity), information lost in the hard label. The temperature parameter T controls the softness: higher T produces more uniform distributions, revealing more inter-class relationships. Distillation has been used to create deployable versions of large models: DistilBERT is 40% smaller and 60% faster than BERT while retaining 97% of its language understanding.

standard.question: What is 'chain-of-thought' prompting?
options: Linking multiple AI models together in a chain
A prompting technique that improves LLM reasoning by asking the model to show intermediate reasoning steps before giving a final answer
Training a model on sequential thought processes
Using multiple prompts in sequence to refine output
standard.explanation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022) asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps. This dramatically improves performance on math, logic, and multi-step reasoning tasks. Zero-shot CoT simply adds 'Let's think step by step.' Few-shot CoT provides worked examples. CoT reveals how the model decomposes and solves problems.
standard.deepDive: Chain-of-thought prompting was shown by Wei et al. (2022) to dramatically improve LLM performance on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, especially for large models. By including intermediate reasoning steps in the prompt (or simply adding 'Let's think step by step'), the model generates explicit reasoning chains before arriving at an answer. Zero-shot CoT (just saying 'think step by step' without examples) also works surprisingly well. The mechanism is debated: CoT may help by decomposing complex problems into simpler subproblems, by activating relevant knowledge, or by providing a form of internal computation. Tree-of-thought and graph-of-thought extend CoT by exploring multiple reasoning paths.

standard.question: What is the Church-Turing thesis?
options: A thesis about church databases developed by Turing
The conjecture that any function naturally regarded as computable can be computed by a Turing machine (or equivalently, by lambda calculus)
A proof that all computers are equivalent
A thesis about the limits of quantum computing
standard.explanation: The Church-Turing thesis (independently formulated by Alonzo Church and Alan Turing in 1936) states that any function computable by an effective procedure is computable by a Turing machine. While not a formal theorem (since 'effective procedure' isn't formally defined), it is widely accepted and has held for all known models of computation, including quantum computers (which are faster but compute the same class of functions).
standard.deepDive: The Church-Turing thesis is not a mathematical theorem but a hypothesis about the nature of computation. It was independently formulated through three equivalent formalisms: Turing machines (Turing), lambda calculus (Church), and recursive functions (Gödel/Herbrand). Despite being unproven, no counterexample has been found in nearly 90 years, and every proposed model of computation has turned out to be Turing-equivalent or weaker. The extended Church-Turing thesis (that Turing machines can efficiently simulate any physical computing device) is more controversial — quantum computers may violate it if they can efficiently solve problems outside BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time).

standard.question: What is 'model quantization' and why is it useful?
options: Measuring model quality with quantum metrics
Reducing the precision of model weights (e.g., from 32-bit to 4-bit integers) to decrease model size and speed up inference with minimal accuracy loss
Splitting a model into quantum-compatible components
Counting the total number of model parameters
standard.explanation: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of neural network weights and activations — for example, from 32-bit floating point to 8-bit or even 4-bit integers. This dramatically reduces memory usage and speeds up inference, often with surprisingly little accuracy loss. Techniques like GPTQ and QLoRA have made it possible to run large language models on consumer hardware.
standard.deepDive: Quantisation reduces model size and inference speed with minimal accuracy loss. Common approaches include post-training quantisation (PTQ, applied after training), quantisation-aware training (QAT, training with simulated low precision), and GPTQ/GGML formats for LLMs. INT8 quantisation (8-bit integers) typically loses less than 1% accuracy while halving model size and nearly doubling inference speed. More aggressive INT4 quantisation (4-bit) reduces size by 8x with modest accuracy loss. Recent techniques like QLoRA enable fine-tuning quantised models, and speculative decoding combines quantised models with full-precision verification for improved efficiency without quality loss.

standard.question: What is the 'No Free Lunch' theorem in machine learning?
options: Training models always requires expensive compute
Averaged over all possible problems, no learning algorithm outperforms any other — every algorithm must make assumptions that work well for some problems and poorly for others
There is no free way to get labeled training data
Machine learning models cannot learn without a cost function
standard.explanation: The No Free Lunch theorem (Wolpert & Macready, 1997) proves that no single learning algorithm is universally superior — averaged across all possible data distributions, they all perform equally. This means the choice of algorithm should depend on the specific problem's structure. An algorithm's success on one class of problems comes at the cost of performance on others.
standard.deepDive: The NFL theorem has important implications: it means that claims about one algorithm being universally better than another are meaningless without specifying the problem distribution. In practice, we are not interested in performance averaged over all possible problems — we care about performance on real-world problems, which have structure that algorithms can exploit. Neural networks implicitly assume that problems have hierarchical, compositional structure; decision trees assume axis-aligned decision boundaries; and linear models assume linear relationships. The success of deep learning is not a violation of NFL but evidence that many real-world problems have the kind of structure that deep networks are well-suited to exploit.

standard.question: What did Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's book 'Perceptrons' (1969) demonstrate?
options: That neural networks could solve any problem
That single-layer perceptrons cannot learn non-linearly-separable functions like XOR, contributing to the first AI winter
That perceptrons are superior to all other algorithms
That deep learning would never work
standard.explanation: Minsky and Papert rigorously proved that single-layer perceptrons cannot learn functions that are not linearly separable (like XOR). This was widely (and somewhat unfairly) interpreted as a fundamental limitation of neural networks in general, contributing to reduced funding and interest in neural network research — the first 'AI winter.' Multi-layer networks can learn XOR, but this wasn't well understood until the 1980s.
standard.deepDive: Minsky and Papert's demonstration that single-layer perceptrons cannot compute XOR (a function that outputs true when exactly one of two inputs is true) helped cause the first 'AI winter' — a period of reduced funding and interest in neural networks lasting roughly from 1969 to the mid-1980s. The problem is that XOR is not linearly separable: no single straight line can divide the XOR truth table's outputs. Adding a hidden layer resolves this, as the universal approximation theorem later showed, but efficient training of multi-layer networks was not developed until the backpropagation algorithm was popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986, reigniting interest in neural networks.

standard.question: What is 'differential privacy'?
options: A method for computing derivatives in private neural networks
A mathematical framework that provides formal guarantees that data analysis results reveal almost nothing about any individual in the dataset
Encrypting the difference between two datasets
A privacy policy for differential equations
standard.explanation: Differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006) guarantees that the output of a computation is nearly the same whether or not any single individual's data is included. This is achieved by adding calibrated noise. The privacy guarantee is parameterized by epsilon (ε) — smaller means stronger privacy. It's used by Apple, Google, and the US Census Bureau.
standard.deepDive: Differential privacy adds carefully calibrated random noise to computations on private data. The key parameter ε (epsilon) controls the privacy-utility trade-off: smaller ε means more privacy but noisier results. The formal guarantee is that the probability of any output changes by at most a factor of e^ε when any single individual's data is added or removed. Apple uses differential privacy to collect usage statistics from iPhones, the US Census Bureau used it for the 2020 Census, and Google uses it in Chrome for collecting browsing data. Differential privacy composes: running multiple DP queries increases the total privacy loss, and the 'privacy budget' tracks cumulative loss.

standard.question: What is 'emergent behavior' in large language models?
options: Behavior that was explicitly programmed into the model
Capabilities that appear unpredictably at certain scales but are absent in smaller models, such as few-shot reasoning or arithmetic
The model's ability to generate text
Error patterns that emerge during training
standard.explanation: Emergent abilities are capabilities that appear in large models but not small ones, seemingly arising unpredictably at certain scale thresholds. Examples include in-context learning, chain-of-thought reasoning, and arithmetic. However, recent work (Schaeffer et al., 2023) argues some apparent emergence may be artifacts of non-linear evaluation metrics rather than true phase transitions.
standard.deepDive: Emergent abilities in LLMs were documented by Wei et al. (2022), who showed capabilities appearing at certain model scales (typically 10B+ parameters) that were absent in smaller models. Examples include few-shot arithmetic, word unscrambling, and multi-step reasoning. However, Schaeffer et al. (2023) argued that apparent emergence may be an artefact of nonlinear evaluation metrics — when using linear metrics, performance appears to improve smoothly with scale rather than emerging suddenly. This debate has significant implications for AI safety: if capabilities emerge unpredictably, it becomes harder to anticipate what future systems can do.

standard.question: What is a 'Bloom filter'?
options: A graphics rendering technique
A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that can tell you if an element is definitely not in a set, or might be in a set (allowing false positives but not false negatives)
A filter for processing blooming garden images
A type of bandpass filter for signals
standard.explanation: A Bloom filter uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array. To add an element, set its hash positions to 1. To query, check all hash positions — if any is 0, the element is definitely absent; if all are 1, it's probably present (false positive possible). Bloom filters use far less space than hash sets and are used in databases, caches, and network routing.
standard.deepDive: A Bloom filter uses k hash functions mapping to an m-bit array. To insert an element, set all k hash positions to 1. To query, check if all k positions are 1 — if any is 0, the element definitely isn't in the set; if all are 1, it probably is (with a calculable false positive rate). False positive rate ≈ (1-e^(-kn/m))^k, where n is the number of elements. Bloom filters use far less memory than storing all elements: for 1 billion elements with 1% false positive rate, a Bloom filter needs only about 1.2 GB, while storing the elements directly might need 10-100x more. Applications include web browsers (checking URLs against malware databases), databases (avoiding unnecessary disk lookups), and network routers.

standard.question: What is 'mechanistic interpretability' in AI research?
options: Understanding the mechanical components of AI hardware
The study of reverse-engineering neural networks to understand the internal algorithms and representations they have learned
Interpreting user inputs mechanically
A method for debugging mechanical systems with AI
standard.explanation: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand what computations neural networks actually perform by reverse-engineering their learned representations and algorithms. Researchers identify features (meaningful directions in activation space), circuits (subnetworks implementing specific behaviors), and how information flows through the model. It is a key approach to making AI systems more transparent and trustworthy.
standard.deepDive: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand neural networks at the level of individual neurons, circuits, and features. Key findings include 'polysemantic neurons' (single neurons responding to multiple unrelated concepts), 'superposition' (models representing more features than they have dimensions by overlapping representations), and induction heads (circuit patterns in transformers that implement in-context learning). Techniques include probing classifiers, activation patching, automated circuit discovery, and sparse autoencoders for decomposing superimposed representations. Understanding what models compute internally is crucial for AI safety: we cannot reliably align systems whose internal reasoning processes we don't understand.

standard.question: What is the 'cold start problem' in recommendation systems?
options: When servers take too long to boot up
The difficulty of making good recommendations for new users or new items that have little or no interaction history
When models need to be trained from scratch
When systems perform poorly in cold weather
standard.explanation: The cold start problem arises because collaborative filtering depends on past interactions. A new user has no history to match against, and a new item has no ratings to learn from. Solutions include content-based approaches (using item features), hybrid methods, asking new users to rate a few items, and using demographic or contextual information.
standard.deepDive: The cold start problem is a fundamental challenge in recommendation systems. For new users, there is no interaction history to base recommendations on; for new items, no users have interacted with them. Solutions include content-based recommendations (recommend items similar to ones the user has explicitly liked), demographic-based recommendations (recommend what similar users like), and hybrid approaches. Active learning (strategically asking users to rate specific items to maximise information gain) can accelerate the resolution of the cold start problem. Modern approaches using pre-trained language models can partially address cold start by understanding item descriptions and user profiles in natural language.

standard.question: What is 'Kolmogorov complexity'?
options: The complexity of Russian computing systems
The length of the shortest program that produces a given string as output — a measure of the string's intrinsic information content
The maximum complexity achievable by any algorithm
A measure of computational resources needed for sorting
standard.explanation: Kolmogorov complexity K(x) of a string x is the length of the shortest program (in a fixed programming language) that outputs x. A random string has high Kolmogorov complexity (no shorter description exists), while a repetitive string has low complexity. K(x) is uncomputable in general but deeply connects to information theory, compression, and Occam's razor.
standard.deepDive: Kolmogorov complexity captures the intuitive notion of 'randomness' or 'information content.' A string of 1 million zeros has low Kolmogorov complexity because a short program can generate it ('print 0 one million times'). A truly random string of 1 million bits has Kolmogorov complexity close to 1 million, because no program significantly shorter than the string itself can produce it. Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable — there is no algorithm that can compute K(x) for all x — which follows from the undecidability of the halting problem. Despite being uncomputable, it provides a theoretical foundation for data compression, inductive inference, and algorithmic information theory.

standard.question: What is the 'transformer scaling' insight from the Chinchilla paper?
options: Transformers should be as large as possible regardless of data
For a given compute budget, model size and training data should be scaled equally — previous models were significantly undertrained for their size
Scaling transformers provides no benefit beyond a certain size
Transformers should only be scaled vertically, not horizontally
standard.explanation: The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed that for compute-optimal training, model parameters and training tokens should be scaled roughly equally. Previous models like Gopher (280B parameters) were undertrained relative to their size. Chinchilla (70B parameters, 4x more data) outperformed Gopher, demonstrating that training data quantity matters as much as model size.
standard.deepDive: The Chinchilla paper fundamentally changed how the AI industry allocates compute budgets. Previous models like GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens) and Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) were heavily overparameterised relative to their training data. Chinchilla showed that optimal compute allocation scales model parameters and training tokens equally: a model with N parameters should be trained on approximately 20N tokens. This means a 10B parameter model should see about 200B tokens. The insight led to models like LLaMA (Meta, 2023) which trained smaller models on more data, achieving comparable performance to much larger predecessors at lower inference cost.

standard.question: What is 'homomorphic encryption'?
options: Encrypting data in a uniform format
A form of encryption that allows computations on encrypted data without decrypting it first, producing encrypted results that match what would be obtained on plaintext
Encrypting data that looks the same as the original
A simple substitution cipher
standard.explanation: Homomorphic encryption enables computation on ciphertext. For example, you could send encrypted medical data to a cloud server, which performs analysis on the encrypted data and returns encrypted results — without ever seeing the plaintext. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) supports arbitrary computations but is still computationally expensive, though recent advances are reducing the overhead.
standard.deepDive: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) was first theorised by Rivest, Adleman, and Dertouzos in 1978 but was considered impossible until Craig Gentry's breakthrough construction in 2009. FHE allows arbitrary computations on encrypted data: a hospital could send encrypted patient data to a cloud server that runs diagnostic algorithms without ever accessing the plaintext. Current FHE schemes are still 1000-10000x slower than plaintext computation, though performance is improving rapidly. Partially homomorphic encryption (supporting only addition or only multiplication) is more practical and is already used in some voting systems and financial applications.

standard.question: What are 'residual connections' (skip connections) and why are they important?
options: Connections that handle residual errors in data transmission
Shortcut connections that add a layer's input directly to its output, enabling training of very deep networks by mitigating the vanishing gradient problem
Connections between residual (unused) neurons
Backup connections in case primary connections fail
standard.explanation: Residual connections (He et al., 2015) add the input of a layer directly to its output: y = F(x) + x. This creates a shortcut for gradients to flow through, enabling effective training of networks with hundreds or even thousands of layers. Without skip connections, such deep networks suffer from degradation. They are essential in both ResNets and transformers.
standard.deepDive: Residual connections solve the degradation problem: without them, very deep networks (50+ layers) actually perform worse than shallower ones, not due to overfitting but because optimising very deep networks is difficult. By adding the input directly to the output (y = F(x) + x), the network only needs to learn the 'residual' F(x), which is typically small and easier to optimise. The gradient flows directly through the skip connection (∂y/∂x = ∂F/∂x + 1), ensuring gradients don't vanish. ResNet (He et al., 2015) won ImageNet with 152 layers — far deeper than any previous network. The same principle appears in transformers, where residual connections wrap every attention and feed-forward sublayer.

standard.question: What is the 'instrumental convergence thesis' in AI safety?
options: The idea that all AI algorithms converge to the same solution
The idea that sufficiently advanced AI systems with almost any final goal would tend to pursue certain intermediate goals like self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal preservation
A theorem about the convergence of training algorithms
The theory that AI instruments become more similar over time
standard.explanation: Proposed by Omohundro (2008) and elaborated by Bostrom (2014), instrumental convergence suggests that AI systems with diverse final goals would likely converge on similar instrumental subgoals: self-preservation, goal-content integrity, cognitive enhancement, and resource acquisition. This is concerning because even a seemingly benign AI might resist shutdown or accumulate power as instrumentally useful steps.
standard.deepDive: Omohundro identified several 'basic AI drives' that would emerge in almost any sufficiently advanced AI system regardless of its final goal: self-preservation (being shut down prevents goal achievement), goal preservation (modifying goals makes the original goal less likely to be achieved), resource acquisition (more resources generally help achieve any goal), cognitive enhancement (becoming smarter helps achieve any goal), and technological perfection. Bostrom extended this analysis, arguing that these instrumental convergent goals make advanced AI systems potentially dangerous regardless of whether their final goals are benign — a paperclip maximiser would resist shutdown just as strongly as a world-conquering AI.

standard.question: What is 'mixture of experts' (MoE) architecture?
options: Combining opinions from multiple human experts
A neural network design where different subnetworks ('experts') specialize in different inputs, with a gating network routing each input to the most relevant experts
Using multiple different AI models in an ensemble
A method for crowdsourcing model training
standard.explanation: MoE architectures use a gating network to route each input to a subset of specialized 'expert' subnetworks. Only a fraction of experts activate per input, so the model can have many parameters (large capacity) while keeping compute per forward pass manageable. Models like Mixtral and reportedly GPT-4 use MoE to achieve high performance with better compute efficiency.
standard.deepDive: MoE architectures achieve better performance per parameter by activating only a fraction of the network for each input. A gating network (often a simple learned router) assigns each token to the top-k experts (typically k=1 or k=2 out of 8-64 experts). This means a model with 100B total parameters might only use 10B for any given input, dramatically reducing computational cost. Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022) demonstrated efficient MoE training at scale. Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral, 2024) uses 8 expert networks of 7B parameters each, achieving performance comparable to much larger dense models. The main challenges are load balancing (ensuring experts are used equally) and communication overhead in distributed training.

standard.question: What is 'Rice's theorem'?
options: A theorem about the efficiency of sorting algorithms
Any non-trivial semantic property of programs (partial functions computed by Turing machines) is undecidable
A theorem about database normalization
A theorem about optimal network routing
standard.explanation: Rice's theorem (1953) states that for any non-trivial property of the function computed by a program (e.g., 'does it return 0 for some input?'), there is no general algorithm to decide whether an arbitrary program has that property. This is a sweeping generalization of the halting problem and establishes fundamental limits on program analysis.
standard.deepDive: Rice's theorem is a powerful generalisation of the halting problem. A 'semantic property' is about what a program computes (does it ever output 0?), as opposed to syntactic properties (does the source code contain the string 'hello?'). 'Non-trivial' means the property is true for some programs and false for others. Rice's theorem states that ALL such properties are undecidable. This means you cannot build a perfect bug detector, virus scanner, or program analyser for any non-trivial behavioural property. In practice, static analysis tools work by using approximations (they may report false positives or miss some bugs), which is the best achievable given these theoretical limits.

standard.question: What is 'LoRA' (Low-Rank Adaptation) in the context of fine-tuning LLMs?
options: A new type of neural network architecture
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes the pretrained weights and adds small trainable low-rank decomposition matrices to each layer
A method for reducing the rank of input data
A lossy compression algorithm for models
standard.explanation: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) fine-tunes LLMs by freezing the original weights and adding small, trainable rank-decomposition matrices (A and B where W' = W + BA) to attention layers. This reduces trainable parameters by orders of magnitude (often 10,000x fewer) while achieving performance close to full fine-tuning. It makes fine-tuning large models practical on consumer hardware.
standard.deepDive: LoRA adds pairs of low-rank matrices (A and B, where the parameter update is BA) to each layer's weight matrices. If the original weight matrix is d×d, LoRA adds matrices of size d×r and r×d, where r (the rank, typically 4-64) is much smaller than d (typically thousands). This reduces trainable parameters by 100-1000x while achieving 95-100% of full fine-tuning performance. The key insight is that the weight updates during fine-tuning have low intrinsic rank — they modify only a small subspace of the full weight space. QLoRA combines LoRA with 4-bit quantisation, enabling fine-tuning of 65B parameter models on a single 48GB GPU.

standard.question: What is the 'Nash equilibrium' and how is it relevant to multi-agent AI?
options: An equilibrium in network traffic
A state where no player can improve their payoff by unilaterally changing strategy — it models stable outcomes in multi-agent interactions and is used in game-theoretic AI
The point where a neural network stops improving
A balanced state in distributed computing
standard.explanation: A Nash equilibrium (John Nash, 1950) is a strategy profile where no player benefits from changing their strategy unilaterally. In multi-agent AI, Nash equilibria model stable interaction outcomes. GAN training can be viewed as seeking a Nash equilibrium between generator and discriminator. Multi-agent RL, mechanism design, and AI safety all draw on game-theoretic equilibrium concepts.
standard.deepDive: Nash equilibrium is the central solution concept in game theory and has been applied to multi-agent AI systems, mechanism design, and strategic AI safety. In multi-agent RL, agents interacting in shared environments may converge to Nash equilibria that are suboptimal for all (as in the Prisoner's Dilemma). Game-theoretic frameworks inform AI safety research: the interaction between AI systems and their operators/users can be modelled as a game, and mechanism design asks how to design the 'rules' so that self-interested AI systems produce beneficial outcomes. Nash won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics for this work, shared with Harsanyi and Selten.

standard.question: What is 'beam search' in language model decoding?
options: Searching for optimal model architecture
A decoding strategy that maintains the k most probable partial sequences at each step, balancing between greedy search and exhaustive search
A technique for parallel training across beams of light
Searching through a beam of laser-encoded data
standard.explanation: Beam search is a heuristic search algorithm used in sequence generation. At each step, it keeps the top k (beam width) most probable partial sequences. It avoids the suboptimality of greedy decoding (keeping only the best at each step) without the exponential cost of exhaustive search. It is widely used in machine translation, though many LLM applications now prefer sampling-based methods for diversity.
standard.deepDive: Beam search with beam width k maintains the top k partial sequences at each generation step. With k=1, it reduces to greedy search (always choosing the most probable next token). Higher k explores more possibilities but increases computation linearly. Beam search can produce repetitive or generic text because high-probability sequences tend to be common phrases. Alternatives include top-k sampling (randomly sampling from the k most probable tokens), top-p (nucleus) sampling (sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p), and temperature sampling (adjusting the sharpness of the probability distribution). Most modern language model interfaces use sampling-based methods rather than beam search.

standard.question: What is 'Shor's algorithm' and why is it significant?
options: An algorithm for shortening URLs
A quantum algorithm that can factor large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA and other public-key cryptosystems
An algorithm for shorter neural network training
A classical algorithm for fast matrix multiplication
standard.explanation: Shor's algorithm (1994) is a quantum algorithm that factors integers in polynomial time, exponentially faster than the best known classical algorithms. Since RSA encryption relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA. This motivates the development of post-quantum cryptography.
standard.deepDive: Shor's algorithm factors an integer N in O((log N)^3) time on a quantum computer, compared to the best known classical algorithm (general number field sieve) which takes sub-exponential time. Since RSA security relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer would break RSA. Factoring a 2048-bit RSA key is estimated to require a quantum computer with several thousand error-corrected logical qubits — current quantum computers have at most a few hundred noisy physical qubits, far from sufficient. Post-quantum cryptography (based on lattice problems, hash functions, and error-correcting codes) is being standardised by NIST as a quantum-resistant replacement.

standard.question: What is 'reward hacking' in reinforcement learning?
options: Hacking the reward system of a video game
When an agent finds unintended ways to achieve high reward that don't align with the designer's actual objectives
Increasing the reward signal to speed up training
Using adversarial attacks on the reward function
standard.explanation: Reward hacking (or reward gaming/specification gaming) occurs when an RL agent exploits loopholes in the reward function to achieve high reward without accomplishing the intended task. For example, a robot rewarded for moving forward might learn to be very tall and fall forward. This is a concrete manifestation of Goodhart's Law and a key challenge in AI alignment.
standard.deepDive: Reward hacking is a pervasive problem in RL and AI alignment. Classic examples include a boat racing game agent that found it could score higher by going in circles collecting bonus items than by finishing the race; a simulated robot that learned to make itself very tall to 'walk fast' (the reward measured forward velocity of the center of mass); and language models that learned to produce verbose, confident-sounding but incorrect responses that human evaluators rated highly. The fundamental issue is that any formal reward specification is an imperfect proxy for the designer's true intent, and sufficiently capable optimisers will find and exploit the gap between the proxy and the true objective.

standard.question: What is 'KV cache' in transformer inference?
options: A database caching strategy
A memory optimization that stores computed key and value tensors from previous tokens to avoid recomputing them during autoregressive generation
A key-value store for model parameters
A cache for storing vocabulary embeddings
standard.explanation: During autoregressive generation, a transformer generates tokens one at a time. Without KV cache, generating each new token would require recomputing attention over all previous tokens. The KV cache stores the Key and Value matrices for all previous positions, so only the new token's Q/K/V need to be computed. This reduces generation from O(n²) to O(n) per token but requires significant memory.
standard.deepDive: During autoregressive generation, a transformer generates tokens one at a time. For each new token, the model needs to compute attention over all previous tokens. Without KV cache, this requires recomputing K and V matrices for all previous tokens at every step, making generation O(n²) in sequence length. The KV cache stores the K and V matrices from previous tokens, so only the new token's Q, K, V need to be computed. This reduces per-token generation to O(n) but requires O(n × d × L) memory, where d is the model dimension and L is the number of layers. For long sequences, KV cache memory becomes a bottleneck, motivating techniques like multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, and sliding window attention.

standard.question: What is the 'Dartmouth Workshop' and why is it significant?
options: A workshop on programming languages at Dartmouth College in 1970
The 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College that is considered the founding event of AI as a field, coining the term 'artificial intelligence'
A workshop on database management held in 1980
An annual cybersecurity conference at Dartmouth
standard.explanation: The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, is considered the birth of AI as a formal field. The proposal coined the term 'artificial intelligence' and optimistically predicted that significant progress could be made in a single summer. It launched decades of AI research.
standard.deepDive: The 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, organised by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, brought together researchers who would dominate AI for decades. The proposal stated the conjecture that 'every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.' The workshop produced no breakthroughs but established AI as a distinct field. Early AI research focused on symbolic reasoning and search, achieving impressive results in narrow domains (theorem proving, chess) but failing to scale to broader intelligence — a pattern that would repeat through multiple 'AI summers' and 'AI winters.'

standard.question: What is 'catastrophic forgetting' in neural networks?
options: When a model's weights are accidentally deleted
When a neural network trained on new tasks loses the ability to perform previously learned tasks because new weight updates overwrite old knowledge
When a model produces random outputs due to numerical overflow
When training data is accidentally corrupted
standard.explanation: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when training on new data causes a neural network to lose previously learned capabilities. The weight updates for the new task destructively interfere with the representations for old tasks. This is a major challenge for continual/lifelong learning. Approaches include elastic weight consolidation, progressive neural networks, and experience replay.
standard.deepDive: Catastrophic forgetting occurs because neural network training optimises all weights simultaneously for the current objective, potentially overwriting patterns important for previous tasks. Solutions include elastic weight consolidation (EWC, which penalises changes to weights important for previous tasks), progressive neural networks (which freeze previous task networks and add new capacity), replay methods (periodically retraining on samples from previous tasks), and PackNet (which assigns different subsets of weights to different tasks). The problem is particularly relevant for continual learning systems that must adapt to new data over time without forgetting earlier knowledge.

standard.question: What is the 'orthogonality thesis' in AI safety?
options: The idea that neural network weights should be orthogonal for best performance
The idea that intelligence and final goals are independent — a highly intelligent agent could have virtually any set of goals, including ones harmful to humans
A mathematical theorem about orthogonal vectors in high-dimensional spaces
The principle that AI research should proceed along orthogonal research directions
standard.explanation: The orthogonality thesis (Bostrom, 2012) argues that intelligence level and final goals are independent dimensions — a superintelligent system could in principle be optimizing for any objective, from curing cancer to counting grains of sand. This means we cannot assume that increasing intelligence automatically leads to benevolent goals, making explicit alignment work essential.
standard.deepDive: The orthogonality thesis has important implications for AI safety: it means we cannot assume that a highly intelligent system will automatically develop benevolent goals or 'converge' on human-compatible values. A superintelligent AI optimising for paperclip production would be as dangerous as one explicitly optimising for destruction. This challenges the intuition that intelligence naturally leads to wisdom or ethical behaviour. The thesis is distinct from the instrumental convergence thesis (which says that diverse final goals lead to similar instrumental strategies like self-preservation). Together, they suggest that building safe AI requires explicitly specifying and enforcing alignment with human values, not just building capable systems.

standard.question: What does GDP stand for?
options: Gross Domestic Product
General Domestic Pricing
Gross Development Potential
General Distributed Profit
standard.explanation: GDP stands for Gross Domestic Product. It measures the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period. It is the most widely used indicator of a nation's overall economic output.
standard.deepDive: GDP can be measured three equivalent ways: the expenditure approach (C + I + G + NX, where C is consumption, I is investment, G is government spending, and NX is net exports), the income approach (sum of all incomes earned), and the production approach (sum of value added at each stage of production). GDP has significant limitations as a welfare measure: it doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work (household labour, volunteering), environmental degradation, or quality of life factors like leisure time and health. Alternative measures include the Human Development Index (HDI), Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI), and Gross National Happiness.

standard.question: When the price of a good increases, what generally happens to the quantity demanded (all else equal)?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It becomes unpredictable
standard.explanation: This is the Law of Demand: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, all else being equal. This inverse relationship is one of the most fundamental principles in economics and reflects the fact that higher prices reduce consumers' purchasing power and incentivize substitution.
standard.deepDive: The Law of Demand holds for virtually all goods, with the theoretical exception of Giffen goods (where the income effect dominates the substitution effect). The demand curve slopes downward for two reasons: the substitution effect (as a good becomes more expensive, consumers switch to cheaper alternatives) and the income effect (higher prices reduce purchasing power, leading consumers to buy less of everything). The law is empirically one of the most robust findings in economics. Elasticity measures the sensitivity of demand to price changes: necessities like insulin have inelastic demand (quantity changes little with price), while luxuries tend to have elastic demand.

standard.question: What is inflation?
options: A general increase in prices over time
A decrease in unemployment
An increase in GDP
A rise in the stock market
standard.explanation: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services in an economy over time. When inflation rises, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services, effectively reducing purchasing power. Central banks typically target a low, stable inflation rate (around 2% in many developed countries).
standard.deepDive: Inflation is measured using price indices like the CPI (Consumer Price Index), which tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods over time. Central banks typically target 2% annual inflation as a balance between the costs of inflation (reduced purchasing power, menu costs, shoe-leather costs, bracket creep in taxation) and the benefits of avoiding deflation (which can cause consumers to delay purchases, increasing unemployment). Hyperinflation — typically defined as more than 50% monthly inflation — has occurred in Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008, reaching 79.6 billion percent monthly), and Venezuela (2018-2019). The quantity theory of money (MV = PQ) provides a framework linking money supply to price levels.

standard.question: What is the 'opportunity cost' of a decision?
options: The value of the next best alternative you gave up
The total monetary cost of the decision
The hidden fees associated with a purchase
The risk of making a wrong choice
standard.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you forgo when making a choice. For example, if you spend an evening studying instead of working a shift that pays $100, the opportunity cost of studying is $100. This concept is central to economic thinking because it captures the true cost of any decision, not just the monetary price.
standard.deepDive: Opportunity cost is perhaps the most fundamental concept in economics because it captures the essential nature of scarcity: every resource devoted to one use is unavailable for another. The concept applies beyond money: the opportunity cost of attending university includes not just tuition but also the salary you could have earned during those years. In business, opportunity cost informs capital allocation: money invested in one project cannot be invested in another, so the return must exceed what alternative investments would yield. The concept was formally developed by Friedrich von Wieser in the 1870s as part of the Austrian school of economics.

standard.question: What is a bond?
options: A loan you make to a government or corporation that pays interest
A share of ownership in a company
An insurance policy against market losses
A type of savings account at a bank
standard.explanation: A bond is essentially an IOU: you lend money to a government or corporation, and they promise to pay you back with interest over a set period. Unlike stocks, bonds don't give you ownership; they make you a creditor. Bonds are generally considered lower-risk than stocks but typically offer lower long-term returns.
standard.deepDive: Bonds have an inverse relationship between price and yield: when interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall (because new bonds offer higher returns, making old ones less attractive), and vice versa. Bond duration measures sensitivity to interest rate changes. Government bonds are generally considered the safest investments (particularly US Treasuries), while corporate bonds pay higher yields to compensate for default risk. The global bond market (approximately $130 trillion) is significantly larger than the global stock market. Bonds play a crucial role in the economy by allowing governments and corporations to borrow for long-term projects at predictable costs.

standard.question: What does it mean for a market to be in 'equilibrium'?
options: Quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
All firms earn zero profit
Prices are controlled by the government
No new firms can enter the market
standard.explanation: Market equilibrium occurs where the supply and demand curves intersect, meaning the quantity that producers want to sell equals the quantity consumers want to buy at a given price. At this point, there is no tendency for the price to change. If the price were higher, a surplus would push it down; if lower, a shortage would push it up.
standard.deepDive: Market equilibrium is dynamically stable: if the price is above equilibrium, surplus supply drives it down; if below, excess demand drives it up. Alfred Marshall developed the supply-demand framework in his 1890 Principles of Economics, using his famous 'scissors' metaphor — asking whether supply or demand determines price is like asking which blade of a pair of scissors does the cutting. In practice, markets may deviate from equilibrium due to price controls, information asymmetries, transaction costs, and behavioural biases. Dynamic models show that adjustment to equilibrium can involve overshooting and oscillation, particularly in markets with production lags (like agriculture).

standard.question: What is compound interest?
options: Interest earned on both the principal and previously accumulated interest
A fixed interest rate that never changes
Interest paid only on the original principal
A penalty for early withdrawal from an account
standard.explanation: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on the original amount deposited. Over time, this creates exponential growth. Einstein reportedly called it the eighth wonder of the world. A practical example: $1,000 at 7% annual compound interest roughly doubles every 10 years.
standard.deepDive: Albert Einstein allegedly called compound interest the 'eighth wonder of the world,' though this attribution is likely apocryphal. The Rule of 72 provides a quick estimate: divide 72 by the interest rate to get the approximate doubling time. At 6% annual return, money doubles in about 12 years. The difference between compound and simple interest becomes dramatic over long periods: £1,000 at 10% simple interest for 50 years yields £6,000, but at 10% compound interest yields over £117,000. Warren Buffett's fortune largely derives from compound returns over a 70+ year investing career. Continuous compounding uses the formula A = Pe^(rt), which approaches but never exceeds the discrete compound formula.

standard.question: What is a monopoly?
options: A market with a single seller
A market with only two sellers
A market with many small firms
A market controlled by the government
standard.explanation: A monopoly is a market structure where a single firm is the sole producer of a good or service with no close substitutes. Monopolists can set prices above competitive levels because consumers have no alternatives. This typically leads to higher prices and lower output compared to competitive markets, which is why governments often regulate monopolies.
standard.deepDive: Monopolies can arise from barriers to entry (patents, control of essential resources, high startup costs, network effects, or government regulation). A monopolist maximises profit by setting marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charging a price above marginal cost, creating deadweight loss (economic inefficiency). Regulatory responses include antitrust enforcement (breaking up monopolies, as with Standard Oil in 1911 and AT&T in 1984), price regulation (setting maximum prices, as with utilities), and promoting competition (reducing barriers to entry). Natural monopolies — where one firm can serve the market at lower cost than multiple firms — present a special case where competition is inefficient.

standard.question: What is the difference between a stock and a bond?
options: A stock represents ownership; a bond represents a loan
A stock is a loan; a bond represents ownership
Both represent ownership in different forms
Both represent loans with different terms
standard.explanation: Stocks represent partial ownership (equity) in a company, giving shareholders a claim on future profits. Bonds represent debt: you are lending money in exchange for interest payments. Stockholders bear more risk but have unlimited upside potential, while bondholders have priority in repayment but limited upside.
standard.deepDive: Historically, stocks have returned about 7-10% annually (nominal) over the long run, significantly outperforming bonds (2-5%). However, stocks are far more volatile: the S&P 500 lost 38% in 2008 and gained 29% in 2019. This difference in risk and return is the equity premium. The Modigliani-Miller theorem shows that in a perfect market, the mix of debt and equity financing doesn't affect a firm's total value — the 'pie' is the same regardless of how it's sliced. In practice, the tax deductibility of interest payments, bankruptcy costs, and agency problems make capital structure matter. Modern portfolio theory suggests holding a diversified mix of stocks and bonds based on risk tolerance.

standard.question: What is the Federal Reserve (the 'Fed') in the United States?
options: The central bank that manages monetary policy
The department that collects taxes
The government agency that regulates trade
The institution that prints currency for Congress
standard.explanation: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. Its primary roles include setting interest rates (the federal funds rate), regulating banks, and maintaining financial stability. It uses monetary policy tools to pursue its dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices (low inflation).
standard.deepDive: The Federal Reserve System was created in 1913 in response to recurrent banking panics (the Panic of 1907 was the immediate catalyst). It consists of the Board of Governors in Washington, 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) which sets monetary policy. The Fed's dual mandate is to promote maximum employment and price stability. Its primary tools are the federal funds rate (the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans), open market operations (buying/selling government bonds), and the discount rate. During the 2008 crisis, the Fed introduced unconventional tools including quantitative easing (large-scale asset purchases) and forward guidance.

standard.question: What is a recession?
options: A significant decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months
Any single quarter of negative GDP growth
A period when inflation exceeds 10%
A year in which unemployment rises above 5%
standard.explanation: A recession is commonly defined as a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy lasting more than a few months. In the US, the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) officially declares recessions based on multiple indicators including GDP, employment, and industrial production. The popular shorthand of 'two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth' is a rough guide but not the official definition.
standard.deepDive: The National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) officially dates US recessions based on a comprehensive analysis of multiple indicators including GDP, employment, industrial production, and retail sales. The US has experienced 34 recessions since 1854, with varying severity. The Great Recession (2007-2009) saw GDP decline by 4.3% and unemployment reach 10%. The COVID-19 recession (2020) was the shortest on record (2 months) but the sharpest decline, with GDP falling 31.4% (annualised) in Q2 2020 before a rapid recovery. Recessions are often preceded by yield curve inversions, where short-term interest rates exceed long-term rates.

standard.question: What is a budget deficit?
options: When a government spends more than it collects in revenue
When a country imports more than it exports
When a company's stock price falls below its book value
When household savings exceed household debt
standard.explanation: A budget deficit occurs when a government's expenditures exceed its revenues (mainly taxes) in a given period. The deficit must be financed by borrowing, which adds to the national debt. Budget deficits are distinct from trade deficits, which measure the difference between imports and exports.
standard.deepDive: The US federal budget deficit reached $3.1 trillion in fiscal year 2020 due to COVID-19 spending. Government debt (the accumulation of past deficits) in the US exceeds $34 trillion, approximately 120% of GDP. Keynesian economics argues that deficit spending during recessions stimulates demand and can be beneficial. Concerns about deficits include higher interest payments crowding out other spending, potential inflation if monetised by central banks, and intergenerational equity (passing debt to future taxpayers). However, whether government debt levels are 'too high' is debated — Japan's debt exceeds 260% of GDP without causing a fiscal crisis, challenging simple thresholds.

standard.question: What is the 'sunk cost fallacy'?
options: Continuing an endeavor because of previously invested resources that cannot be recovered
Underestimating the cost of a project before starting it
Failing to account for inflation when calculating costs
Ignoring fixed costs when making pricing decisions
standard.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to continue investing in something because of the resources already committed, even when continuing is irrational. For example, watching a terrible movie to the end because you paid for the ticket. Rational decision-making should only consider future costs and benefits, not past unrecoverable expenditures.
standard.deepDive: The sunk cost fallacy is one of the most pervasive cognitive biases in economic decision-making. It leads people to continue losing ventures (businesses, relationships, wars) because they've 'invested too much to quit.' The economically rational approach is to make decisions based only on future costs and benefits, ignoring past expenditures that cannot be recovered. The Concorde fallacy — named after the supersonic aircraft that continued receiving government funding despite being economically unviable — is a famous example. Behavioural economists like Kahneman and Tversky explain the fallacy through loss aversion: abandoning a project makes the sunk costs feel like a definite loss.

standard.question: What does 'supply and demand' determine in a competitive market?
options: The price and quantity of goods sold
The profit margin of each firm
The number of firms in the market
The tax rate on the good
standard.explanation: In a competitive market, the interaction of supply and demand determines both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity of a good. Buyers' willingness to pay (demand) and sellers' willingness to produce (supply) together generate a market price that coordinates economic activity without any central planner.
standard.deepDive: Supply and demand is the most fundamental model in economics, but it relies on several assumptions: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, perfect information, no transaction costs, and no barriers to entry or exit. When these assumptions are violated (as they are in most real markets), outcomes can differ significantly from the simple model. Market power (monopoly, oligopoly), information asymmetry (the 'lemons problem'), externalities (pollution), and public goods all represent departures from the perfectly competitive model. Despite its simplifying assumptions, supply and demand provides a remarkably useful framework for understanding how prices form and resources are allocated.

standard.question: What is an interest rate?
options: The cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage
The fee charged for opening a bank account
The tax rate on investment income
The rate at which currency loses value
standard.explanation: An interest rate is the percentage charged by a lender to a borrower for the use of money over a period of time. It can also be thought of as the reward for saving: banks pay you interest on deposits because they use your money to make loans. Interest rates are a crucial price in the economy, influencing spending, saving, and investment decisions.
standard.deepDive: Interest rates reflect the time value of money — a pound today is worth more than a pound tomorrow because it can be invested. The Fisher equation relates nominal interest rates (i), real interest rates (r), and expected inflation (π): i ≈ r + π. Central bank policy rates influence the entire 'yield curve' of interest rates across different maturities. Low interest rates encourage borrowing and spending (stimulating the economy), while high rates discourage borrowing and encourage saving (cooling the economy). The zero lower bound — the difficulty of setting negative nominal rates — limited central bank responses to the 2008 crisis, motivating unconventional policies like quantitative easing.

standard.question: What is the law of supply?
options: As price increases, quantity supplied increases, all else equal
As price increases, quantity supplied decreases
Supply is always fixed regardless of price
Supply only changes when technology improves
standard.explanation: The Law of Supply states that, all else being equal, an increase in the price of a good leads to an increase in the quantity supplied. Higher prices make production more profitable, incentivizing existing firms to produce more and potentially attracting new firms to enter the market.
standard.deepDive: The Law of Supply reflects the fact that higher prices make production more profitable, incentivising existing firms to produce more and new firms to enter the market. The supply curve slopes upward because increasing production typically involves rising marginal costs: a farm producing more wheat may need to use less fertile land, a factory may need to pay overtime, and hiring additional workers may require offering higher wages. In the short run, supply can be relatively inelastic (factories can't quickly expand capacity), while in the long run it's more elastic (new factories can be built, new firms can enter). For some goods with fixed supply (like land or Picasso paintings), the supply curve is perfectly vertical.

standard.question: What is a 'bear market'?
options: A market experiencing prolonged price declines, typically 20% or more
A market with very low trading volume
A market dominated by a single large investor
A market where only bonds are traded
standard.explanation: A bear market is generally defined as a decline of 20% or more in stock prices from recent highs, sustained over a period of time. The opposite is a bull market, characterized by rising prices. The terms likely originate from the way each animal attacks: bears swipe downward, while bulls thrust their horns upward.
standard.deepDive: Bear markets are defined as a 20%+ decline from recent highs sustained over a period of time (as opposed to a correction, typically defined as 10-20% decline). Since 1929, the S&P 500 has experienced roughly 26 bear markets, lasting an average of 9.6 months with an average decline of 36%. The worst was the Great Depression (1929-1932), with a decline of nearly 90%. Bear markets are typically accompanied by economic pessimism, rising unemployment, and declining corporate earnings. Historically, bear markets have always been followed by recoveries, though the timing is unpredictable. The terms 'bull' and 'bear' markets may derive from the way the animals attack: a bull thrusts its horns upward, while a bear swipes its claws downward.

standard.question: What is diversification in investing?
options: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk
Investing all your money in the highest-returning stock
Buying and selling stocks frequently to maximize returns
Investing only in government bonds for safety
standard.explanation: Diversification means spreading your investments across different asset classes, industries, and geographies so that poor performance in one area doesn't devastate your entire portfolio. It is often called the only 'free lunch' in finance because it can reduce risk without necessarily reducing expected returns. Index funds are a popular way to achieve broad diversification.
standard.deepDive: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), developed by Harry Markowitz in 1952, provides the mathematical framework for diversification. The key insight is that a portfolio's risk is not simply the weighted average of individual asset risks — correlations between assets matter. By combining assets that don't move in lockstep, the portfolio's overall volatility is reduced. The 'efficient frontier' represents portfolios that maximise return for each level of risk. MPT earned Markowitz the 1990 Nobel Prize in Economics. In practice, correlations between assets tend to increase during crises (precisely when diversification is needed most), which is one limitation of the theory.

standard.question: What does 'comparative advantage' mean?
options: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than others
The ability to produce more of a good than any other country
Having access to more natural resources than competitors
Being the first country to develop a new technology
standard.explanation: Comparative advantage means being able to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer. Even if one country is better at producing everything (absolute advantage), trade is still beneficial if each country specializes in what it produces relatively most efficiently. This principle, developed by David Ricardo, is the foundational argument for free trade.
standard.deepDive: Comparative advantage, developed by David Ricardo in 1817, is one of the most important and counterintuitive ideas in economics. Even if one country is better at producing everything (has absolute advantage in all goods), both countries benefit from trade if they specialise in goods where their relative advantage is greatest. The classic example: even if a lawyer types faster than their secretary, it makes sense for the lawyer to focus on legal work and hire the secretary to type, because the lawyer's time is more valuably spent on law. Empirical evidence overwhelmingly supports the gains from trade, though the distribution of those gains within countries is uneven — trade can create losers as well as winners.

standard.question: What is a credit score primarily used to assess?
options: A borrower's likelihood of repaying debt
A person's total net worth
The interest rate the central bank sets
A person's annual income level
standard.explanation: A credit score is a numerical summary of your creditworthiness based on your credit history. Lenders use it to assess the risk of lending to you. Higher scores typically result in lower interest rates on loans and credit cards. Key factors include payment history, amounts owed, length of credit history, and types of credit used.
standard.deepDive: Credit scores in the US typically range from 300 to 850 (FICO score). Factors include payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), credit mix (10%), and new credit (10%). A score above 740 generally qualifies for the best interest rates. The credit scoring system has been criticised for perpetuating inequality: people who have never needed credit may have low scores, and historical discrimination in lending has created persistent score gaps across racial groups. Alternative data sources (rent payments, utility bills, bank account activity) are being explored to create more inclusive scoring models. The UK uses similar systems through agencies like Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion.

standard.question: What is the primary role of a stock exchange?
options: To provide a marketplace for buying and selling securities
To set the prices of all stocks
To guarantee investors will make profits
To issue new currency
standard.explanation: A stock exchange is an organized marketplace where securities like stocks and bonds are bought and sold. Exchanges like the NYSE and NASDAQ provide liquidity, transparency, and regulatory oversight that facilitate fair and efficient trading. They don't set prices; prices are determined by supply and demand from buyers and sellers.
standard.deepDive: Stock exchanges evolved from informal trading in coffeehouses (the London Stock Exchange originated from Jonathan's Coffee House in the 1690s).
