The computational overhead of running real-time safety monitors during inference
The regulatory compliance burden placed on AI developers by government agencies
standard.explanation: The alignment tax refers to the additional cost (in capability, compute, development time) of building an aligned AI system compared to an unaligned one. If the tax is high, competitive pressures incentivize cutting corners on safety. A key goal is reducing this tax — ideally to zero or negative, where aligned systems work better than unaligned ones. Paul Christiano has emphasized that low alignment tax is essential for adoption.
standard.deepDive: The alignment tax is the capability difference between an aligned system and an equally resourced unaligned system. If the tax is high (alignment significantly reduces capability), competitive pressures incentivise building unaligned systems. If the tax is zero or negative (aligned systems are equally or more capable), there is no competitive reason to skip alignment. Reducing the alignment tax is a key goal of alignment research. Approaches include making alignment techniques that improve rather than degrade capabilities (like RLHF, which makes models more helpful), developing interpretability tools that aid debugging, and creating evaluation frameworks that catch alignment failures early.

standard.question: What is the halting problem, and why is it significant in theoretical computer science?
options: The problem of knowing when to stop training a neural network; significant for practical ML engineering
The problem of deciding whether a given program halts or runs forever on a given input; it is undecidable, proving fundamental limits of computation
The problem of stopping runaway processes in operating systems; significant for system reliability
The problem of deciding when an iterative algorithm has converged; significant for numerical analysis
standard.explanation: Turing (1936) proved that no general algorithm can decide, for all program-input pairs, whether the program eventually halts. The proof uses diagonalization: assuming a halting decider H exists, construct a program that does the opposite of what H predicts, yielding contradiction. This established fundamental limits on computability and was the first concrete undecidability result, spawning an entire field of computability theory.
standard.deepDive: Turing's proof uses diagonalisation. Assume halting decider H(P, I) exists, returning 'halts' or 'loops' for program P on input I. Define D(P) = { if H(P,P)='halts' then loop forever; else halt }. Running D(D): if H(D,D)='halts', D loops — contradiction; if H(D,D)='loops', D halts — contradiction. Therefore H cannot exist. The proof technique generalises: Rice's theorem shows that any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Practically, this means no tool can automatically detect all bugs, verify all specifications, or determine all security vulnerabilities.

standard.question: In computational complexity theory, what relationship holds between P, NP, and NP-complete?
options: P = NP = NP-complete; they are all the same complexity class
P is a subset of NP; NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; whether P = NP is open
NP is a subset of P; NP-complete problems are the easiest problems in NP
P and NP are disjoint sets with NP-complete at the boundary
standard.explanation: P (polynomial-time solvable) is contained in NP (polynomial-time verifiable). NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP: every problem in NP reduces to any NP-complete problem in polynomial time (Cook-Levin showed SAT is NP-complete). Whether P = NP is the most important open question in computer science — if any single NP-complete problem turns out to be in P, then P = NP and all NP problems become efficiently solvable.
standard.deepDive: P ⊆ NP because any problem solvable in polynomial time is trivially verifiable in polynomial time (just solve it). Whether P = NP is the most important open problem in theoretical computer science. NP-complete problems are the 'hardest' in NP: every NP problem reduces to every NP-complete problem in polynomial time (Cook-Levin theorem for SAT, Karp's 21 reductions for others). If any NP-complete problem has a P algorithm, then P = NP and ALL NP problems become efficiently solvable. The class co-NP contains problems whose NO instances are verifiable in polynomial time; it is open whether NP = co-NP.

standard.question: In the original transformer paper ('Attention Is All You Need'), what scaling factor is applied to dot products in scaled dot-product attention, and why?
options: 1/d_k — to normalize by the key dimension and bound the attention weights
1/sqrt(d_k) — to counteract dot product magnitude growth that pushes softmax into saturated regions with vanishing gradients
1/n — to normalize by sequence length for consistent attention distributions
1/sqrt(n) — to account for the number of attention heads in multi-head attention
standard.explanation: The dot products are divided by sqrt(d_k) where d_k is the key dimension. Vaswani et al. explain that when Q and K components have unit variance, the dot product has variance d_k, which grows with dimension. Large-magnitude dot products push the softmax into regions where gradients are extremely small. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance, keeping softmax in a well-behaved gradient regime.
standard.deepDive: The scaling factor 1/√d_k prevents the softmax function from producing nearly one-hot distributions. When Q and K entries are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k (sum of d_k independent products). For d_k = 64, dot products have standard deviation 8, which pushes softmax into extreme saturation where gradients are near zero. Dividing by √d_k = 8 restores unit variance. This simple but crucial trick enables effective gradient flow through the attention mechanism and was one of the key design decisions in the original transformer paper.

standard.question: In Constitutional AI (CAI) as developed by Anthropic, what replaces human preference labels in the RLHF pipeline?
options: A rule-based constraint checker that filters outputs against fixed safety patterns
AI-generated feedback where the model critiques and revises its own outputs according to a set of written principles
Automated unit tests verifying factual accuracy against a knowledge base
A separate smaller model trained exclusively on curated safety examples
standard.explanation: Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) replaces human feedback with AI self-critique. The model generates responses, critiques them according to a set of principles (the 'constitution'), revises its outputs, and then preference pairs from this process train a reward model (RLAIF — RL from AI Feedback). This scales oversight beyond human labeling while making the desired behavior explicit through written principles.
standard.deepDive: Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) replaces human preference labelling with AI self-supervision. In the 'constitutional AI' pipeline: (1) the model generates responses to prompts, (2) the model critiques its own responses according to written principles ('the constitution'), (3) the model revises its responses based on the critiques, and (4) the original-revised pairs form preference data for training a reward model (RLAIF — RL from AI Feedback). This dramatically reduces the need for human annotation while making the training values explicit. The constitution can be inspected, debated, and modified, providing greater transparency than opaque human preference data.

standard.question: What does Rice's theorem in computability theory establish?
options: Every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable
Every program can be compressed to a Turing machine with at most 2 states
There exists a universal program simulating any other in polynomial time overhead
The set of all computable functions is countably infinite
standard.explanation: Rice's theorem states that for any non-trivial property of the partial function computed by a program (where 'non-trivial' means some programs satisfy it and some don't), no algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program has that property. This vastly generalizes the halting problem — you can't algorithmically determine if a program computes a prime, ever outputs 42, or satisfies any other semantic (as opposed to syntactic) property.
standard.deepDive: Rice's theorem is proved by reduction from the halting problem. Given any non-trivial semantic property P (true for some programs, false for others), and a program that computes the empty function (never halts), we can construct a reduction: to decide whether program M halts on input x, construct a program M' that first runs M on x, then computes a function with property P. If M halts, M' has property P; if M doesn't halt, M' computes the empty function (doesn't have P). Deciding P for M' would decide halting for M, which is impossible. The theorem implies that perfect virus detection, perfect type inference, and perfect program optimisation are all impossible in general.

standard.question: What does the Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) actually guarantee about neural networks?
options: A single-hidden-layer network can learn any function from finite training data with gradient descent
A sufficiently wide single-hidden-layer network with non-linear activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary accuracy
Deep networks can represent any computable function using polynomially many parameters
Any Boolean function can be exactly represented by a network with two hidden layers
standard.explanation: The UAT states that a feedforward network with one hidden layer containing finitely many neurons with a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of R^n to arbitrary precision. Crucially, it is an existence result about representational capacity, not learnability: it says nothing about whether SGD will find the right parameters, how many neurons are needed (potentially exponentially many), or how the network will generalize.
standard.deepDive: The Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees existence but says nothing about learnability, required width, or generalisation. A single hidden layer might need exponentially many neurons to approximate certain functions, and the theorem provides no algorithm for finding the right weights. In practice, deeper networks (more layers) are generally more efficient than wider ones for approximating hierarchical functions, which is why deep learning outperforms shallow networks despite the UAT applying to both. The theorem has been extended to various activation functions and network architectures, including ReLU networks and residual networks.

standard.question: What is the 'Lottery Ticket Hypothesis' (Frankle & Carlin, 2019)?
options: Dense randomly-initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks that, when trained in isolation from their original initialization, can match the full network's accuracy
Only about 1% of training examples contribute meaningfully to final model performance
The final weights of a trained network are determined almost entirely by the random initialization seed
Training large models is computationally equivalent to exhaustive architecture search over all possible subnetworks
standard.explanation: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis states that dense, randomly-initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks ('winning tickets') that — when trained in isolation from the same original initialization — can match the full network's test accuracy. The analogy: training a large network is like buying many lottery tickets, succeeding because at least one subnetwork happens to be well-initialized. This has significant implications for model compression, pruning strategies, and understanding why overparameterization helps training.
standard.deepDive: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis challenges the conventional understanding of neural network training. It suggests that overparameterisation helps training not because all parameters are needed for the final solution, but because having many parameters increases the probability that a good sparse subnetwork ('winning ticket') is present in the random initialisation. The hypothesis has been refined: the original formulation required rewinding to exact initial weights, but later work showed that rewinding to weights early in training (rather than initialisation) also works. The hypothesis connects to pruning (removing unnecessary weights after training), neural architecture search, and theoretical questions about the loss landscape of neural networks.

standard.question: What does the First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics state?
options: Every competitive equilibrium maximizes total social welfare
Every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient, given complete markets and no externalities
Government intervention always reduces aggregate welfare
Free markets always produce equitable distributions of resources
standard.explanation: The First Welfare Theorem states that under certain conditions (complete markets, no externalities, no market power, perfect information), every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient — no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. It says nothing about equity; a Pareto efficient outcome can be extremely unequal. The Second Welfare Theorem addresses distribution, stating any Pareto efficient allocation can be achieved via competitive equilibrium with appropriate lump-sum transfers.
standard.deepDive: The First Welfare Theorem requires several conditions: complete markets (a market exists for every good), no externalities, no market power (price-taking behaviour), no information asymmetries, and local non-satiation (agents always prefer more). When any condition fails, the equilibrium may not be Pareto efficient — this is the theoretical foundation for government intervention. The theorem says nothing about equity: an allocation where one person has everything is Pareto efficient. The Second Welfare Theorem addresses equity: any Pareto efficient allocation can be achieved as a competitive equilibrium with appropriate lump-sum transfers.

standard.question: What did Akerlof's 'Market for Lemons' (1970) demonstrate about markets with asymmetric information?
options: Bad products always drive good products out of the market through price competition
Information asymmetry can cause adverse selection, potentially collapsing the market as high-quality sellers exit
Consumers always systematically undervalue all used goods regardless of true quality
Government quality certification is the only possible solution to information asymmetry
standard.explanation: Akerlof showed that when sellers know more about product quality than buyers (using used cars as the example), buyers discount prices to account for the risk of getting a 'lemon.' This drives high-quality sellers out, lowering average quality further, potentially leading to complete market collapse through adverse selection. The paper was initially rejected by multiple journals — it later won Akerlof the Nobel Prize and became foundational to information economics.
standard.deepDive: Akerlof's paper was rejected by the American Economic Review and the Review of Economic Studies before being published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1970. The 'lemons' insight has been applied to markets far beyond used cars: insurance (sicker people buy more insurance), labour markets (the best workers leave if pay is cut across the board), financial markets (toxic assets), and online platforms. Market mechanisms that mitigate adverse selection include signalling (education as a signal of ability — Spence, 1973), screening (insurers offering menu of contracts — Stiglitz, 1975), and reputation systems (eBay ratings).

standard.question: What is the 'Stolper-Samuelson theorem' in international trade theory?
options: Free trade always benefits all factors of production in both countries
A rise in the price of a good raises the real return to the factor used intensively in its production and lowers the return to the other factor
Countries with similar factor endowments will trade more with each other
Tariffs always reduce aggregate national welfare without exception
standard.explanation: The Stolper-Samuelson theorem (1941), within the Heckscher-Ohlin framework, shows that when the price of a good rises (e.g., due to opening trade), the real return to the factor used intensively in that good rises, while the real return to the other factor falls. This means trade creates winners and losers within a country — a country's abundant factor gains but its scarce factor loses, providing a rigorous basis for understanding distributional effects of trade.
standard.deepDive: The Stolper-Samuelson theorem has direct policy relevance: it predicts that trade liberalisation creates winners and losers within each country, which helps explain why trade is politically contentious despite being net beneficial. In a capital-abundant country like the US, free trade is predicted to benefit capital owners and harm unskilled workers. Empirical evidence on the 'China shock' (Autor, Dorn, Hanson 2013) confirms that US regions most exposed to Chinese imports experienced significant declines in manufacturing employment and wages. This has motivated calls for trade adjustment assistance and redistribution to compensate losers from trade.

standard.question: What is 'moral hazard' in economics, and what is a canonical example?
options: The risk that people act immorally when unobserved; example: shoplifting increases at night
When one party takes greater risks because another party bears the costs; example: insured drivers being less careful
The tendency for markets to produce outcomes that violate moral norms; example: price gouging after disasters
The risk of fraud in financial transactions; example: embezzlement by bank employees
standard.explanation: Moral hazard occurs when a party insulated from risk behaves differently than if they bore the full consequences of their actions. The canonical example is insurance: an insured driver may take less care because the insurer pays for accidents. Other key examples include banks deemed 'too big to fail' taking excessive risks, and employees with guaranteed salaries shirking. Despite its name, moral hazard is about incentives under asymmetric risk-bearing, not morality per se.
standard.deepDive: Moral hazard is distinct from adverse selection: adverse selection involves hidden information before a contract (one party knows more about their risk), while moral hazard involves hidden action after a contract (one party changes behaviour because of the contract). Solutions include monitoring (surveillance cameras, audits), incentive design (deductibles, co-payments, performance bonuses), and reputation mechanisms. The 2008 financial crisis illustrated systemic moral hazard: banks that were 'too big to fail' took excessive risks, knowing that losses would be socialised while profits remained private. The Dodd-Frank Act attempted to address this through increased capital requirements and resolution planning.

standard.question: What is a 'Pigouvian tax' designed to accomplish?
options: Raise maximum government revenue with minimum economic distortion
Correct a negative externality by taxing the activity at a rate equal to the marginal external cost
Implement a progressive income distribution through graduated tax rates
Protect domestic industries by taxing imported goods from lower-cost producers
standard.explanation: A Pigouvian tax (named after Arthur Pigou) corrects a negative externality by setting the tax equal to the marginal external cost at the socially optimal output level. This internalizes the externality, aligning private costs with social costs. A carbon tax is the archetypal modern example. The optimal Pigouvian tax achieves the first-best outcome, whereas command-and-control quantity regulations may not (though they have other advantages like certainty about quantity).
standard.deepDive: The Pigouvian tax is theoretically elegant but practically challenging. Setting the correct tax rate requires knowing the marginal external cost at the socially optimal level of output — information that is difficult to obtain. For carbon emissions, estimates of the social cost of carbon range from $50 to over $200 per tonne, depending on the discount rate, damage function, and climate sensitivity. Despite these difficulties, a carbon tax is widely considered by economists to be the most efficient instrument for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, preferable to command-and-control regulation. Over 40 national and subnational jurisdictions have implemented carbon pricing as of 2024.

standard.question: What is the 'Ricardian equivalence' proposition in macroeconomics?
options: Government bonds and corporate equity are equivalent investment vehicles
Under certain assumptions, whether the government finances spending through debt or taxes has equivalent macroeconomic effects
All countries have equivalent productive capacity when adjusted for natural resources
Monetary and fiscal policy have equivalent effects on aggregate demand
standard.explanation: Ricardian equivalence (formalized by Barro, 1974) states that under strong assumptions (rational forward-looking consumers, perfect capital markets, lump-sum taxes, altruistic bequests creating effectively infinite horizons), the choice between tax and debt financing is irrelevant — rational consumers anticipate future taxes needed to service debt and save accordingly. While rarely holding perfectly in practice (liquidity constraints, finite horizons, distortionary taxes), it's a crucial theoretical benchmark for evaluating fiscal policy.
standard.deepDive: Ricardian equivalence was originally suggested by David Ricardo (who was sceptical of it) and rigorously formulated by Robert Barro in 1974. The strong assumptions it requires are rarely satisfied: many consumers are credit-constrained (cannot borrow at the same rate as the government), have finite horizons (don't fully account for taxes their grandchildren will pay), or are not perfectly rational. Empirical evidence generally rejects strict Ricardian equivalence — tax cuts do stimulate consumption — but the degree of departure varies. The theorem remains important as a benchmark: deviations from Ricardian equivalence tell us which of its assumptions are most violated in practice.

standard.question: What does the Coase theorem state about externalities?
options: Externalities can only be efficiently resolved through government taxation or regulation
With well-defined property rights and zero transaction costs, bargaining produces efficient outcomes regardless of the initial rights allocation
The social cost of an externality always exceeds its private benefit
Private markets invariably fail when externalities are present
standard.explanation: The Coase theorem states that with well-defined property rights and zero transaction costs, private bargaining between parties will reach an efficient outcome regardless of who holds the initial rights. The rights assignment affects the distribution (who pays whom) but not efficiency. In practice, transaction costs are rarely zero — which is precisely why externalities often require regulatory solutions, a point Coase himself emphasized strongly.
standard.deepDive: Coase's theorem, from his 1960 paper 'The Problem of Social Cost' (one of the most cited law articles ever), challenges the Pigouvian approach by showing that government intervention is not always necessary to resolve externalities. If transaction costs are zero, the polluter and the affected party will negotiate an efficient solution regardless of who has the legal right. However, Coase himself emphasised that transaction costs are usually significant (especially for large-scale externalities like air pollution involving millions of parties), making his theorem more of a theoretical benchmark than a practical prescription. The theorem has profoundly influenced law and economics, particularly the analysis of property rights and liability rules.

standard.question: What is a 'liquidity trap' in monetary economics?
options: When banks accumulate excess reserves but cannot find profitable lending opportunities
When interest rates are at or near zero and expansionary monetary policy becomes ineffective because people hoard cash
When a country's currency becomes illiquid in foreign exchange markets during a crisis
When financial regulations prevent institutions from converting assets to cash quickly enough
standard.explanation: A liquidity trap occurs at the zero lower bound: interest rates are so low that people are indifferent between bonds (yielding ~0%) and cash, so additional money injection doesn't stimulate spending. Keynes described this phenomenon. It became highly relevant during Japan's stagnation and after the 2008 crisis, motivating unconventional policies like quantitative easing, negative interest rates, and forward guidance.
standard.deepDive: Japan's experience from the 1990s-2010s is the most studied case of a liquidity trap. Despite the Bank of Japan cutting interest rates to zero and implementing massive quantitative easing, the economy experienced two decades of near-zero growth and mild deflation. Paul Krugman argued (1998) that the BOJ needed to commit to future inflation — a 'credible promise to be irresponsible' — to raise inflation expectations and reduce real interest rates. The experience motivated the development of unconventional monetary policy tools: negative interest rates, yield curve control, and massive asset purchases. Whether these policies succeeded remains debated.

standard.question: What is Ostrom's key contribution regarding the 'Tragedy of the Commons'?
options: She proved mathematically that commons always lead to overexploitation
She showed that many real-world commons are sustainably managed through community institutions, without requiring privatization or state control
She demonstrated that only government ownership prevents resource depletion
She showed that the tragedy applies only to environmental resources, not economic ones
standard.explanation: Elinor Ostrom (Nobel Prize 2009) challenged Hardin's claim that commons are inevitably overexploited by documenting numerous cases where communities successfully managed shared resources through local institutions, norms, and governance mechanisms — without privatization or top-down government control. She identified design principles for successful commons management, including clear group boundaries, proportional costs and benefits, collective choice arrangements, and effective monitoring.
standard.deepDive: Elinor Ostrom (the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics, 2009) identified eight design principles for successful commons management: clearly defined boundaries, rules adapted to local conditions, collective choice arrangements, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution mechanisms, recognition of self-governance by higher authorities, and nested enterprises for larger-scale resources. Her work challenged the assumption that commons inevitably lead to tragedy (Hardin 1968) and showed that local communities can develop sophisticated institutional arrangements for sustainable resource management. Examples include irrigation systems in Spain and Nepal, fisheries in Maine and Turkey, and forest management in Japan and Switzerland.

standard.question: What is 'comparative advantage' and how does it differ from 'absolute advantage'?
options: Comparative advantage means producing more output per hour; absolute advantage means lower total production cost
A country has comparative advantage if it produces a good at lower opportunity cost, even if it has no absolute advantage in anything
Comparative advantage applies only to developing countries; absolute advantage to developed ones
They are interchangeable terms describing the same economic concept
standard.explanation: Comparative advantage (Ricardo, 1817) concerns relative efficiency: even if Country A produces both wine and cloth more efficiently than Country B (absolute advantage in both), trade still benefits both if each specializes where its opportunity cost is lowest. This is perhaps the most powerful and counterintuitive insight in economics — it shows trade can benefit all parties, even seemingly 'inferior' producers.
standard.deepDive: Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage (1817) used the example of England and Portugal producing cloth and wine. Even if Portugal was better at producing both goods (absolute advantage in both), both countries benefit from specialisation and trade. The key insight is that trade is driven by differences in relative (opportunity) costs, not absolute costs. Empirical support comes from studies showing that countries export goods in which they have comparative advantage, as predicted by the Ricardian and Heckscher-Ohlin models. The theory provides the primary economic argument for free trade and against protectionism.

standard.question: What is 'hyperbolic discounting' and why does it matter for economics?
options: Discounting at extremely high rates; it explains why developing countries have low savings
A pattern where people are disproportionately impatient about near-future delays versus far-future ones, causing time-inconsistent preferences
Discounting only financial outcomes; it explains why people value experiences over money
A mathematical technique for computing present values using hyperbolic functions
standard.explanation: Under standard exponential discounting, the discount rate between consecutive periods is constant. Hyperbolic discounting features a higher rate for near-future tradeoffs than far-future ones, creating time inconsistency: you might prefer $110 in 31 days over $100 in 30 days, but prefer $100 today over $110 tomorrow — even though both involve waiting 1 day for $10 extra. This explains procrastination, undersaving, and addiction, and motivates commitment devices.
standard.deepDive: Hyperbolic discounting creates time-inconsistent preferences. A person might prefer £110 in 31 days over £100 in 30 days (patient choice), but prefer £100 now over £110 tomorrow (impatient choice) — even though both involve a 1-day wait for an extra £10. Standard exponential discounting (used in economic models) cannot produce this pattern. The β-δ model captures hyperbolic discounting: the discount factor between the present and any future period is βδ^t, where β < 1 represents the extra impatience about immediate versus future rewards. This explains procrastination, undersaving, and addiction. Commitment devices (automatic savings plans, pre-commitment contracts) can help overcome time inconsistency.

standard.question: What is the 'Efficient Market Hypothesis' in its strong form (Fama, 1970)?
options: All financial markets reach equilibrium within a single trading session
Asset prices reflect all information including private/insider information, making even insider trading unable to generate excess returns
All investors earn exactly the market return over sufficiently long horizons
Transaction costs in financial markets trend toward zero over time
standard.explanation: The strong EMH states that prices fully reflect ALL information — public and private. Even insider trading shouldn't generate excess returns. The semi-strong form says prices reflect all public information; the weak form says they reflect all historical price data. The strong form is generally rejected empirically (insider trading is profitable), but the semi-strong form has substantial support. The EMH remains among the most debated propositions in finance.
standard.deepDive: The strong form of the EMH is the most extreme claim: if prices reflect ALL information (including insider information), even insider trading cannot generate excess returns. This is generally rejected — insider trading does generate abnormal returns, which is why it is illegal. The semi-strong form (prices reflect all public information) has more empirical support: event studies show that prices adjust to public information (earnings announcements, economic data) within minutes. The weak form (prices reflect all past trading data) implies that technical analysis (predicting prices from historical patterns) cannot generate excess returns, which is broadly supported by evidence.

standard.question: What is NAIRU and why is it important for monetary policy?
options: A measure of government debt sustainability; important for fiscal policy
The unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation — below it, inflation accelerates; central banks use it to guide interest rate decisions
The minimum wage level that maximizes employment; important for labor market regulation
The optimal tax rate that maximizes government revenue (the peak of the Laffer curve)
standard.explanation: NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment) is the unemployment rate at which inflation remains stable. Below NAIRU, tight labor markets accelerate wage and price growth; above it, slack pushes inflation down. Central banks try to estimate NAIRU to calibrate monetary policy, though it's unobservable and varies over time, making it controversial in practice.
standard.deepDive: NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment) is the unemployment rate at which inflation is stable — neither accelerating nor decelerating. Below NAIRU, labour markets are tight, wages rise faster than productivity, and firms pass costs to consumers, accelerating inflation. Above NAIRU, slack in the labour market puts downward pressure on wages and inflation. NAIRU is unobservable and must be estimated, typically around 4-5% for the US. It varies over time with structural changes in the economy. The concept has been criticised for being too imprecise to guide policy and for potentially locking in unnecessary unemployment.

standard.question: What did the Phillips curve originally describe, and how did Friedman's critique change the understanding?
options: A permanent tradeoff between inflation and GDP growth; Friedman showed growth matters more than inflation
An inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment in the short run; Friedman showed no long-run tradeoff exists because expectations adjust
A positive relationship between government spending and inflation; Friedman showed monetary policy was more important
A relationship between money supply and interest rates; Friedman showed the relationship was unstable
standard.explanation: The original Phillips curve (1958) showed an empirical inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation. Friedman (1968) and Phelps argued the tradeoff is only short-run: in the long run, inflation expectations adjust and the economy returns to its natural rate of unemployment. The stagflation of the 1970s — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously — confirmed this critique. Modern New Keynesian Phillips curves incorporate expectations explicitly.
standard.deepDive: The original Phillips curve (1958) showed an empirical inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in UK data spanning nearly a century. Friedman's Presidential Address to the AEA (1968) and Phelps's independent work argued that the trade-off was temporary: in the short run, unexpected inflation could reduce real wages and temporarily boost employment, but in the long run, expectations adjust and unemployment returns to its natural rate. The 1970s stagflation (high inflation AND high unemployment) confirmed their prediction. Modern New Keynesian Phillips curves incorporate forward-looking expectations and supply shocks.

standard.question: In game theory, what is a Nash Equilibrium?
options: The outcome where all players achieve their maximum possible payoff simultaneously
The outcome that maximizes total social welfare across all players
A strategy profile where no player can unilaterally improve their payoff by changing only their own strategy
The unique optimal outcome that must occur in any rational strategic interaction
standard.explanation: A Nash Equilibrium is a strategy profile where each player's strategy is a best response to all other players' strategies — no one benefits from unilaterally deviating. Nash Equilibria need not be socially optimal: the Prisoner's Dilemma is a classic case where the Nash Equilibrium is Pareto dominated. Nash (1950) proved every finite game has at least one equilibrium (possibly in mixed strategies), earning him the Nobel Prize.
standard.deepDive: Nash equilibrium is the central solution concept in game theory. Pure strategy Nash equilibria (where each player deterministically chooses one action) don't always exist, but Nash proved that mixed strategy equilibria (where players randomize) always exist in finite games. Computing Nash equilibria is PPAD-complete (a complexity class believed harder than polynomial time but easier than NP-complete). In practice, many games have multiple Nash equilibria, and selecting among them requires refinement concepts like subgame perfection, trembling hand perfection, or evolutionary stability.

standard.question: What does the Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem prove about bilateral trade under asymmetric information?
options: Bilateral trade always reaches efficiency given sufficient rounds of bargaining
No mechanism simultaneously achieves ex-post efficiency, individual rationality, incentive compatibility, and budget balance when buyer and seller have private overlapping valuations
Auction mechanisms strictly dominate bilateral negotiation in all settings
The buyer always extracts more surplus than the seller in any incentive-compatible mechanism
standard.explanation: The Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem (1983) is a fundamental impossibility result: when a buyer and seller have private valuations whose supports overlap, no mechanism can simultaneously be incentive compatible (truth-telling is optimal), individually rational (no party is forced to lose), ex-post efficient (trade happens iff the buyer values it more), and budget balanced. This explains why real-world bargaining inevitably involves some inefficiency — it's not a failure of design but a fundamental information-theoretic constraint.
standard.deepDive: The Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem shows that in bilateral trade with private overlapping valuations, no mechanism can simultaneously achieve all four desirable properties. The gap between efficiency and incentive compatibility can be quantified: the expected welfare loss grows with the overlap between buyer and seller valuation distributions. The theorem explains why real-world bargaining is often inefficient (some mutually beneficial trades fail to occur) and provides theoretical justification for intermediaries (brokers, market makers) who subsidise trade to increase efficiency. The result extends to more general multi-agent settings through the work of Myerson on optimal mechanism design.

standard.question: In Arrow's Impossibility Theorem, which of these is NOT one of Arrow's conditions on social welfare functions?
options: Pareto efficiency (unanimous individual preference implies social preference)
Independence of irrelevant alternatives
Non-dictatorship
Majority rule (social preference follows the majority)
standard.explanation: Arrow's four conditions are: (1) Unrestricted domain (all preference orderings are admissible), (2) Pareto efficiency, (3) Independence of irrelevant alternatives (the social ranking of A vs B depends only on individuals' rankings of A vs B), and (4) Non-dictatorship. Majority rule is NOT one of Arrow's conditions — in fact, majority rule can produce intransitive social preferences (Condorcet's paradox), violating the requirement that the output be a complete, transitive ordering.
standard.deepDive: Arrow's four conditions are: (1) Universal Domain (any configuration of individual preferences is admissible), (2) Pareto Efficiency (if all individuals prefer A to B, society prefers A to B), (3) Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (the social ranking of A vs B depends only on individual rankings of A vs B), and (4) Non-Dictatorship (no single individual always determines the social preference). Majority rule is not one of Arrow's conditions — it is a specific voting procedure that satisfies some of Arrow's conditions but can produce Condorcet cycles (violating transitivity of social preferences). Arrow showed no social welfare function can satisfy all four conditions simultaneously for three or more alternatives.

standard.question: In the Arrow-Debreu model of general equilibrium, what role do 'contingent commodities' play?
options: They represent goods that may or may not be produced depending on aggregate demand
They extend the commodity space to include state-contingent delivery, enabling complete markets for uncertainty
They are goods whose prices are set by a central authority rather than by markets
They represent goods whose delivery is contingent on the buyer making full advance payment
standard.explanation: In the Arrow-Debreu framework, a commodity is defined not just by physical properties but by the state of the world in which it is delivered. An 'umbrella if it rains' is a different commodity from an 'umbrella if it's sunny.' This elegant device allows the competitive equilibrium framework to handle uncertainty — with complete contingent markets, the First Welfare Theorem extends to economies under uncertainty. The obvious limitation is that complete contingent markets don't exist in reality.
standard.deepDive: In the Arrow-Debreu framework, a commodity is specified by its physical properties, the location of delivery, the time of delivery, AND the state of the world in which delivery occurs. An 'umbrella delivered if it rains on Tuesday' is a different commodity from 'umbrella delivered if it's sunny on Tuesday.' This ingenious extension allows the standard competitive equilibrium machinery to handle uncertainty: complete markets in contingent commodities achieve Pareto efficient risk sharing. In practice, complete contingent markets don't exist (there are too many possible states of the world), which is why real-world risk sharing is incomplete and financial innovation (insurance, derivatives, securities) attempts to fill the gaps.

standard.question: What is the 'revenue equivalence theorem' in auction theory?
options: All auction formats generate identical government tax revenue from the sale
Under risk-neutral bidders with independent private values, all standard auctions (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch) yield the same expected seller revenue
Seller revenue from any auction always equals exactly the second-highest bidder's valuation
Auction revenue is equivalent to revenue from optimal posted pricing in all settings
standard.explanation: The revenue equivalence theorem (Vickrey 1961, Myerson 1981, Riley & Samuelson 1981) shows that under independent private values, risk-neutral symmetric bidders, and any mechanism allocating to the highest bidder with zero surplus for the lowest type, expected revenue is the same regardless of auction format. First-price, second-price, English, and Dutch auctions all yield identical expected revenue. The result breaks down with risk aversion, asymmetric bidders, or correlated values.
standard.deepDive: Revenue equivalence holds under independent private values (each bidder knows their own valuation, drawn independently from the same distribution) and risk neutrality. Under these conditions, all four standard auction formats produce the same expected revenue. The intuition: with symmetric risk-neutral bidders and independent values, the auction format only affects who pays what in which state, not the expected amount. Revenue equivalence breaks in several ways: risk-averse bidders pay more in first-price auctions (they shade bids less to reduce risk); correlated values favour English auctions (the 'linkage principle': observing others' bids provides information that reduces the winner's curse); and asymmetric bidders may prefer different formats.

standard.question: What did the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem prove about voting mechanisms?
options: All voting systems produce equally fair outcomes when voters are sincere
Any deterministic, surjective voting rule for 3+ candidates that is non-dictatorial is susceptible to strategic manipulation
Proportional representation systems are always superior to plurality voting
Two-party systems inevitably emerge from any single-member district election rule
standard.explanation: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem (independently proved 1973/1975) shows that any voting procedure choosing among 3+ candidates must be either dictatorial, restricts outcomes to at most 2 alternatives, or is manipulable (some voter can benefit by misreporting preferences). Closely related to Arrow's theorem, it is a fundamental impossibility result in mechanism design and social choice theory, showing that strategic voting is an inescapable feature of democratic systems with three or more options.
standard.deepDive: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem is closely related to Arrow's Impossibility Theorem — indeed, some proofs derive one from the other. It has practical implications: in any voting system, some voters will have incentive to vote strategically (misrepresenting their true preferences). Under plurality voting, this manifests as the 'wasted vote' problem (voting for a frontrunner rather than your preferred candidate). Under ranked-choice voting, strategic manipulation is harder to execute but still theoretically possible. The theorem motivates research into mechanisms that minimize the gains from strategic behaviour and into alternative voting systems (approval voting, quadratic voting, liquid democracy) that may be more resistant to manipulation in practice.

standard.question: What is the 'hard problem of consciousness' as formulated by David Chalmers?
options: Explaining how the brain processes and integrates sensory information
Explaining why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience (phenomenal consciousness)
Determining experimentally whether non-human animals possess consciousness
Building an artificial system that can pass behavioral tests for consciousness
standard.explanation: Chalmers (1995) distinguished the 'hard problem' — explaining why there is subjective experience at all, why physical processing is accompanied by phenomenal consciousness — from 'easy problems' like explaining discrimination, attention, or reportability. Even a complete functional/neural explanation of the brain might leave the hard problem untouched: knowing all the neural correlates of seeing red need not explain why there is 'something it is like' to see red.
standard.deepDive: Chalmers formulated the hard problem in his 1995 paper 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness.' The 'easy problems' (which may still be scientifically hard) include explaining discrimination, categorisation, integration of information, reportability, attention, and deliberate control. These are 'easy' because they are problems of function — explaining how the brain processes information. The hard problem asks why information processing is accompanied by subjective experience. Even a complete neural account of how the brain discriminates red from green leaves unexplained why there is something it is like to see red. This 'explanatory gap' (Levine) has motivated property dualism, panpsychism, mysterianism, and various physicalist responses.

standard.question: What is the 'veil of ignorance' in John Rawls' theory of justice?
options: The principle that justice requires ignoring all cultural and religious differences between people
A thought experiment where principles of justice are chosen without knowing one's place in society
The philosophical claim that no one can truly comprehend the suffering of others
A legal principle requiring judges to remain ignorant of defendants' social standing
standard.explanation: Rawls' veil of ignorance (A Theory of Justice, 1971) asks us to choose principles of justice from an 'original position' where we don't know our race, sex, class, talents, or conception of the good. Rawls argued rational agents behind this veil would choose (1) equal basic liberties, and (2) the 'difference principle' — inequalities are only justified if they benefit the worst-off members of society. This is a contractualist approach to deriving fair principles for the basic structure of society.
standard.deepDive: Rawls's veil of ignorance eliminates knowledge that could bias the choice of principles. Behind the veil, you don't know your race, sex, class, talents, religion, or conception of the good life. This ensures that whatever principles you choose, you could accept regardless of your position. Rawls argues this leads to his two principles: (1) equal basic liberties for all, and (2) inequalities arranged to benefit the least advantaged (difference principle). Critics include Harsanyi (who argued the veil leads to utilitarianism, not maximin), Nozick (who argued historical entitlements matter more than ideal distributions), and communitarian critics like Sandel (who argued the 'unencumbered self' behind the veil is incoherent).

standard.question: In Derek Parfit's 'Reasons and Persons,' what does the teletransportation thought experiment challenge?
options: The possibility of faster-than-light travel
Whether personal identity persists through physical discontinuity — is the copy on Mars the same person?
The ethical permissibility of human cloning technology
Whether consciousness requires a biological substrate
standard.explanation: Parfit imagines a device that scans your body, destroys it, and creates an exact replica on Mars. Is the person on Mars you? Parfit argued that what matters in survival is not some deep fact of identity but rather psychological continuity and connectedness — memories, personality, intentions. He controversially concluded that personal identity is 'not what matters,' with radical implications for how we think about future selves, death, and moral responsibility.
standard.deepDive: Parfit's teletransportation challenges the common assumption that personal identity is a deep, all-or-nothing fact. If the replica on Mars has all your memories, personality, and psychological continuity, many find it hard to deny it 'is' you. But the original body was destroyed — so are you dead? Parfit argued that what matters for survival is not strict identity (numerical sameness) but psychological continuity and connectedness — the relation that holds between your current self and your self five minutes ago. Since the replica has full psychological continuity with you, Parfit argues 'this is as good as survival.' The thought experiment has implications for the ethics of brain uploading, teleportation, and personal identity over time.

standard.question: What is Hume's 'is-ought problem' (sometimes called 'Hume's guillotine')?
options: The difficulty of determining which moral obligations we actually ought to follow
The logical gap between descriptive statements (what IS the case) and prescriptive statements (what OUGHT to be)
The problem of whether moral obligations exist independently of human belief
The challenge of implementing moral ideals within practical political constraints
standard.explanation: Hume observed that many moral arguments slip from descriptive premises (facts about the world) to normative conclusions (what should be done) without adequate justification. You cannot derive 'ought' from 'is' alone — no purely factual premise logically entails an evaluative conclusion. This remains one of the most important principles in metaethics. G.E. Moore's 'naturalistic fallacy' is related but distinct — it concerns identifying moral properties with natural properties.
standard.deepDive: Hume's is-ought gap has been central to metaethics for nearly three centuries. The gap holds that from purely descriptive premises ('humans desire happiness,' 'cooperation promotes survival'), no normative conclusion ('you ought to promote happiness,' 'cooperation is morally good') logically follows without adding a normative premise. This challenges moral naturalism (deriving ethics from human nature) and evolutionary ethics (deriving ethics from evolution). Defenders of the gap include non-cognitivists (moral claims aren't factual, so they can't be derived from facts) and Kantians (morality is grounded in pure practical reason, not empirical facts). Those who challenge the gap include Philippa Foot and Alasdair MacIntyre, who argue that certain facts about human nature and flourishing do entail normative conclusions.

standard.question: What is Peter Singer's central argument in 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972)?
options: Charitable giving is supererogatory — morally praiseworthy but never obligatory
If we can prevent suffering without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do so — implying strong obligations on the affluent
Government foreign aid is always more effective than individual charitable donations
Our moral obligations extend only to members of our own political community
standard.explanation: Singer's argument is deceptively simple: (1) suffering and death from lack of food, shelter, and medicine are bad; (2) if we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to; (3) geographic distance and number of other potential helpers don't diminish the obligation. The radical conclusion is that affluent people should give until they reach the point where giving more would cause comparable suffering to themselves. This paper was foundational to the effective altruism movement.
standard.deepDive: Singer's argument has had enormous practical impact through the effective altruism movement. The key premises are: (1) suffering from lack of food, shelter, and medical care is bad; (2) if we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do so; (3) by donating to effective charities, we can prevent such suffering. The argument implies that the affluent have much stronger obligations to the global poor than conventionally recognised. GiveWell estimates that the most effective global health charities can save a life for approximately $3,000-5,000. Singer's 'Effective Altruism' movement has directed billions to high-impact causes.

standard.question: What is the 'experience machine' thought experiment designed to test?
options: Whether removing negative experiences would make people happier overall
Whether we value things beyond subjective experience — Nozick argues most would reject a life of perfectly simulated pleasure
Whether simulated experiences count as knowledge for epistemological purposes
Whether sharing experiences between minds is theoretically possible
standard.explanation: Nozick (1974) asks whether you would plug into a machine that provides any desired experiences (you'd believe them real). He argued most would refuse, suggesting we value things beyond subjective experience: actually doing things, being a certain kind of person, and genuine contact with reality. This is widely considered a powerful challenge to hedonistic utilitarianism, though some philosophers question whether the intuition survives careful reflection or whether it merely reflects status quo bias.
standard.deepDive: Nozick designed the experience machine as a challenge to hedonistic utilitarianism — the view that only subjective experiences matter. If hedonism were correct, plugging in would be rational: the experiences would be indistinguishable from reality and could include any pleasures you desire. Yet most people resist, suggesting we value: (1) actually doing things, not just experiencing them; (2) being a certain kind of person, not just having the experience of being one; (3) contact with reality, not just convincing simulation. The thought experiment anticipates modern debates about virtual reality, social media (which offers curated, filtered experiences), and AI-generated content.

standard.question: What is 'moral realism' in metaethics?
options: The view that moral claims should be grounded in realistic assessments of human capacity
The view that there are objective, mind-independent moral facts
The view that moral rules must be based on realistic assumptions about human psychology
The view that only empirically observable consequences determine moral status
standard.explanation: Moral realism holds that objective moral truths exist independently of anyone's beliefs, attitudes, or conventions. Key variants include naturalistic realism (moral facts are natural facts), non-naturalistic realism (moral facts are sui generis, as in Enoch's robust realism), and Cornell realism. Opponents include expressivists (moral utterances express attitudes, not beliefs), error theorists (all positive moral claims are false), and constructivists (moral truths are constructed, not discovered).
standard.deepDive: Moral realism is the view that there are objective moral facts independent of what anyone thinks or believes. This doesn't mean moral truths are easy to discover or that disagreement doesn't exist — there are objective truths about quantum physics that are also difficult to discover. Main arguments for realism: our moral practice presupposes it (we treat moral claims as genuinely true or false, open to discovery and error), and moral realism best explains moral progress (the abolition of slavery, expansion of rights). Main arguments against: the 'queerness' argument (Mackie), evolutionary debunking arguments, and the argument from persistent moral disagreement.

standard.question: What is the 'demandingness objection' to consequentialism?
options: That consequentialism requires too much cognitive effort to calculate all possible consequences
That consequentialism demands excessive philosophical sophistication from ordinary agents
That consequentialism may require enormous personal sacrifices whenever doing so would produce better overall outcomes
That consequentialism demands universal agreement on what constitutes a 'good' consequence
standard.explanation: The demandingness objection holds that consequentialism requires agents to sacrifice their own interests, projects, and relationships whenever doing so produces greater overall good — potentially demanding you give most of your income, abandon personal goals, etc. Bernard Williams argued this fails to respect the importance of personal integrity and 'ground projects.' Responses include satisficing consequentialism (you only need to produce 'good enough' outcomes), agent-relative options, and simply accepting the demanding conclusion.
standard.deepDive: The demandingness objection applies to any version of consequentialism that requires maximisation. If you could always produce more good by donating more money, time, or effort, consequentialism seems to require constant self-sacrifice. Bernard Williams argued this 'alienates' agents from their own projects and commitments — the things that make life worth living. Consequentialist responses include rule consequentialism (following moderate rules produces better outcomes), agent-relative consequentialism (giving special weight to your own projects is itself good), and satisficing (actions are right if they produce sufficiently good outcomes, not necessarily the best possible).

standard.question: What does Hilary Putnam's 'Twin Earth' thought experiment demonstrate?
options: That all knowledge is inevitably relative to one's cultural framework
That the meaning of natural kind terms is partly determined by the external world, not just by what's 'in the head'
That consciousness necessarily requires a biological physical substrate
That meaningful language is impossible without sustained social interaction
standard.explanation: Putnam (1975) imagines Twin Earth, identical to Earth except 'water' there is XYZ (not H2O) but looks and behaves identically. Your Twin Earth counterpart has the same internal mental states, yet their 'water' refers to XYZ while yours refers to H2O. Therefore meaning 'ain't in the head' — external factors partly determine reference. This is a foundational argument for semantic externalism, with implications for philosophy of mind and language.
standard.deepDive: Putnam's Twin Earth experiment establishes semantic externalism — the view that the meanings of at least some terms are partly determined by the external world, not just by what's 'in the head.' On Twin Earth, a molecule called XYZ has all the same superficial properties as water (H2O) — it looks, tastes, and flows like water. Twin Earthlings call it 'water.' Putnam argues that the word 'water' on Earth refers to H2O, while 'water' on Twin Earth refers to XYZ, even if Earthlings and Twin Earthlings have identical mental states. Therefore, meaning 'ain't in the head.' This has implications for philosophy of mind (what we think about depends on our environment) and AI (can a system that lacks environmental grounding truly understand language?).

standard.question: What is the 'repugnant conclusion' in population ethics, as identified by Derek Parfit?
options: That all ethical systems inevitably produce some conclusions we find deeply repugnant
That total utilitarianism implies a vast population of barely-happy lives is better than a smaller population of very happy lives
That overpopulation necessarily leads to the collapse of moral institutions
That we have absolutely no moral obligations to people who don't yet exist
standard.explanation: The repugnant conclusion follows from total utilitarianism: for any world of very happy people (population A), there exists a much larger population (Z) whose members have lives barely worth living but whose total welfare exceeds A's. If total welfare is what matters, Z is better than A. Parfit considered this deeply counterintuitive. Avoiding it while retaining other plausible axioms has proven remarkably difficult — most alternatives face their own paradoxes.
standard.deepDive: The repugnant conclusion is generated by three premises: (1) for any population of happy people A, there exists a larger population B whose total welfare exceeds A's, where each individual in B has slightly lower welfare; (2) slightly reducing everyone's welfare while adding more people can increase total welfare; (3) iterating this process eventually reaches a vast population of people with lives barely worth living (Z). Since Z has more total welfare than A, total utilitarianism ranks Z above A. Proposed solutions include average utilitarianism (vulnerable to the 'mere addition paradox'), critical-level theories (only counting welfare above a threshold), and person-affecting views (which face the non-identity problem). Gustaf Arrhenius has shown that avoiding the repugnant conclusion while satisfying other plausible conditions is impossible.

standard.question: What is Nick Bostrom's simulation argument?
options: A proof that we are definitely living inside a computer simulation
A trilemma: either civilizations rarely survive to create simulations, or they rarely choose to, or we are almost certainly in one
An argument that computer simulations can never produce genuine consciousness
A claim that the physical universe is itself running on some deeper computational substrate
standard.explanation: Bostrom's simulation argument (2003) is not a claim that we're simulated — it's a trilemma. At least one must be true: (1) almost all civilizations go extinct before reaching simulation capability, (2) virtually no civilization that reaches that level runs ancestor simulations, or (3) we are almost certainly living in a simulation. The reasoning is probabilistic: if mature civilizations do run many simulations, simulated beings vastly outnumber biological ones.
standard.deepDive: Bostrom's simulation argument is a trilemma, not an argument that we are in a simulation. At least one of three propositions must be true: (1) almost all civilizations at our level go extinct before becoming technologically capable of running high-fidelity ancestor simulations; (2) almost all such civilizations choose not to run such simulations; (3) we are almost certainly living in a simulation. The argument is purely probabilistic: if (1) and (2) are false, then many civilizations run many simulations, and simulated beings vastly outnumber real beings, making (3) probable. The argument has implications for existential risk (proposition 1), the future of technology (proposition 2), and the nature of reality (proposition 3).

standard.question: What distinction does Philippa Foot draw between 'doing' and 'allowing' harm?
options: Doing harm is always illegal while allowing harm is merely immoral
Actively causing harm is morally worse than failing to prevent equivalent harm — the act/omission distinction
There is no moral difference; Foot argued they should be treated identically by any consistent ethical theory
Doing harm is worse only when the agent has malicious intent; otherwise they are equivalent
standard.explanation: Foot argued (and many deontologists agree) that there is a morally significant difference between actively causing harm and merely failing to prevent it. This underpins the act/omission distinction: killing someone seems worse than failing to save them, even with identical outcomes. Consequentialists typically reject this distinction. The debate remains central to medical ethics (killing vs. letting die), trolley problems, and Peter Singer's arguments about global poverty obligations.
standard.deepDive: Foot's doing/allowing distinction (also called the act/omission distinction) is one of the most debated issues in normative ethics. Deontologists generally hold that there is a morally significant difference between killing someone (doing harm) and letting someone die (allowing harm) — even when the outcomes are identical. This is why most people judge the trolley switch case (diverting harm) differently from the transplant case (actively killing one to save five). Consequentialists typically reject the distinction: the outcome (one death vs five deaths) is the same either way. The distinction has practical importance in medical ethics (active euthanasia vs withdrawing treatment), international law (duty to rescue), and charitable giving (are we responsible for deaths we could have prevented?).

standard.question: What is the difference between 'act utilitarianism' and 'rule utilitarianism'?
options: Act utilitarianism judges each individual action by its consequences; rule utilitarianism judges actions by conformity to rules that would maximize utility if generally followed
Act utilitarianism applies only to deliberate actions; rule utilitarianism also covers omissions
Act utilitarianism was Bentham's view; rule utilitarianism was developed in the 20th century by Rawls
They are mathematically equivalent and always produce identical moral prescriptions
standard.explanation: Act utilitarianism evaluates each action directly by its consequences in that specific situation. Rule utilitarianism says the right action follows rules whose general adoption would maximize utility. They can diverge: act utilitarianism might justify a beneficial lie, while rule utilitarianism might forbid it because universal lying would be catastrophic. Critics argue rule utilitarianism either collapses into act utilitarianism (via increasingly specific rules) or irrationally fetishizes rules.
standard.deepDive: The act/rule distinction cuts across consequentialist theories. An act utilitarian evaluates each specific action by its consequences in that particular situation; a rule utilitarian evaluates rules by the consequences of their general adoption. These can diverge: an act utilitarian might justify breaking a promise when doing so maximises utility in a specific case, while a rule utilitarian would condemn promise-breaking because a general rule permitting it would undermine trust and produce worse overall outcomes. Rule utilitarianism is often seen as capturing the consequentialist appeal of utilitarianism while avoiding its most counterintuitive implications.

standard.question: What is the 'problem of evil' and what is Plantinga's influential response?
options: The question of why humans commit evil acts; Plantinga argues it's due to original sin

The apparent incompatibility of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God with the existence of evil; Plantinga's free will defense argues God cannot create genuinely free beings who are guaranteed never to choose evil
The question of how to define evil objectively; Plantinga argues evil is the absence of good
The difficulty of punishing evil fairly; Plantinga argues divine justice resolves the problem
standard.explanation: The logical problem of evil argues that an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God is logically incompatible with the existence of evil. Plantinga's free will defense (1974) argued it's possible that a world with genuinely free creatures who sometimes choose evil is more valuable than a world of automata, and that even an omnipotent God cannot create free beings guaranteed to never choose evil (a logical impossibility). Most philosophers accept this resolves the logical version, though the evidential problem of evil (why so much suffering?) remains hotly debated.
standard.deepDive: Plantinga's Free Will Defense addresses the logical problem of evil — the claim that God's existence is logically incompatible with the existence of evil. Plantinga argues that it's logically possible that God cannot create beings with genuine libertarian free will who are guaranteed never to choose evil. If free will is a sufficiently great good (making possible love, moral virtue, genuine relationship), then God may be justified in creating free beings even knowing some will choose evil. Most philosophers of religion consider the logical problem of evil resolved by Plantinga's defense. The evidential problem (why so much suffering, including animal suffering predating human free will?) remains more challenging.

standard.question: What is 'effective altruism' as a philosophical position?
options: A charity evaluation methodology based primarily on measuring administrative overhead ratios
A philosophical movement combining the obligation to help others with rigorous evidence about which interventions do the most good
A political advocacy movement focused exclusively on increasing government foreign aid budgets
A form of virtue ethics emphasizing the cultivation of generosity and compassion as character traits
standard.explanation: Effective altruism combines the moral motivation to benefit others (drawing on arguments by Singer, among others) with evidence-based methods to determine which interventions are most effective. Core principles include cause impartiality (comparing across cause areas like global health, animal welfare, and existential risk), cost-effectiveness analysis, counterfactual reasoning, and prioritizing problems that are large in scale, neglected, and tractable. It was developed by philosophers including William MacAskill and Toby Ord.
standard.deepDive: Effective altruism combines moral motivation (the belief that we should help others) with evidence-based reasoning about how to help most effectively. Key principles include cause impartiality (not favouring causes based on emotional appeal), cost-effectiveness analysis (comparing the impact per dollar across different interventions), and a focus on scale, neglectedness, and tractability (the INT framework) for cause prioritisation. Priority areas include global health (GiveWell-recommended charities), animal welfare (reducing factory farming), existential risk reduction (AI safety, biosecurity), and building the EA community itself. The movement has been shaped by the philosophical work of Singer, Parfit, Ord, and MacAskill.

standard.question: In Kripke's 'Naming and Necessity,' what does the concept of a 'rigid designator' mean?
options: A name whose reference cannot be changed once established by a formal naming ceremony
A term that refers to the same object in every possible world in which that object exists
A logical constant that maintains the same truth value across all interpretations of a formal language
A definite description that uniquely singles out a single object in the actual world
standard.explanation: Kripke argued that proper names are 'rigid designators' — they pick out the same individual in every possible world. 'Aristotle' refers to Aristotle even in worlds where he never studied philosophy. Definite descriptions like 'the teacher of Alexander' are non-rigid — they pick out different people in different possible worlds. This undermined the Frege-Russell view that names are disguised descriptions, and grounded the necessity of identity (if Hesperus = Phosphorus, this is necessarily true).
standard.deepDive: Kripke's concept of rigid designation overturned the description theory of reference (Frege, Russell), which held that names refer via descriptions ('Aristotle' = 'the student of Plato who taught Alexander'). Kripke showed that names track the same individual across possible worlds, while descriptions may pick out different individuals. 'Aristotle might not have been a philosopher' is meaningful (he could have become a farmer), but 'the teacher of Alexander might not have been the teacher of Alexander' is not. This has consequences for necessary truths: 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is necessary (they're the same object in all worlds) despite being discovered empirically.

standard.question: In decision theory, how do Causal Decision Theory (CDT) and Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) diverge on Newcomb's Problem?
options: CDT recommends two-boxing (your choice can't causally change the prediction); EDT recommends one-boxing (one-boxers are predicted to get the million)
CDT and EDT agree on all well-defined decision problems; Newcomb's Problem is considered ill-formed
CDT recommends one-boxing; EDT recommends two-boxing
CDT applies only to deterministic scenarios; EDT applies only to probabilistic ones
standard.explanation: In Newcomb's Problem, a highly accurate predictor placed $1M in an opaque box if it predicted you'd one-box, $0 if it predicted you'd two-box. CDT says two-box: your current choice can't causally alter the already-fixed prediction, so you're always $1000 richer taking both boxes. EDT says one-box: the evidence is that one-boxers almost always get $1M. This reveals a deep disagreement about whether rational choice tracks causal influence or evidential correlation. Functional Decision Theory (FDT) offers a third approach by asking what decision procedure yields the best outcomes.
standard.deepDive: Newcomb's problem (Nozick 1969) splits decision theorists into two camps. CDT reasons: the prediction is already made; my choice cannot causally change the box contents; taking both boxes dominates (I get $1000 more regardless of the prediction). EDT reasons: one-boxing is evidence that the predictor put $1M in the box; the expected value of one-boxing is much higher. Almost all one-boxers actually get $1M and almost all two-boxers get only $1000 — CDT advocates are 'right' but poor. FDT (Yudkowsky & Soares 2017) offers a third perspective: evaluate the output of the decision algorithm, not the individual decision. Since the predictor simulates your algorithm, the algorithm that outputs 'one-box' gets $1M.

standard.question: What is the 'mere addition paradox' and why does it create a crisis for population ethics?
options: Adding a happy person to any world always makes it better; paradoxical because it implies infinite value
Three separately plausible steps — mere addition of happy people, equalizing redistribution, and transitivity — lead inexorably to the repugnant conclusion
Adding people to a community always reduces per-capita welfare; paradoxical for immigration policy
It's a version of the sorites paradox applied to the question of when a population becomes 'too large'
standard.explanation: Parfit showed that three seemingly reasonable principles — (1) merely adding happy lives can't make things worse (mere addition), (2) equalizing redistribution while maintaining total welfare is an improvement, (3) 'better than' is transitive — lead step by step from a small very happy population (A) to a vast barely-happy population (Z). Each step seems acceptable, but the endpoint is the repugnant conclusion. This forces abandoning at least one principle, and each option has severe costs, creating what Temkin and others call an impossibility in population ethics.
standard.deepDive: The mere addition paradox creates a chain of reasoning from an intuitively good world (A: small, very happy population) to the repugnant conclusion (Z: vast, barely-happy population). Step 1: mere addition (adding happy people without harming anyone) seems permissible, yielding A+. Step 2: equalising redistribution (from unequal A+ to equal B) seems good. Step 3: transitivity (if A+ is at least as good as A, and B is better than A+, then B is better than A). Repeating this process leads from A to Z. To block the argument, we must reject one premise: that mere addition is never bad, that equalising redistribution is always good, or that the 'better than' relation is transitive. Each rejection has counterintuitive implications.

standard.question: How does the 'explanatory gap' argument against physicalism differ from the 'zombie conceivability' argument?
options: They are identical arguments expressed with different terminology
The explanatory gap is epistemic (we lack understanding of why physical processes produce experience); the zombie argument is metaphysical (if zombies are conceivable, consciousness is non-physical)
The explanatory gap concerns neuroscience methodology; the zombie argument concerns quantum mechanics
The explanatory gap is an empirical observation; the zombie argument is a deductive proof of dualism
standard.explanation: Levine's explanatory gap (1983) is epistemic: complete physical knowledge seems to leave unexplained WHY those processes produce THIS experience. It might be compatible with physicalism (perhaps we just can't grasp the explanation). Chalmers' zombie argument is metaphysical and stronger: if a being physically identical to you but lacking consciousness is conceivable (not logically contradictory), then consciousness is not logically entailed by the physical, suggesting physicalism is false. The gap might reflect our limitations; zombies, if truly conceivable, would refute physicalism outright.
standard.deepDive: Levine's explanatory gap (1983) is an epistemic claim: even with complete physical/functional knowledge of the brain, we would still lack an explanation of why those processes produce the particular subjective experiences they do. Why does C-fibre stimulation feel painful rather than pleasurable or like nothing at all? This gap might be compatible with physicalism if the gap is merely epistemic (we lack the concepts to bridge it) rather than metaphysical. Chalmers's zombie argument is metaphysical: if zombies (physical duplicates without consciousness) are conceivable, they are metaphysically possible, which means consciousness is not necessitated by physical facts.
