standard.deepDive: During autoregressive generation (producing text one token at a time), the model must store the key and value vectors from all previous tokens so it can attend to them when generating each new token. This stored information is called the KV cache, and it grows linearly with context length and the number of attention heads. For a model like Llama 3.1 405B with 128 attention heads and a 128K token context window, the KV cache at full context can consume hundreds of gigabytes of GPU memory per request. GQA reduces this by using fewer key-value heads than query heads (Llama 3 uses 128 query heads but only 8 KV heads), shrinking the cache by 16x while preserving most of the model's quality.

standard.question: What is 'top-p' (nucleus) sampling in LLM text generation?
options: Selecting from the top p most probable tokens
Selecting from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p
Setting the probability threshold for each individual token
Sampling p tokens in parallel and choosing the best
standard.explanation: Top-p (nucleus) sampling dynamically selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probabilities add up to threshold p (typically 0.9-0.95), then renormalizes probabilities among that set. Unlike top-k (which fixes the number of candidates), top-p adapts: when the model is confident, fewer tokens are considered; when uncertain, more are included.
standard.deepDive: Top-p sampling works by sorting all tokens in the vocabulary by their probability (highest to lowest), then including tokens until their cumulative probability reaches the threshold p. The key advantage over top-k (which always selects exactly k tokens) is adaptability: when the model is very confident, top-p might include only 2-3 candidates, maintaining coherence; when it is uncertain, it might include hundreds, allowing creative variety. Most production systems combine temperature adjustment with top-p sampling for optimal text generation quality.

standard.question: What was the key finding of the Chinchilla paper that contradicted earlier scaling law advice?
options: Training data quality matters more than quantity
Model size and training data should scale equally with compute budget
Smaller models always outperform larger ones
Pre-training is unnecessary if you do enough fine-tuning
standard.explanation: The Kaplan et al. (2020) scaling laws from OpenAI suggested prioritizing model size over data, leading to under-trained giants like GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens). The 2022 Chinchilla paper showed that model size and data should scale equally: for every doubling of model size, training tokens should also double. This meant models like GPT-3 and Gopher were significantly over-sized for their data budget.
standard.deepDive: The Kaplan scaling laws (OpenAI, 2020) had recommended allocating compute roughly 73% to model size and 27% to data. This led to 'over-parameterised' models like GPT-3 (175B parameters trained on only 300B tokens, about 1.7 tokens per parameter). The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind, 2022) tested over 400 models and found the optimal ratio is approximately equal scaling: roughly 20 tokens per parameter. This meant GPT-3 should have been either 10x smaller or trained on 10x more data, and Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) outperformed the much larger Gopher (280B params) it was designed to test against.

standard.question: How many trillion tokens was Llama 3.1 (405B) pre-trained on?
options: 1.5 trillion
5 trillion
15.6 trillion
50 trillion
standard.explanation: Llama 3.1 405B was pre-trained on over 15.6 trillion tokens, using 30.84 million GPU hours. This is far beyond the Chinchilla-optimal ratio (which would suggest ~8T tokens for 405B params), reflecting a deliberate 'over-training' strategy -- spending extra compute on data rather than parameters makes the final model cheaper to run at inference time.
standard.deepDive: The 15.6 trillion tokens make Llama 3.1 405B one of the most data-intensive training runs ever conducted, processing roughly 38 tokens per parameter -- nearly double the Chinchilla-optimal ratio. This 'over-training' strategy deliberately spends extra compute on data during training to make the final model cheaper to run during inference, because inference cost depends on model size but not on how much data was used during training. The 30.84 million GPU hours represents an enormous computational investment, equivalent to running approximately 16,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs continuously for about 80 days.

standard.question: What is 'red teaming' in AI safety?
options: Training the model on adversarial examples to improve robustness
Systematic attempts to make a model behave in unintended or harmful ways
A technique for compressing model weights
Deploying multiple models that check each other's outputs
standard.explanation: Red teaming means systematically and strategically attempting to cause a model to violate the developer's policies or act in unintended ways. Best practice involves both automated adversarial prompt generation and human red team members who explore creative attack approaches. Major labs conduct red team exercises before deployment and schedule periodic re-testing every 3-6 months.
standard.deepDive: Red teaming in AI borrows the concept from military and cybersecurity practice, where a 'red team' simulates adversarial attacks to expose vulnerabilities. In the AI context, red teamers systematically probe the model for harmful outputs, policy violations, and unexpected behaviours by crafting adversarial prompts and multi-turn attack strategies. Modern red teaming combines automated methods (using other AI models to generate thousands of attack prompts) with human expertise (domain specialists who understand how real adversaries think). Major AI labs conduct red team exercises before deployment and periodically afterwards, typically every 3-6 months.

standard.question: What is the relationship between the original Transformer's encoder and decoder, and modern LLMs like GPT?
options: Modern LLMs use only the encoder
Modern LLMs use only the decoder
Modern LLMs use both encoder and decoder
Modern LLMs use neither -- they use a completely different architecture
standard.explanation: The original 2017 Transformer ('Attention Is All You Need') had both an encoder and decoder. Modern autoregressive LLMs like GPT, Claude, and Llama use only the decoder stack. The decoder uses 'causal' (masked) self-attention so each token can only attend to previous tokens, enabling left-to-right text generation. Encoder-only models like BERT are used for different tasks.
standard.deepDive: The original 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' Transformer was designed for machine translation and had an encoder (which reads the full input sentence using bidirectional attention) and a decoder (which generates the translation token by token using causal attention that only looks backward). Modern autoregressive LLMs like GPT, Claude, and Llama use only the decoder stack because their task inherently requires left-to-right processing. Encoder-only models like BERT use only the encoder stack and are better suited for tasks like classification where seeing the full input is beneficial.

standard.question: In Constitutional AI (developed by Anthropic), what replaces human feedback in the RL phase?
options: Randomly generated rewards
AI-generated feedback based on a set of principles
Automated grammar checking
User engagement metrics
standard.explanation: Constitutional AI uses RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback) -- the model itself evaluates pairs of responses based on a 'constitution' of principles, replacing human raters entirely for the harmlessness signal. The supervised phase involves self-critique and revision: the model generates a harmful response, critiques it against the principles, then revises it. Anthropic found this produces a 'Pareto improvement' -- both more helpful AND more harmless.
standard.deepDive: The Constitutional AI process for generating preference data works as follows: the model is presented with pairs of its own responses to the same prompt, and asked which better follows a specific constitutional principle. The model's choices become the preference labels that train a reward model, removing the need for human raters in the preference labelling step -- a major bottleneck in standard RLHF. Anthropic found that this RLAIF approach produces a 'Pareto improvement': the resulting model is both more helpful and more harmless compared to models trained with human preference labels alone.

standard.question: Why do transformers need positional encoding?
options: To reduce memory usage during training
Because self-attention treats tokens as an unordered set, so position information must be explicitly added
To convert words into numerical vectors
To enable the model to generate text in multiple languages
standard.explanation: Unlike RNNs which process tokens sequentially, a transformer's self-attention mechanism processes all tokens in parallel and is permutation-invariant -- it has no inherent notion of token order. Positional encodings add order information explicitly. The original Transformer used sinusoidal encodings; modern models use Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) which encode position directly into the attention computation.
standard.deepDive: The self-attention mechanism computes attention scores between all pairs of tokens using dot products, and this operation is inherently permutation-invariant -- swapping token order produces the same scores. Without positional information, 'The cat sat on the mat' would be processed identically to 'mat the on sat cat the.' The original Transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings (fixed mathematical functions added to token embeddings), but these have been largely replaced by Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), which encode position by rotating query and key vectors so that the dot product depends on relative distance rather than absolute position.

standard.question: As of early 2026, which AI benchmarks are considered essentially 'saturated' (frontier models score near-perfectly)?
options: ARC-AGI-2 and GPQA Diamond
GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, and SQuAD
AIME 2026 and HLE
FrontierMath and Humanity's Last Exam
standard.explanation: GSM8K (grade school math), CommonsenseQA, and SQuAD (reading comprehension) are essentially saturated by frontier models -- gains are marginal and the focus has shifted to calibration, hallucination, and safety. Harder benchmarks like GPQA Diamond (expert science), AIME (competition math), ARC-AGI-2, and HLE (Humanity's Last Exam) are where meaningful differentiation still occurs.
standard.deepDive: Benchmark saturation occurs when frontier models consistently score above 95%, making the benchmark unable to discriminate between models. GSM8K (grade-school math), CommonsenseQA, and SQuAD (reading comprehension) are essentially saturated. The field has shifted to harder benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond (graduate-level science), AIME (competition math), ARC-AGI-2 (novel pattern-recognition tasks designed to be impossible to memorise from training data), and HLE (Humanity's Last Exam). On contamination-resistant benchmarks, Chinese frontier models score at the level Western models achieved 6-8 months earlier.

standard.question: What key technical innovation makes DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) simpler than standard RLHF?
options: It uses a larger reward model
It eliminates the need for a separate reward model by deriving an implicit reward from the policy itself
It replaces human preferences with synthetic data
It uses supervised learning on the reward model's outputs
standard.explanation: DPO's key insight is a mathematical reparameterization: using the Bradley-Terry preference model, you can express the reward function in terms of the policy and reference policy, and the intractable partition function cancels out. This lets you optimize directly on preference pairs using a supervised loss, without training a separate reward model or running RL. The global optimizers of RLHF and DPO are theoretically identical.
standard.deepDive: The mathematical derivation works by expressing the reward function in terms of the model's own output probabilities, which introduces a term called the 'partition function' Z. The partition function Z requires summing the reward over all possible outputs -- a computation that is completely intractable. DPO's breakthrough insight is that when computing the probability of preferring response A over response B using the Bradley-Terry model, Z appears in both terms and cancels out. This means the preference probability can be computed directly from model probabilities without ever estimating Z or training a separate reward model.

standard.question: What is GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), and which model demonstrated its power?
options: A data augmentation technique; GPT-5 demonstrated it
A reward-free RL method using relative group advantage; DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated it
A model compression algorithm; Llama 4 demonstrated it
A new attention mechanism; Gemini 3 demonstrated it
standard.explanation: GRPO updates the policy based on relative advantage within a group of sampled responses, using rank-based penalties instead of a learned reward model. DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated that pure RLVR (RL with Verifiable Rewards) combined with GRPO can produce emergent reasoning capabilities, with the model spontaneously developing chain-of-thought reasoning without being explicitly taught to do so.
standard.deepDive: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) works by generating a group of responses to each prompt, scoring them, and updating the policy based on how each response compares to the group average rather than to an absolute reward model. DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated GRPO's power by developing sophisticated reasoning capabilities through pure reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The model spontaneously developed chain-of-thought reasoning, self-verification, and error-correction behaviours without being explicitly taught these strategies, suggesting that RL training with clear success criteria can elicit emergent cognitive strategies.

standard.question: What is the purpose of the KL divergence penalty in RLHF training with PPO?
options: To speed up training convergence
To prevent the policy from diverging too far from the reference model, mitigating reward hacking
To increase the diversity of generated responses
To regularize the reward model's predictions
standard.explanation: Without the KL penalty, the model can exploit inaccuracies in the reward model (reward hacking), generating nonsensical or repetitive outputs that score high on the proxy reward but are actually low quality. The KL divergence term penalizes the policy for moving too far from the initial supervised fine-tuned model. Implementations typically use an adaptive KL controller that adjusts the penalty coefficient to keep KL within a target range of about 3-10.
standard.deepDive: Without the KL penalty, the reinforcement learning process can find degenerate solutions -- outputs that score very highly on the reward model but are actually low quality, such as verbose, repetitive, confident-sounding text. This is called 'reward hacking' and is a practical manifestation of Goodhart's Law. The KL divergence measures how different the RL-trained model's output distribution has become from the original supervised fine-tuned model. By penalising large KL values, the training process forces the model to stay close to the SFT model's behaviour, which serves as a regularising anchor.

standard.question: What is FlashAttention's core innovation?
options: Approximate attention using random projections
IO-aware exact attention using tiling to minimize GPU memory transfers
Replacing attention with linear layers
Using sparse attention patterns to skip irrelevant tokens
standard.explanation: FlashAttention (by Tri Dao et al., NeurIPS 2022) computes exact attention while being IO-aware -- it uses tiling to minimize reads/writes between GPU HBM (high bandwidth memory) and on-chip SRAM. The key insight was that attention's bottleneck wasn't compute but memory bandwidth. FlashAttention-3 (2024) further exploits Hopper GPU features like asynchronous tensor cores and FP8 support.
standard.deepDive: Standard attention requires materialising an N x N attention matrix (where N is sequence length) in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which becomes prohibitively expensive for long sequences. FlashAttention avoids this by computing attention in tiles: small blocks that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip SRAM (about 20 MB on an H100) rather than the larger but slower HBM (80 GB). The key insight by Tri Dao was that the bottleneck in attention is not arithmetic but memory bandwidth -- reading and writing the massive attention matrix. By keeping computation in SRAM, FlashAttention reduces HBM accesses and achieves 2-4x speedups while computing mathematically identical results.

standard.question: DeepSeek-V3 introduced Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA). By how much does it reduce KV cache usage?
options: About 50%
About 75%
About 93%
About 99%
standard.explanation: Multi-Head Latent Attention reduces KV cache usage by 93.3% compared to standard multi-head attention, dramatically lowering memory requirements during inference. Unlike Grouped Query Attention (GQA), which reduces KV heads, MLA compresses key-value information into a low-dimensional latent space and reconstructs it, achieving much more aggressive compression without the quality loss seen in other methods.
standard.deepDive: In standard multi-head attention, the model stores separate key and value vectors for every token at every attention head, requiring enormous GPU memory. MLA replaces this with a compression step: keys and values are projected into a much smaller 'latent' representation, and only these compressed latents are stored in the KV cache. When the model needs to compute attention, it reconstructs approximations of the full keys and values using a learned up-projection. Because the compression is learned (optimised during training) rather than fixed, MLA achieves much more aggressive compression (93.3%) than alternative methods while maintaining quality.

standard.question: In transformer training, what is the standard optimizer, and why was it specifically developed?
options: SGD with momentum, for its simplicity
Adam, for its adaptive learning rates per parameter
AdamW, because standard Adam incorrectly couples weight decay with gradient updates
RMSprop, for its handling of sparse gradients
standard.explanation: AdamW is the standard optimizer for transformers. The key insight was that the original Adam optimizer applied L2 regularization incorrectly -- the regularization term was scaled by Adam's adaptive learning rate, making it inconsistent across parameters. AdamW 'decouples' weight decay, applying it directly to weights rather than through the loss function. Standard practice uses weight_decay of 0.01-0.1 with learning rates of 1e-4 to 3e-4.
standard.deepDive: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) maintains running averages of both the gradient and the squared gradient for each parameter, using these to adaptively scale the learning rate. The problem with standard Adam was that its L2 regularisation (a technique to prevent overfitting) was incorrectly coupled with the adaptive learning rate: parameters with large gradients received less regularisation. AdamW fixes this by applying weight decay directly to the parameters, independent of the gradient computation. This 'decoupling' ensures consistent regularisation regardless of gradient history.

standard.question: What are the three distinct stages of modern LLM post-training (after pre-training)?
options: Pruning, quantization, deployment
SFT, preference optimization, and RL with verifiable rewards
Tokenization, embedding, and classification
Distillation, fine-tuning, and evaluation
standard.explanation: Modern post-training has evolved into three stages: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for instruction following, (2) Preference optimization (DPO/RLHF) for alignment with human preferences, and (3) RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for reasoning capabilities. The key 2025-era shift was from human-labeled rewards to automated verification and self-play, as demonstrated by DeepSeek-R1's emergent reasoning.
standard.deepDive: This three-stage pipeline represents the evolution of post-training from the original two-stage approach (SFT then RLHF). Stage 1 (SFT) teaches instruction following. Stage 2 (preference optimisation via DPO or RLHF) aligns with human preferences. Stage 3 (RLVR -- reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) was pioneered by DeepSeek-R1 and uses automated verification of correct answers to train reasoning capabilities. This third stage is the key 2025-era innovation: rather than relying on human judgments, it uses objective correctness as the training signal.

standard.question: What is RoPE (Rotary Positional Embedding) and why did it replace sinusoidal encodings?
options: A learned embedding table; it's more memory efficient
A rotation applied to query and key vectors in attention; it encodes relative position and generalizes better to longer contexts
A fixed binary encoding; it's faster to compute
A random projection; it prevents overfitting to position
standard.explanation: RoPE rotates query and key vectors based on their positions, so that the dot product between them depends on their relative distance. Unlike additive sinusoidal encodings, RoPE bakes position directly into the attention computation and generalizes better to longer contexts. Llama 3 uses RoPE with a base frequency of 500,000, enabling stable context windows up to 128K tokens.
standard.deepDive: RoPE encodes position by rotating the query (Q) and key (K) vectors by an angle proportional to their position in the sequence. When the model computes the dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n, the rotation means this dot product depends on the relative distance (m-n) rather than the absolute positions individually. The 'base frequency' parameter controls how quickly the rotations cycle: Llama 3 uses a base frequency of 500,000, which allows stable attention patterns across contexts up to 128K tokens, compared to Llama 2's base frequency of 10,000 which limited it to much shorter contexts.

standard.question: What is quantization in the context of LLM deployment, and what precision is commonly used?
options: Converting continuous outputs to discrete tokens; 8-bit
Reducing the numerical precision of model weights; 4-bit is common for deployment
Compressing the vocabulary size; 16-bit
Encrypting model weights for security; 128-bit
standard.explanation: Quantization reduces the precision of model weights from the 16-bit or 32-bit floats used during training to lower precisions like 8-bit or 4-bit integers. This dramatically reduces memory and speeds up inference. QLoRA combines 4-bit quantized weights with LoRA fine-tuning, saving ~33% GPU memory (though at ~39% increased training runtime). The key tradeoff is maintaining model quality despite lower precision.
standard.deepDive: During training, model weights are stored in 16-bit or 32-bit format for precise gradient computation. Quantization reduces these to 8-bit or even 4-bit format for deployment, shrinking the model by 4-8x and speeding up inference proportionally. The tradeoff is precision: a 32-bit float can represent about 4 billion distinct values, while a 4-bit integer represents only 16. Clever techniques like GPTQ, AWQ, and NF4 minimise quality loss by concentrating precision on the most important weight values. A 70B-parameter model shrinks from 140 GB in BF16 to about 35 GB at 4-bit, fitting on a single high-end consumer GPU.

standard.question: Kimi K2 (2025) pushed MoE to an unprecedented scale. How many total vs. active parameters does it have?
options: 100B total / 10B active
671B total / 37B active
1 trillion total / 32B active
2 trillion total / 100B active
standard.explanation: Kimi K2 has 1 trillion total parameters with only 32 billion active per token, using 384 experts with top-8 routing. Each expert sub-network contains approximately 4 billion parameters, and only about 2% of total weights are used at inference time. For comparison, DeepSeek-V3 uses 671B total / 37B active.
standard.deepDive: Kimi K2's trillion-parameter scale with only 32B active parameters represents a more extreme MoE design than DeepSeek-V3: K2 activates only about 3.2% of its total parameters per token, compared to DeepSeek-V3's 5.5%. With 384 experts and top-8 routing, each expert sub-network contains roughly 2.6 billion parameters. The practical implication is enormous knowledge capacity (the full trillion parameters) while maintaining inference costs comparable to a 32B dense model. This trend toward ever-larger MoE models with proportionally smaller active counts suggests the industry is finding ways to scale knowledge without proportionally scaling compute cost.

standard.question: Why is 'learning rate warmup' used at the start of transformer training?
options: To gradually load training data into GPU memory
To allow Adam's moment estimates to stabilize before making large parameter updates
To pre-compute the attention matrices
To test the training pipeline for bugs
standard.explanation: During warmup, the learning rate increases linearly from 0 over the first 1-5% of training steps. This is crucial because Adam's momentum estimates (first and second moments) are initialized to zero, making early gradient estimates unreliable. Starting with a high learning rate would destabilize attention weights. After warmup, a cosine schedule typically decays the learning rate back down.
standard.deepDive: Adam's first moment (running average of gradients) and second moment (running average of squared gradients) are both initialised to zero at the start of training. Since they are exponential moving averages, early values are biased toward zero because the averages have not yet accumulated enough history. If the learning rate is already high during this period, parameter updates will be based on unreliable gradient estimates, potentially destabilising training. The warmup period (typically the first 1-5% of steps) gradually increases the learning rate from near-zero, allowing Adam's moment estimates to stabilise before large updates are made.

standard.question: What is knowledge distillation?
options: Extracting key facts from a training corpus
Training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the outputs of a larger 'teacher' model
Removing redundant parameters from a neural network
Converting model weights to a different format
standard.explanation: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student model to reproduce the probability distributions (soft targets) of a larger teacher model, not just the hard labels. The soft targets contain rich information about inter-class similarities that hard labels lack. A common workflow in 2025 is to first prune a model, then quantize it, and use distillation to fine-tune and recover any lost performance.
standard.deepDive: Knowledge distillation, introduced by Geoffrey Hinton in 2015, exploits a key insight: the 'soft' probability distribution output by a teacher model contains far more information than hard labels. For example, when classifying an image of a '7', the teacher's output reveals that '7' looks somewhat like '1' and '2' -- inter-class similarity information that helps the student learn more efficiently. In the LLM context, distillation is commonly used after pruning and quantization to recover lost quality. DeepSeek-R1's reasoning capabilities were distilled into smaller models, producing the R1-Distill series that brought reasoning abilities to models small enough to run on consumer hardware.

standard.question: What is 'circuit breaking' in AI safety?
options: Shutting down GPUs when they overheat
Directly altering model representations to prevent harmful outputs, using representation engineering
Adding a separate safety classifier after generation
Limiting the model's context window for safety
standard.explanation: Circuit breakers are an adversarially robust alignment technique inspired by representation engineering. Rather than relying on RLHF or output filters, they directly alter harmful representations within the model to halt unsafe outputs before they're generated. This approach reduces harmful request compliance by 87-90% across models, making it significantly more robust against unseen attacks than traditional approaches.
standard.deepDive: Circuit breaking operates at a deeper level than RLHF or output filtering: rather than training the model to refuse harmful requests (which sophisticated attacks can circumvent) or filtering outputs after generation (which misses subtle content), it directly modifies internal representations that precede harmful generation. Using techniques from representation engineering, researchers identify the directions in the model's activation space that correspond to harmful behaviour, then apply transformations that project these representations into an orthogonal space. The reported 87-90% reduction in harmful compliance was measured against strong adversarial attacks that successfully bypassed RLHF-based defences.

standard.question: What is the typical vocabulary size of a modern frontier LLM, and how has it trended?
options: Around 5,000 tokens, staying stable
Around 30,000-50,000, staying stable
From ~32K to over 200K tokens, growing rapidly
Over 1 million tokens, growing rapidly
standard.explanation: Vocabulary sizes have grown dramatically: Llama 2 (2023) used 32K tokens, GPT-2 used ~50K, Llama 3 expanded to 128K tokens (100K tiktoken + 28K non-English), and Gemini 3 (2025) reportedly uses ~262K -- an 8x increase in three years. Larger vocabularies improve compression (Llama 3's tokenizer gets 3.94 characters/token vs. 3.17 for Llama 2) and handle multilingual text better.
standard.deepDive: Vocabulary size reflects a fundamental tradeoff: smaller vocabularies require more tokens per sentence (increasing compute cost) but each token is well-represented in training data, while larger vocabularies compress text better but require more embedding parameters. The dramatic growth from 32K (Llama 2) to 262K (Gemini 3) reflects the increasing importance of multilingual capabilities: languages with different scripts need dedicated tokens, and a 32K vocabulary must share its limited space among all languages. Llama 3's 128K vocabulary improved compression and multilingual performance substantially.

standard.question: Why is DeepSeek-V3's use of FP8 training significant?
options: FP8 is a new GPU architecture
It was the first to validate FP8 mixed-precision training at extreme scale, with loss error below 0.25% vs BF16
FP8 eliminates the need for gradient checkpointing
FP8 allows training without GPUs
standard.explanation: DeepSeek designed an FP8 mixed-precision training framework and validated it on their 671B-parameter model -- the first time FP8 training was shown to work at such extreme scale. The relative loss error compared to the BF16 (16-bit) baseline remained consistently below 0.25%, within normal training randomness. This achieved both faster training and reduced GPU memory usage, contributing to their remarkably low training cost.
standard.deepDive: Most AI training uses BF16 (16-bit) floating-point precision. FP8 uses only 8 bits, halving memory requirements and doubling NVIDIA Tensor Core throughput. The challenge is that 8 bits can represent only 256 distinct values (vs 65,536 for 16 bits), introducing rounding errors. DeepSeek's innovation was a mixed-precision framework using FP8 for bulk computation while maintaining higher precision for critical operations like gradient accumulation. The fact that quality loss was below 0.25% at 671B-parameter scale validated this approach for production use, meaning future training runs can get twice the computation from the same hardware.

standard.question: What architecture does Llama 3.1 405B use for its feed-forward layers?
options: Standard ReLU-activated FFN
GELU-activated FFN
SwiGLU-activated FFN
Sparse mixture of FFN experts
standard.explanation: Llama 3.1 uses SwiGLU activation in its feed-forward networks, replacing the older GELU. SwiGLU uses two linear layers with element-wise multiplication, where one branch passes through the Swish activation acting as a gate. This gating mechanism can model more complex interactions (even learning quadratic functions), and has been shown to produce better perplexity scores than GELU or ReLU in large models.
standard.deepDive: SwiGLU replaces the standard two-layer feed-forward network with a three-layer structure incorporating a learnable gate. In a standard FFN, the computation is y = W2 * GELU(W1 * x). SwiGLU changes this to y = W2 * (Swish(W1 * x) * W3 * x), where the Swish function on one branch acts as a gate for the other branch. This gating mechanism allows the network to selectively amplify or suppress features, enabling more complex interactions including quadratic functions. SwiGLU consistently produces better perplexity scores than ReLU, GELU, or other activations in large models.

standard.question: What did Epoch AI identify as a likely physical constraint on frontier training runs by around 2027?
options: Running out of training data
A 9-month training time limit
GPU memory ceiling
Internet bandwidth for distributed training
standard.explanation: Epoch AI found that frontier AI systems will hit a ~9-month training time limit by around 2027 (90% CI: 2025-2029). Beyond this duration, runs become impractical due to hardware failure rates, opportunity costs, and the pace of algorithmic improvement. If training time stops increasing, compute growth must come from larger clusters or multi-cluster training, rather than longer runs.
standard.deepDive: The 9-month training time limit reflects several practical constraints. Hardware failure rates compound over time: with tens of thousands of GPUs, individual component failures occur daily, requiring robust checkpointing. The opportunity cost of tying up a cluster becomes prohibitive as both hardware and algorithms improve. Competitive dynamics mean a model completed sooner can be deployed and generate revenue faster. If training duration stops increasing, further compute scaling must come from larger GPU clusters rather than longer runs.

standard.question: What is RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards)?
options: RL where a human verifies each reward signal
RL where correctness is automatically checked via programmatic verification (e.g., math/code execution)
RL using verified internet sources as reward
RL where the reward model is formally verified
standard.explanation: RLVR trains models on tasks where correctness can be automatically checked -- math problems verified by solution checking, code verified by execution, logical puzzles verified by constraint satisfaction. The reward signal comes from programmatic verification rather than a learned reward model. DeepSeek-R1 showed that pure RLVR can produce emergent reasoning capabilities, with the model spontaneously developing chain-of-thought.
standard.deepDive: RLVR differs from standard RLHF in a crucial way: instead of relying on a learned reward model to judge output quality, it uses programmatic verification -- checking math answers against solutions, executing code and checking test cases, verifying logical constraints. This eliminates the reward model as a source of error and reward hacking. DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated that training with RLVR alone can produce models that spontaneously develop chain-of-thought reasoning, self-correction, and backtracking behaviours, suggesting that clear success criteria are sufficient to elicit sophisticated problem-solving strategies.

standard.question: As of February 2026, which model leads on the GPQA-Diamond benchmark (expert-level science questions)?
options: GPT-5.3 Codex at 94.3%
Claude Opus 4.6 at 94.3%
Gemini 3.1 Pro at 94.3%
Qwen3.5-plus at 94.3%
standard.explanation: As of February 2026, Gemini 3.1 Pro leads GPQA-Diamond at 94.3%, followed by Claude Opus 4.6 at 91.3%, Qwen3.5-plus at 88.4%, and GPT-5.3 Codex at 81%. GPQA-Diamond tests expert-level graduate science questions and remains one of the harder benchmarks that isn't yet saturated, unlike GSM8K or CommonsenseQA.
standard.deepDive: GPQA-Diamond (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A) consists of expert-crafted science questions where even domain experts need significant time to answer, and the questions resist simple web searches. The 94.3% score by Gemini 3.1 Pro approaches domain-expert human performance, suggesting frontier models are nearing human-level on expert scientific reasoning. However, the multiple-choice format allows process of elimination, and newer benchmarks like HLE (Humanity's Last Exam) and ARC-AGI-2 continue to show substantial gaps between AI and human performance.

standard.question: What role does synthetic data play in frontier model pre-training as of 2025?
options: It has completely replaced web-crawled data
It works best when mixed with web data like Common Crawl, not used alone
It is only used for safety training, not pre-training
It performs worse than real data in all cases
standard.explanation: Research shows pure synthetic data doesn't outperform Common Crawl, and textbook-style synthetic data actually performs notably worse. However, mixing any type of synthetic data with web-crawled data substantially improves performance. In 2025, 'source rephrasing' became the dominant paradigm, with Kimi K2, Qwen-2.5, Grok, and GPT-5 all reporting meaningful gains from rephrasing web data with LLMs.
standard.deepDive: The finding that synthetic data works best when mixed with web data rather than used alone has important implications: synthetic data augments rather than replaces web crawling. 'Source rephrasing' -- using LLMs to rewrite web-crawled text in cleaner, more informative forms -- emerged as the dominant strategy because it combines real-world diversity with AI-generated quality. Pure synthetic data underperforms likely because it lacks diversity and real-world grounding: synthetic text tends to be formulaic and may reinforce the generating model's biases rather than providing genuinely new information.

standard.question: How many layers and attention heads does the Llama 3.1 405B model have?
options: 96 layers, 96 heads
126 layers, 128 heads
160 layers, 160 heads
80 layers, 64 heads
standard.explanation: Llama 3.1 405B uses 126 layers with 128 attention heads, a token representation dimension of 16,384, and 8 key-value heads (via GQA). It was trained for 30.84 million GPU hours total. The 128K-token vocabulary (100K tiktoken + 28K non-English tokens) improved compression from 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token.
standard.deepDive: The 126-layer depth and 128 attention heads make Llama 3.1 405B one of the deepest and widest transformers in production use. The 8 key-value heads (vs 128 query heads) implement a 16:1 GQA ratio, reducing KV cache memory by about 16x without significantly degrading quality. The hidden dimension of 16,384 means each token is represented as a 16,384-dimensional vector, with each attention head operating on 128-dimensional slices. The total 30.84 million GPU hours of training is equivalent to running about 16,000 H100 GPUs continuously for approximately 80 days.

standard.question: What happens during the supervised learning phase of Constitutional AI?
options: Humans label thousands of preference pairs
The model generates harmful responses, critiques them against principles, revises them, then is fine-tuned on the revisions
The model is trained on a curated safe dataset
A separate safety model filters training data
standard.explanation: In Constitutional AI's supervised phase, the model is deliberately prompted to generate harmful content, then generates self-critiques based on the constitution's principles, then generates revised (harmless) responses. The original model is fine-tuned on these revised responses. This is followed by the RLAIF phase, where AI-generated preference labels replace human raters for training the preference model.
standard.deepDive: The supervised learning phase of Constitutional AI deliberately generates harmful content as a starting point: the model is prompted with red-team-style queries. These harmful responses are critiqued by the model itself using constitutional principles, then revised. This critique-and-revise cycle can be repeated multiple times, progressively improving the response. The original model is fine-tuned on the final revised responses, teaching it to produce thoughtful, principled responses. This is followed by the RLAIF phase, which uses AI-generated preference comparisons to further refine the model.

standard.question: What is DAPO, and what problem does it address?
options: A data augmentation method for pre-training
A post-training technique addressing instability when training reasoning models with long chain-of-thought outputs
A distributed computing framework for parallelism
A new attention mechanism for document processing
standard.explanation: DAPO (from ByteDance/Tsinghua, 2025) tackles instabilities that arise when training reasoning models that produce very long chain-of-thought outputs. It introduces four techniques: Clip-Higher (to prevent reward collapse), Dynamic Sampling (to handle variable-length outputs), Token-level Policy Gradient Loss (for finer-grained optimization), and Overlong Reward Shaping (to handle extremely long generations).
standard.deepDive: DAPO addresses a specific instability in training reasoning models: these models produce very long chain-of-thought outputs (sometimes thousands of tokens) before reaching a final answer, and RL struggles to assign credit across such long sequences. Clip-Higher prevents 'reward collapse' by asymmetrically clipping the policy ratio. Dynamic Sampling handles enormous variation in reasoning chain lengths. Token-level Policy Gradient Loss applies the RL update at each token rather than per-sequence. Overlong Reward Shaping handles chains that exceed the maximum context window by providing shaped rewards rather than simply truncating.

standard.question: In the context of LLM training, what does the '6N' rule refer to?
options: 6 GPUs per node is optimal
It costs approximately 6 FLOPs per parameter per training token
Models should have 6 times as many neurons as layers
Training should run for 6 epochs
standard.explanation: The '6N' rule (from the Kaplan scaling laws) states that processing one training token through a model with N parameters costs approximately 6N floating-point operations (FLOPs) -- 2N for the forward pass multiplied by 3 (forward, backward for weights, backward for activations). So total training compute C is approximately 6 * N * D, where D is the number of training tokens.
standard.deepDive: The 6N rule can be derived from neural network computational structure: processing a single token through a transformer requires 2N operations for the forward pass (one multiply and one add per parameter), and approximately 4N for the backward pass (2N for activation gradients, 2N for weight gradients), totaling 6N per token. This formula is used extensively for planning training runs: total compute C = 6 x N x D, where N is parameters and D is training tokens. The Chinchilla scaling laws use this formula to determine optimal allocation of compute between N and D.

standard.question: What is the NVIDIA B200's expected performance improvement over the H100?
options: About 25% faster
About 2.5x faster in practical scenarios
About 10x faster
About the same speed but cheaper
standard.explanation: The NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell architecture) is expected to be approximately 2.5x faster than H100/H200 in most practical AI scenarios. As of 2026, B200 availability remains the primary constraint, with most supply allocated to hyperscalers who placed orders in 2024-2025, leaving new buyers facing 12-18 month wait times. Pricing ranges from $30,000-$70,000 per GPU.
standard.deepDive: The 2.5x practical speedup comes from several Blackwell architecture improvements: 208 billion transistors (vs H100's 80 billion), NVLink 5 doubling interconnect bandwidth to 1.8 TB/s, and HBM3e memory providing 8 TB/s bandwidth (vs 3.35 TB/s). The availability constraint is significant: despite shipping since late 2024, most B200 supply through 2025-2026 was allocated to hyperscale cloud providers who placed orders years in advance, creating 12-18 month waitlists for other buyers. Pricing ranges from $30,000-$70,000 per GPU.

standard.question: In the Kaplan et al. (2020) scaling laws, what are the approximate exponents for optimal allocation of compute between model size (N) and data (D)?
options: N^0.5 and D^0.5 (equal split)
N^0.73 and D^0.27 (favoring model size)
N^0.27 and D^0.73 (favoring data)
N^0.9 and D^0.1 (heavily favoring model size)
standard.explanation: Kaplan et al. found optimal exponents of ~0.73 for model size and ~0.27 for data, meaning compute should disproportionately go to making models bigger. This implied a tokens-per-parameter ratio of about 3. This was later overturned by Chinchilla, which found both should scale equally (exponent ~0.5 each), recommending ~20 tokens per parameter. The Kaplan exponents led to 'over-parameterized' models like GPT-3.
standard.deepDive: The Kaplan scaling laws proposed that loss L decreases as a power law with model size: L ~ N^(-0.076). The small exponent means diminishing returns are steep: to reduce loss by just 17%, you need a 10x increase in parameters. These power-law relationships held consistently across many orders of magnitude, suggesting scaling is governed by smooth, predictable laws. However, the Chinchilla paper later challenged the Kaplan exponents, finding both model size and data should scale roughly equally, rather than the 73/27 split Kaplan proposed.

standard.question: In DPO's mathematical derivation, why does the intractable partition function cancel out?
options: It's approximated using Monte Carlo sampling
When computing the reward difference between winning and losing responses, the partition function appears in both terms and cancels
It's set to 1 by assumption
It's absorbed into the KL divergence term
standard.explanation: DPO's critical insight: by reparameterizing the reward in terms of the policy and reference policy, the reward for any response contains a log-partition-function term Z. When you compute the preference probability (reward_win - reward_lose) under the Bradley-Terry model, the Z term appears identically in both and cancels completely. This is what makes the direct optimization approach feasible without needing to estimate Z.
standard.deepDive: The partition function Z is defined as the sum over all possible outputs of exp(reward/temperature), requiring evaluation of the reward for every possible text -- a number exceeding the atoms in the observable universe. DPO's insight is that when computing the Bradley-Terry preference probability P(y_win > y_lose), the expression becomes sigmoid(r_win - r_lose), where each r contains a +log(Z) term. Since both terms contain the same Z, the difference r_win - r_lose cancels Z entirely, converting an intractable optimisation into simple supervised learning.

standard.question: What is the mathematical formula for the cross-entropy loss used in next-token prediction?
options: L = sum(y * log(y_hat))
L = -sum(y * log(y_hat)), which for one-hot targets simplifies to -log(p(correct_token))
L = (y - y_hat)^2
L = |y - y_hat|
standard.explanation: The cross-entropy loss is L = -sum(y_i * log(p_i)) where y is the true distribution and p is the predicted distribution. Since the true distribution is one-hot (probability 1 on the correct next token, 0 elsewhere), this simplifies to -log(p(correct_token)). The model is penalized proportionally to how surprised it is by the actual next token. Perplexity is simply exp(average_loss).
standard.deepDive: The cross-entropy loss L = -sum(y_i * log(p_i)) compares the true distribution y (one-hot, with probability 1 on the correct next token) against the model's predicted distribution p. Since y is one-hot, this simplifies to -log(p(correct_token)). The model is penalised proportionally to how 'surprised' it is: assigning probability 0.01 yields a high loss of 4.6, while probability 0.9 yields a low loss of 0.1. Perplexity, the standard evaluation metric, is simply exp(average_loss), making it the geometric mean of inverse prediction probabilities.

standard.question: In multi-head attention, what are the Query, Key, and Value matrices conceptually doing?
options: Q finds relevant database entries, K indexes them, V returns the content
Q represents what each token is looking for, K represents what each token offers to be matched against, V represents the actual information to be passed if matched
Q encodes position, K encodes semantics, V encodes syntax
Q, K, V are interchangeable names for the same transformation
standard.explanation: The attention mechanism works like a soft lookup: Q (Query) represents what information each token is seeking, K (Key) represents what each token advertises it contains, and V (Value) represents the actual content to pass along. Attention scores are computed as softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), and these scores weight the V vectors. The sqrt(d_k) scaling prevents dot products from growing too large with high dimensions.
standard.deepDive: The attention mechanism works like a soft lookup: Q (Query) represents what information each token is seeking, K (Key) represents what each token advertises it contains, and V (Value) represents the actual content to pass along. Attention scores are computed as softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), and these scores weight the V vectors. The multi-head mechanism runs this process in parallel across multiple 'heads,' each with different Q, K, V projections, allowing the model to attend to different types of relationships simultaneously (syntactic, semantic, positional, etc.).

standard.question: Why is the attention score divided by sqrt(d_k) in the transformer?
options: To normalize for the number of attention heads
Because dot products of high-dimensional vectors grow with dimension, pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients
To account for the batch size
To convert from logits to probabilities
standard.explanation: When d_k (key dimension) is large, dot products tend to grow in magnitude proportional to sqrt(d_k), because they're sums of d_k random products. Large dot product values push the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients (saturation), making learning very slow. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the variance of the dot products at approximately 1, ensuring healthy gradient flow.
standard.deepDive: When d_k (key dimension) is large, dot products of random d_k-dimensional vectors have variance proportional to d_k, meaning their standard deviation grows as sqrt(d_k). For d_k = 128, dot products would have standard deviation about 11 times larger than for d_k = 1. Large values push the softmax into saturated regions where gradients are extremely small, making learning nearly impossible. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) rescales dot products to have approximately unit variance regardless of d_k, keeping softmax in its healthy gradient region.

standard.question: In RLHF with PPO, what typical target range is used for the adaptive KL penalty coefficient?
options: KL divergence of 0.001-0.01
KL divergence of 0.1-1.0
KL divergence of 3-10
KL divergence of 100-1000
standard.explanation: Many PPO-RLHF implementations use an adaptive KL controller that dynamically adjusts the penalty coefficient beta to keep the observed KL divergence within a target range of approximately 3-10 nats. Too low means the policy barely changes from the SFT model (underfitting); too high means the policy has drifted far enough to risk reward hacking and mode collapse.
standard.deepDive: The adaptive KL controller works by comparing the observed KL divergence after each training batch to a target value and adjusting the penalty coefficient accordingly. A KL of 3 means the model's output distribution has changed modestly from the SFT baseline; a KL of 10 means it has changed substantially. Going beyond 10 typically indicates reward hacking -- generating nonsensical outputs that exploit the reward model. The specific target range varies across implementations, with some using fixed coefficients instead of adaptive ones.

standard.question: What is the relationship between model parallelism strategies (tensor, pipeline, data) in large-scale training?
options: You use one strategy and it handles everything
Tensor parallelism splits within layers (intra-node), pipeline parallelism splits across layers (inter-node), data parallelism replicates the model across groups
They are different names for the same technique
Pipeline parallelism is only used for inference, not training
standard.explanation: Large-scale training uses all three: Tensor parallelism splits individual layer operations across GPUs within a node (requires high-bandwidth NVLink). Pipeline parallelism assigns different layers to different nodes (tolerates lower inter-node bandwidth). Data parallelism replicates the full model across groups and splits the batch. These compose hierarchically: e.g., 8-way tensor within a node, 16-way pipeline across nodes, 4-way data across pipeline replicas.
standard.deepDive: These three parallelism strategies address different bottlenecks. Tensor parallelism splits individual layer operations across GPUs within a single server, requiring the highest bandwidth (NVLink). Pipeline parallelism assigns different layer groups to different servers, tolerating higher latency (InfiniBand). Data parallelism replicates the entire model across groups and splits the training data. These compose hierarchically: for example, Llama 3.1 405B training used 8-way tensor within each server, 16-way pipeline across servers, and data parallelism across pipeline replicas.

standard.question: How does SwiGLU differ from standard feed-forward networks in transformers, structurally?
options: It uses three linear transformations instead of two, with one branch gated by the Swish activation
It replaces linear layers with convolutions
It adds a residual connection inside the FFN
It uses dropout instead of activation functions
standard.explanation: A standard FFN has two linear transformations with an activation in between: FFN(x) = W2 * activation(W1 * x). SwiGLU uses THREE linear transformations: SwiGLU(x) = W2 * (Swish(W1 * x) elementwise_multiply W3 * x). The Swish(W1*x) branch acts as a learned gate for the W3*x branch. This gating mechanism lets the network learn which features to pass through, enabling more complex interactions including quadratic functions.
standard.deepDive: The structural difference is that a standard FFN has two weight matrices while SwiGLU has three. In SwiGLU, the input x is processed through two parallel paths: W1*x passes through the Swish activation, and W3*x passes through unmodified. These are combined by element-wise multiplication, and the result is projected back by W2. The Swish path acts as a learned gate controlling how much information passes to the output. Because the gate is multiplicative, the network can learn quadratic functions of its input, which standard FFNs with a single activation cannot do.

standard.question: What compute was used to train GPT-4, and how does it compare to the threshold Epoch AI considers 'frontier scale'?
options: ~2x10^23 FLOP, well below the 10^25 threshold
~2x10^25 FLOP, roughly at the 10^25 threshold that defines frontier scale
~2x10^27 FLOP, well above frontier scale
~2x10^20 FLOP, far below any notable threshold
standard.explanation: GPT-4's pre-training used approximately 2.15 x 10^25 FLOP. Epoch AI uses 10^25-10^26 FLOP as a rough threshold for frontier-scale models. The first model estimated above 10^26 FLOP was Grok-3 (February 2025). By 2026, Epoch AI projected about 10 models would exceed 10^26 FLOP, growing to 80+ by 2028.
standard.deepDive: GPT-4's estimated 2.15 x 10^25 FLOP places it close to the 10^25 threshold Epoch AI uses for 'frontier scale.' The first model above 10^26 FLOP was xAI's Grok-3 (February 2025). By 2026, Epoch AI projected about 10 models above 10^26, growing to 80+ by 2028. The rapid pace at which the frontier advances means governance thresholds based on absolute compute levels have limited useful lifespan -- what qualifies as 'frontier' today will be routine within a few years.

standard.question: In the original Transformer paper, what is the formula for scaled dot-product attention?
options: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T) * V
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V
Attention(Q,K,V) = sigmoid(QK^T / d_k) * V
Attention(Q,K,V) = ReLU(QK^T) * V / sqrt(d_k)
standard.explanation: The exact formula is Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where d_k is the dimension of the key vectors. The QK^T computes attention scores (which tokens attend to which), softmax normalizes them to probabilities, and multiplication by V produces the weighted combination of value vectors. The 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling prevents gradient vanishing in the softmax.
standard.deepDive: Breaking down the formula: QK^T computes dot products between every query and every key, producing an N x N matrix of attention scores. Division by sqrt(d_k) prevents these scores from becoming too large and saturating softmax. The softmax converts each row into a probability distribution. Multiplying by V takes a weighted average of value vectors according to these probabilities. The result is that each token's output representation is a mixture of all other tokens' information, weighted by how relevant each token's key is to the current token's query.

standard.question: What is the 'over-training' strategy used by models like Llama 3.1 405B, and why is it done?
options: Training past the point of convergence to improve generalization
Training on far more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal (15.6T tokens for 405B params vs the ~8T Chinchilla would recommend) to reduce inference cost
Using excessive data augmentation
Running multiple training epochs on the same data
standard.explanation: Chinchilla optimization minimizes training compute for a given quality level. But inference cost depends on model size, not training data. By 'over-training' a smaller model on more data, you get similar quality to a larger Chinchilla-optimal model but with cheaper inference. Llama 3.1 405B used 15.6T tokens (~38 tokens/parameter vs Chinchilla's ~20), deliberately spending more on training to make the deployed model more efficient.
standard.deepDive: The over-training strategy exploits an asymmetry between training and inference cost. Training cost is proportional to parameters times tokens (C = 6*N*D). Inference cost per token is proportional to roughly 2*N (just parameters). A Chinchilla-optimal 800B model would have similar quality to a 405B model over-trained on more data, but the 405B model costs about half as much per query. Since a deployed model may serve billions of queries, the savings from a smaller model far outweigh the extra training cost.

standard.question: What precision format do most frontier models use during pre-training, and why?
options: FP32 (32-bit float) for maximum accuracy
BF16 (bfloat16) because it has the same exponent range as FP32 but halves memory
INT8 (8-bit integer) for speed
FP64 (64-bit double) for numerical stability
standard.explanation: BF16 (Brain Floating Point 16) is the standard for pre-training. It uses 8 exponent bits (same as FP32) and 7 mantissa bits, giving it the same dynamic range as FP32 but with half the memory and bandwidth. FP16 has only 5 exponent bits, making it prone to overflow/underflow during training. DeepSeek-V3 pioneered FP8 for training, but BF16 remains the baseline most models compare against.
standard.deepDive: BF16 (Brain Floating Point 16, developed by Google Brain) uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 7 mantissa bits, giving it the same dynamic range as FP32. Standard FP16 uses 5 exponent bits, limiting its range and causing frequent overflow and underflow during training. BF16 avoids these issues entirely by matching FP32's range, at the cost of less mantissa precision (7 bits vs FP16's 10), which has been found to be an acceptable tradeoff. DeepSeek-V3 pioneered FP8 for training, but BF16 remains the standard baseline.

standard.question: What properties did Anthropic find worked best for constitutional principles?
options: Long, detailed rules covering every edge case
Short, broad principles that large models could generalize from
Principles written in formal logic notation
Principles derived from user surveys
standard.explanation: Anthropic found that short and broad principles worked better than long and specific ones. Large dialogue models can generalize effectively from a concise constitution. The current Claude constitution draws from sources including the UN Declaration of Human Rights, trust and safety best practices, DeepMind's Sparrow Principles, non-western perspectives, and empirically effective principles. An updated 80-page constitution was published in January 2026.
standard.deepDive: Anthropic experimented with constitutions of varying specificity and found that shorter, more general principles consistently outperformed longer, more detailed ones. The likely mechanism is that large language models have extensive world knowledge and can infer the implications of broad principles without needing them spelled out. The current Claude constitution draws from diverse sources including the UN Declaration of Human Rights, trust and safety best practices, and non-Western perspectives to avoid cultural bias. An expanded 80-page version published in January 2026 provided more detailed guidance while maintaining broad, generalisable rules.

standard.question: In FlashAttention's tiling algorithm, what are the two levels of GPU memory hierarchy being optimized?
options: CPU RAM and GPU RAM
GPU HBM (high-bandwidth memory) and on-chip SRAM
L1 cache and L2 cache
System memory and SSD storage
standard.explanation: FlashAttention optimizes data movement between GPU HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory, the main GPU memory -- large but slower) and on-chip SRAM (small but very fast, located directly on the GPU chip). Standard attention materializes the full N x N attention matrix in HBM. FlashAttention tiles the computation so that each tile fits in SRAM, avoiding the costly HBM round-trips. This is purely an IO optimization -- the math is identical.
standard.deepDive: GPU memory exists in two tiers: HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory, 80 GB on H100, ~3.35 TB/s bandwidth) is the main memory, large enough for model weights and intermediate results. On-chip SRAM (~20 MB on H100, ~20 TB/s bandwidth) is much smaller but dramatically faster. Standard attention materialises the full N x N attention matrix in HBM, requiring O(N^2) memory reads and writes. FlashAttention restructures the computation into tiles that fit entirely in SRAM, never materialising the full matrix in HBM. Since HBM access is the bottleneck, this IO-optimisation achieves 2-4x speedups.

standard.question: What is ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) and how does it differ from RoPE?
options: ALiBi uses learned position embeddings; RoPE uses fixed ones
ALiBi removes input-layer positional embeddings and adds position-dependent biases directly to attention scores; RoPE rotates Q and K vectors
ALiBi and RoPE are identical methods with different names
ALiBi is for vision transformers; RoPE is for language models
standard.explanation: ALiBi completely removes traditional positional embeddings from the input layer. Instead, it adds a linear bias to attention scores based on the distance between tokens: closer tokens get higher scores, with the slope varying per head. RoPE, by contrast, rotates query and key vectors so their dot product depends on relative position. Both encode relative position, but through different mechanisms. Most frontier LLMs in 2025 use RoPE.
standard.deepDive: ALiBi adds a negative linear bias to attention scores based on distance: if tokens are d positions apart, a penalty of -m*d is added (where m is a head-specific slope). This naturally makes the model attend less to distant tokens. RoPE instead rotates query and key vectors in a complex-valued space, with the dot product depending only on positional difference. Both encode relative position, but RoPE has become dominant because it generalises better to context lengths much longer than those seen during training. Most frontier LLMs in 2025-2026 use RoPE.

standard.question: Why is Anthropic's characterization of RLAIF data as 'low-noise, high-bias' significant?
options: It means AI feedback is always better than human feedback
It means AI feedback is easy to scale but can introduce systematic biases that human data wouldn't have
It means the data is more accurate than human labels
It means the data requires less storage
standard.explanation: Anthropic characterizes human preference data as 'high-noise, low-bias' -- hard to collect consistently but provides reliable signal. AI feedback is 'low-noise, high-bias' -- easy to generate at scale with consistent formatting, but can have systematic blind spots that are uniformly represented in the data. This means RLAIF scales better but can produce tricky second-order effects from the teacher model's own biases.
standard.deepDive: The noise/bias tradeoff maps to a fundamental statistics distinction: high-noise data has high variance (different annotators rate differently) but low systematic error. High-bias data has low variance (AI evaluator is consistent) but may have systematic errors uniformly present in every rating. For training, this means RLAIF can scale cheaply and consistently, but any systematic blind spot of the AI evaluator will be uniformly reinforced across the entire training set. This makes RLAIF-trained models potentially more susceptible to systematic failure modes that are harder to detect.

standard.question: What is the 'Bradley-Terry model' used in preference-based LLM training?
options: A neural network architecture for reward modeling
A statistical model where the probability of preferring response A over B is a logistic function of the difference in their latent reward scores
A method for generating training data
A technique for model compression
standard.explanation: The Bradley-Terry model is the most popular statistical model for preferences in LLM training. It posits P(A preferred over B) = sigmoid(r(A) - r(B)), where r is a latent reward function. Both RLHF (for training the reward model) and DPO (for direct optimization) are grounded in Bradley-Terry. DPO's key trick is expressing r in terms of the policy itself, eliminating the need for a separate reward model.
standard.deepDive: The Bradley-Terry model, originally developed in 1952 for comparing chess players, assumes each response has a latent quality score, with preference probability being a logistic function of score differences: P(A > B) = sigmoid(r(A) - r(B)). In RLHF, the reward model is trained to output these latent scores. In DPO, the same model is used but the reward is expressed directly in terms of log-probability ratios between the policy and reference model. The framework's assumption that preferences are transitive may not always hold for human preferences, motivating exploration of alternative models.

standard.question: What specific power consumption challenge does Epoch AI project for frontier training by 2030?
options: 100 megawatts per training run
4-16 gigawatts per training run, enough to power millions of US homes
1 terawatt per training run
Power will no longer be a constraint due to nuclear fusion
standard.explanation: Epoch AI projects that by 2030, individual frontier training runs will likely draw 4-16 gigawatts (GW) of power. For context, a typical US nuclear power plant produces about 1 GW, and a GW can power roughly 750,000 homes. The power required for the largest training runs has been growing by more than 2x per year, making energy one of the fundamental constraints on scaling.
standard.deepDive: The 4-16 GW range by 2030 is derived from extrapolating current compute growth trends. A single gigawatt is approximately the output of one large nuclear power plant and can power roughly 750,000 American homes. Practical constraints make these projections uncertain: building 16 GW of dedicated power generation requires years of construction, grid infrastructure must deliver that power to a single location, and the cooling requirements are unprecedented. Energy availability is increasingly seen as the primary physical constraint on AI scaling.

standard.question: What are ARC-AGI-2 and Pencil Puzzle Bench designed to prevent that plagues older benchmarks?
options: Overly easy questions
Data contamination -- they use tasks that are novel by construction
Bias toward English speakers
Excessive computational requirements
standard.explanation: ARC-AGI-2 and Pencil Puzzle Bench are specifically designed to be contamination-resistant: their tasks are novel by construction, meaning they cannot appear in training data. This is crucial because benchmark contamination is well-documented for older tests -- frontier models achieve near-90% on HumanEval, but training set contamination inflates scores. On these contamination-resistant benchmarks, Chinese frontier models score at the level Western models achieved 6-8 months earlier.
standard.deepDive: Data contamination occurs when test questions appear in the model's training data, artificially inflating scores. ARC-AGI-2 addresses this with novel visual pattern-recognition tasks that are procedurally generated and never published before testing. Pencil Puzzle Bench uses algorithmically generated logic puzzles unique by construction. These benchmarks provide more honest capability assessments: on contamination-resistant benchmarks, Chinese frontier models score at the level Western models achieved 6-8 months earlier, suggesting some apparent performance gaps on older benchmarks may be artificial.

standard.question: In the LoRA paper, approximately what rank (r) is typically used, and why does it work?
options: r = 1024, because large ranks are needed for good performance
r = 4 to 64, because weight updates during fine-tuning are empirically low-rank
r = 1, because a single dimension captures all task-specific information
r = 4096, matching the model's hidden dimension
standard.explanation: LoRA typically uses ranks of 4 to 64. The key insight is that weight changes during fine-tuning are empirically low-rank -- the update matrix delta_W can be well-approximated by a product of two small matrices A (d x r) and B (r x d) where r << d. This means fine-tuning doesn't need to move all parameters independently; the changes live in a low-dimensional subspace. This is why LoRA can reduce trainable parameters by 10,000x with minimal quality loss.
standard.deepDive: The key theoretical justification for LoRA is the 'intrinsic dimensionality' hypothesis: fine-tuning does not require moving all parameters independently but rather along a low-dimensional subspace. The rank r determines this subspace's dimension: r=4 is sufficient for simple tasks, with diminishing returns beyond r=64. Instead of storing a separate full model for each fine-tuned specialisation, you store the base model once and swap in tiny LoRA adapters (often less than 100 MB each) at serving time, making it feasible to serve dozens of specialised variants from a single base model.

standard.question: In the Chinchilla paper, how many models were trained to determine the optimal scaling laws, and over what parameter range?
options: 50 models from 1M to 1B parameters
Over 400 models from 70M to over 16B parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens
10 models from 1B to 100B parameters
1000 models from 100K to 10B parameters
standard.explanation: Hoffmann et al. trained over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens to establish the Chinchilla scaling laws. This systematic sweep across both model sizes and data quantities was far more comprehensive than the Kaplan study, which had models clustered at smaller scales. The breadth of this sweep is what gave the Chinchilla results their authority.
standard.deepDive: The scale of the Chinchilla study -- over 400 models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens -- was far more comprehensive than the Kaplan study. Kaplan et al. had trained fewer models clustered at smaller sizes, which may have biased findings toward overweighting model size. The systematic sweep across both axes gave Chinchilla's 20-tokens-per-parameter rule high confidence. The implications were stark: GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) should have used roughly 3.5 trillion tokens, and Google's Gopher (280B params) should have used about 5.6 trillion.

standard.question: In DeepSeek-V3's FP8 training framework, what was the maximum relative loss error compared to the BF16 baseline?
options: Below 0.025%
Below 0.25%
Below 2.5%
Below 25%
standard.explanation: DeepSeek reported that the relative loss error of their FP8-trained model remained consistently below 0.25% compared to the BF16 baseline, a level they described as well within the acceptable range of normal training randomness. This was the first validation of FP8 training at the scale of a 671B-parameter model, demonstrating that the 2x memory and compute savings of FP8 don't come at a meaningful quality cost.
standard.deepDive: The 0.25% relative loss error means the FP8-trained model's loss differed from the BF16-trained model's by less than 0.25%, indistinguishable from normal run-to-run variation. This validation was critical because the research community had been sceptical about FP8 precision at extreme scale, where small numerical errors can compound across billions of operations. DeepSeek's success demonstrated that carefully designed mixed-precision frameworks (FP8 for bulk computation, higher precision for sensitive operations) achieve the theoretical 2x speedup without meaningful quality degradation.

standard.question: What is the exact RoPE base frequency used in Llama 3, and what context length does it support?
options: 10,000; supports 4K tokens
100,000; supports 32K tokens
500,000; supports 128K tokens
1,000,000; supports 256K tokens
standard.explanation: Llama 3 uses RoPE with a base frequency of 500,000, which supports stable context windows up to 128K tokens. The base frequency determines how quickly the rotary embeddings cycle through their period. Higher base frequencies allow the model to distinguish positions at greater distances. Earlier models like Llama 2 used much lower base frequencies (10,000) and were limited to shorter contexts.
standard.deepDive: The RoPE base frequency determines the period of the rotational encoding: higher values mean rotation angles increase more slowly with position, allowing the model to maintain distinct representations for distant tokens. With base frequency 10,000 (Llama 2), encoding patterns repeat at around 4,096 positions. Llama 3's base frequency of 500,000 extends this by 50x. The base frequency acts as a tradeoff parameter: very high values support long contexts but may slightly reduce sensitivity to fine-grained positional relationships between nearby tokens.

standard.question: What are the four specific techniques DAPO introduces to stabilize training of reasoning models?
options: Gradient clipping, batch normalization, dropout, early stopping
Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, Token-level Policy Gradient Loss, Overlong Reward Shaping
Reward scaling, value normalization, entropy bonus, GAE lambda
Curriculum learning, progressive resizing, warmup restarts, gradient accumulation
standard.explanation: DAPO (ByteDance/Tsinghua, 2025) introduces: (1) Clip-Higher -- prevents reward collapse by asymmetrically clipping the policy ratio, (2) Dynamic Sampling -- handles variable-length chain-of-thought outputs during training, (3) Token-level Policy Gradient Loss -- applies finer-grained optimization at each token rather than per-sequence, and (4) Overlong Reward Shaping -- specifically handles extremely long generations that exceed context limits.
standard.deepDive: Each DAPO technique addresses a specific failure mode. Clip-Higher modifies PPO's clipping by asymmetrically widening the upper bound, preventing the policy from becoming overly conservative. Dynamic Sampling adjusts batch composition for extreme variation in chain-of-thought lengths. Token-level Policy Gradient Loss replaces per-sequence rewards with per-token credit assignment, identifying which specific reasoning steps caused success or failure. Overlong Reward Shaping provides graduated penalties for reasoning chains approaching context limits, rather than harsh truncation.

standard.question: In the leaked GPT-4 architecture details, how many MoE experts are used and how many are routed per forward pass?
options: 8 experts, 1 routed
16 experts, 2 routed
64 experts, 4 routed
128 experts, 8 routed
standard.explanation: According to widely reported leaks (never confirmed by OpenAI), GPT-4 uses a Mixture of Experts architecture with 16 experts, each with ~111B MLP parameters, routing 2 experts per forward pass. This means the ~1.8T total parameters yield an effective forward-pass cost closer to a ~220B dense model. This was a sharp contrast to GPT-3's fully dense 175B architecture.
standard.deepDive: The 16-expert, 2-routed architecture means each token passes through 2 of 16 expert networks, plus shared attention layers. Each expert's MLP has roughly 111 billion parameters. The forward-pass cost is approximately that of a 220B dense model (2 experts x 111B each, plus shared attention), giving GPT-4 the knowledge capacity of 1.8T parameters with the speed of a much smaller model. The GPT-3-to-GPT-4 transition from dense to MoE was a fundamental architectural shift enabling a massive capability jump without proportional inference cost increase.

standard.question: What specific improvement does FlashAttention-3 make over FlashAttention-2 for Hopper (H100) GPUs?
options: It uses sparse attention patterns
It exploits asynchronous tensor cores and TMA for overlapping computation with data movement via warp-specialization, plus FP8 block quantization
It reduces attention to linear complexity
It replaces softmax with ReLU
standard.explanation: FlashAttention-3 develops three techniques specific to Hopper GPUs: (1) exploiting asynchrony between Tensor Cores and the TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) to overlap computation and data movement via warp-specialization, (2) block quantization leveraging hardware FP8 support for faster attention computation, and (3) incoherent processing to maintain accuracy despite lower precision. These are hardware-specific optimizations absent in FlashAttention-2.
standard.deepDive: FlashAttention-3 was designed to exploit Hopper GPU (H100) features unavailable when FlashAttention-2 was developed.
