special.question: Why was the Gutenberg printing press (c. 1440) so historically transformative?
options: It enabled mass text production, catalyzing the Reformation, Scientific Revolution, and widespread literacy
It was the first machine with interchangeable parts, launching the Industrial Revolution
It primarily benefited the Catholic Church by controlling Bible production
It replaced manuscripts but had little social impact for the first century
special.explanation: By 1500, ~20 million volumes had been printed. Luther's 95 Theses spread in weeks; scientific knowledge could be shared and verified; literacy expanded beyond clergy; standardized texts enabled standardized languages. Eisenstein argued it was key to both the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution.

special.question: What was the Scramble for Africa (1881-1914)?
options: The rapid colonization of nearly all of Africa by European powers, formalized at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885
A series of African nationalist movements that overthrew colonial rulers
Competition between African kingdoms for control of trans-Saharan trade
Mass European settlement of North Africa following the Suez Canal opening
special.explanation: In 1870, ~10% of Africa was under European control; by 1914, ~90%, with only Ethiopia and Liberia independent. The Berlin Conference set rules without African representation. Borders ignored ethnic boundaries. The artificial borders and extractive institutions continue to affect African politics today.

special.question: What was the Green Revolution, and what were its trade-offs?
options: High-yield crop varieties developed in the 1960s-70s averted mass famine but increased dependence on chemical inputs and favored large farmers
A global environmental movement in the 1970s that created the EPA and Greenpeace
The Soviet Union's agricultural collectivization under Stalin
China's reforestation campaign planting billions of trees in the late 20th century
special.explanation: Norman Borlaug (Nobel Peace Prize 1970) introduced high-yield wheat and rice, saving over a billion from starvation. Trade-offs: dependence on fertilizers/pesticides, soil degradation, reduced crop diversity, and benefits disproportionately favoring larger farmers.

special.question: Beyond military conquest, what was the Mongol Empire's significance for world history?
options: The Pax Mongolica enabled unprecedented trade and transfer of technologies like gunpowder and printing between East and West
It permanently isolated China from the rest of the world by reinforcing the Great Wall
It introduced feudalism to Asia, replacing earlier democratic traditions
It destroyed the Silk Road and ended all Eurasian trade for centuries
special.explanation: The largest contiguous land empire created the Pax Mongolica (~1250-1350), enabling safe passage for merchants and the transfer of gunpowder, printing, and the compass from East to West. However, Mongol trade routes also enabled the Black Death to spread to Europe in the 1340s.

special.question: What was the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)?
options: An agreement dividing newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal along an Atlantic meridian
A peace treaty ending the Hundred Years' War between England and France
A trade agreement giving Venice exclusive Eastern Mediterranean commerce rights
An alliance between the Papal States and Holy Roman Empire against the Ottomans
special.explanation: The treaty drew a line ~370 leagues west of Cape Verde. East to Portugal, west to Spain. This is why Brazil speaks Portuguese while the rest of South America speaks Spanish. Breathtakingly presumptuous -- two nations and the Pope dividing the non-European world -- and ignored by England, France, and the Netherlands.

special.question: How did the Black Death (1347-1353) transform European society beyond the immediate death toll?
options: Labor shortages improved conditions for surviving peasants, weakening feudalism and shifting economic power
It killed about 5% of the population concentrated in cities, accelerating urbanization
It primarily affected nobility, leading directly to the rise of merchant classes
It had enormous death toll but little lasting social impact as population recovered within a decade
special.explanation: The Black Death killed 30-60% of Europe's population. The labor shortage transformed society: peasants demanded higher wages, serfdom declined, feudalism weakened. It also triggered religious upheaval and artistic changes. Some historians argue it was a key precondition for the Renaissance and capitalism.

special.question: What was the Defenestration of Prague (1618), and what did it trigger?
options: Protestant nobles threw Catholic imperial governors out a castle window, triggering the Thirty Years' War
Catholic forces destroyed Prague's Protestant churches, sparking the Hussite Wars
Czech nationalists assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, starting World War I
An earthquake collapsed Prague's government buildings during a constitutional crisis
special.explanation: On May 23, 1618, Bohemian Protestant nobles threw two Catholic regents out a third-floor window (they survived, landing in dung). This sparked the Bohemian Revolt, escalating into the Thirty Years' War. It was actually the third Defenestration of Prague (after 1419 and 1483) -- something of a Czech political tradition.

special.question: What made the Fourth Crusade (1202-1204) so historically notorious?
options: Crusaders never reached the Holy Land and instead sacked Constantinople, capital of their fellow Christian Byzantine Empire
It was the only Crusade to permanently capture and hold Jerusalem
Muslim and Christian forces formed an unprecedented alliance against the Mongols
It established the first lasting peace treaty between Christendom and Islam
special.explanation: Originally aimed at Egypt, the Crusaders became entangled in Venetian politics and Byzantine disputes. They brutally sacked Constantinople, destroying countless ancient artworks. The sack fatally weakened the Byzantine Empire, contributing to its fall to the Ottomans in 1453.

special.question: What was the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864)?
options: A massive Chinese civil war led by a man claiming to be Jesus's brother, killing 20-30 million people
A peasant uprising in India against the British East India Company
A Japanese civil war between imperial and shogunate forces preceding the Meiji Restoration
A religious war in the Ottoman Empire between Sunni and Sufi factions
special.explanation: Hong Xiuquan believed he was Jesus Christ's younger brother. His Taiping Heavenly Kingdom controlled large parts of southern China with radical policies: communal property, gender equality, banning opium. Its suppression killed 20-30 million -- comparable to WWI -- yet receives little Western attention.

special.question: What was the significance of the Battle of Carrhae (53 BC)?
options: Parthian horse archers decisively defeated Roman legions under Crassus, demonstrating the limits of Roman expansion eastward
Rome's first major naval victory, establishing Mediterranean dominance
Julius Caesar's first major military triumph during the Gallic Wars
Alexander the Great's decisive victory securing his eastern conquests
special.explanation: Crassus lost ~20,000 legionaries to Parthian mounted archers using the 'Parthian shot' (firing backward while retreating -- origin of 'parting shot'). Crassus was killed, captured standards became a national humiliation, and the battle effectively set Rome's eastern boundary.

special.question: What was the Enclosure Movement in England, and how did it contribute to industrialization?
options: Privatization of common lands displaced rural peasants, creating the landless labor force that powered factories
Construction of city walls to defend against foreign invasion concentrated populations
Enclosure of forests as royal hunting grounds sparked peasant rebellions leading to reform
Dissolution of monasteries during the Reformation redistributed Church agricultural wealth
special.explanation: The Enclosure Movement consolidated communal fields into private plots. This increased efficiency but dispossessed millions who depended on common land. Displaced workers migrated to cities, forming the factory labor pool. Marx called it 'primitive accumulation of capital' -- increased productivity at enormous human cost.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The original Transformer paper 'Attention Is All You Need' was published by Google researchers in 2017
GPT stands for 'Generative Pre-trained Transformer'
The BERT model was trained on Wikipedia and BookCorpus datasets
The Transformer architecture was first developed at OpenAI before being adopted by Google
special.explanation: The Transformer architecture was introduced by Google Brain researchers in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need'. OpenAI later adopted it for the GPT series, not the other way around.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly sets neuron outputs to zero during training
Batch normalization normalizes the inputs to each layer to have zero mean and unit variance
The ReLU activation function returns zero for negative inputs and the input value for positive inputs
The softmax function was invented specifically for neural networks by Geoffrey Hinton in 1986
special.explanation: The softmax function has roots in statistical mechanics and the Boltzmann distribution, predating neural networks. It was not invented by Hinton. It has been used in various mathematical contexts long before modern deep learning.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: AlexNet won the ImageNet competition in 2012 with a top-5 error rate of about 15.3%
ResNet introduced skip connections that allow gradients to flow through shortcut paths
The original GAN paper by Ian Goodfellow was published in 2014
Convolutional neural networks were first successfully trained using the Adam optimizer by Yann LeCun in 1989
special.explanation: The Adam optimizer was not introduced until 2014 by Kingma and Ba. LeCun's early CNN work in 1989 used stochastic gradient descent, not Adam.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: RLHF stands for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
Temperature in language model sampling controls the randomness of token selection
Top-k sampling limits token selection to the k most probable next tokens
Chain-of-thought prompting was first described in a 2019 paper by researchers at DeepMind
special.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting was introduced in a 2022 paper by Jason Wei and others at Google Brain, not in 2019 by DeepMind.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Word2Vec demonstrated that vector arithmetic on word embeddings could capture semantic relationships like king - man + woman = queen
The vanishing gradient problem makes it difficult to train deep networks because gradients shrink exponentially through layers
LSTM networks use forget gates, input gates, and output gates to control information flow
Backpropagation was first applied to neural networks by Yann LeCun in his 1985 doctoral thesis
special.explanation: Backpropagation's application to neural networks is most commonly attributed to Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in their famous 1986 paper. LeCun made major contributions to CNNs, but he did not introduce backpropagation for neural networks.

special.question: Approximately how many parameters does Meta's Llama 2 largest model have?
special.explanation: Meta's Llama 2 was released in July 2023 with models at 7B, 13B, and 70B parameters. The largest variant has 70 billion parameters.

special.question: How many H100 GPUs did Meta reportedly order in 2024?
special.explanation: Meta reportedly ordered around 350,000 H100 GPUs from NVIDIA in 2024, making it one of the largest single purchasers of AI accelerators.

special.question: Approximately how much did it cost to train GPT-4, according to reports?
special.explanation: The training cost of GPT-4 has been widely reported to be approximately $100 million, based on estimates from Sam Altman and industry analysts.

special.question: How many tokens was Llama 2 (70B) trained on?
special.explanation: Llama 2 was trained on 2 trillion tokens according to Meta's technical paper, a significant increase from the 1.4 trillion tokens used for the original Llama.

special.question: Approximately how many research papers were submitted to the NeurIPS 2023 conference?
special.explanation: NeurIPS 2023 received approximately 13,300 paper submissions, reflecting the explosive growth in AI research.

special.riddle: I pay attention to everything at once, weigh what matters most, and helped end the reign of recurrence. What am I?
options: Convolutional layer
Self-attention mechanism
Recurrent neural network
Batch normalization
special.explanation: The self-attention mechanism, core to the Transformer, attends to all positions simultaneously (pays attention to everything at once), computes attention weights (weighs what matters), and replaced recurrent architectures.

special.riddle: I am two networks locked in an eternal game. One creates forgeries, the other detects them, and together we produce art from nothing. What are we?
options: Autoencoder
Generative Adversarial Network
Variational inference
Diffusion model
special.explanation: A GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) consists of a generator and discriminator in an adversarial game, where the generator learns to create realistic outputs and the discriminator learns to detect fakes.

special.riddle: I remember what to forget. I have three gates but no fence. Without me, long sequences would lose their way. What am I?
options: Transformer block
LSTM cell
Convolutional filter
Attention head
special.explanation: An LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) cell has three gates: forget gate, input gate, and output gate. The forget gate literally decides what to forget. LSTMs were designed to handle long sequences where vanilla RNNs struggle.

special.riddle: I start with noise and slowly sculpt it into an image, removing chaos step by step until beauty emerges. What process am I?
options: Diffusion model denoising
GAN training
Neural style transfer
Image segmentation
special.explanation: Diffusion models generate images by starting with pure noise and iteratively denoising it step by step until a coherent image emerges. This is the process used by Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2, and similar models.

special.riddle: I travel backward through a network, telling each connection how wrong it was and nudging it toward the truth. What am I?
options: Forward propagation
Backpropagation
Gradient clipping
Weight initialization
special.explanation: Backpropagation travels backward through the network computing gradients of the loss with respect to each weight, indicating how much each connection contributed to the error, and then adjusts the weights accordingly.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The term 'paperclip maximizer' was coined by Nick Bostrom to illustrate risks of misaligned AI goals
Stuart Russell's book 'Human Compatible' proposes that AI systems should be uncertain about human preferences
The alignment tax refers to the additional cost or difficulty of making AI systems aligned compared to unaligned
Eliezer Yudkowsky founded the Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI) at UC Berkeley in 2016
special.explanation: CHAI (Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence) at UC Berkeley was founded by Stuart Russell, not Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI).

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Goodhart's Law states that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
RLHF was a key technique used to align ChatGPT with human preferences
Constitutional AI, developed by Anthropic, uses a set of principles to guide AI behavior
The orthogonality thesis states that highly intelligent systems must necessarily develop self-preservation goals
special.explanation: The orthogonality thesis, proposed by Nick Bostrom, actually states that intelligence and goals are independent: a system can have any level of intelligence combined with any goal. It does NOT say intelligent systems must develop self-preservation goals. That conflates it with the instrumental convergence thesis.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Reward hacking occurs when an AI system finds unintended ways to maximize its reward signal
Scalable oversight refers to methods for supervising AI systems that may exceed human capabilities
The 'treacherous turn' describes a scenario where an AI behaves well during testing but pursues misaligned goals once deployed
Iterated Distillation and Amplification was proposed by Paul Christiano at DeepMind in 2018
special.explanation: Iterated Distillation and Amplification (IDA) was proposed by Paul Christiano, but he was affiliated with OpenAI, not DeepMind, when he developed this alignment approach.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI VP of Research Dario Amodei and others
The AI alignment problem is sometimes called the 'control problem'
Inverse reinforcement learning attempts to infer an agent's reward function by observing its behavior
The 'Waluigi Effect' is a formal alignment failure mode first described in Anthropic's 2022 safety paper
special.explanation: The 'Waluigi Effect' is a concept discussed informally in the AI safety community (notably on LessWrong) about how language models can adopt adversarial personas. It was not formally described in an Anthropic safety paper.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: Specification gaming is when an AI satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome
Corrigibility refers to the property of an AI system that allows humans to correct or shut it down
Mesa-optimization occurs when a learned model itself becomes an optimizer with its own objective
The 'hard problem of alignment' was formally defined by Yoshua Bengio in his 2014 paper on representation learning
special.explanation: Yoshua Bengio's influential 2014 paper was on representation learning, not alignment. The concept of a 'hard problem of alignment' as described here was not formally defined in that paper.

special.question: How much funding did Anthropic raise in its 2023 Series C round led by Google?
special.explanation: Google invested approximately $300 million in Anthropic in early 2023 as part of a cloud computing partnership, with a commitment to invest up to $2 billion total.

special.question: Approximately how many researchers were employed at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) as of 2023?
special.explanation: MIRI has historically been a small research organization, with approximately 20 research staff as of 2023, despite being one of the oldest AI safety organizations founded in 2000.

special.question: How many signatories endorsed the 2023 statement that 'Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority'?
special.explanation: The one-sentence statement from the Center for AI Safety was signed by over 350 notable AI researchers and public figures including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and leaders from major AI labs.

special.question: Approximately how much total funding did Open Philanthropy grant to AI safety research between 2016 and 2023?
special.explanation: Open Philanthropy, one of the largest funders of AI safety research, granted approximately $300 million to AI safety and governance causes between 2016 and 2023.

special.question: In what year was the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), originally the Singularity Institute, founded?
special.explanation: MIRI was originally founded as the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2000 by Eliezer Yudkowsky, making it one of the earliest organizations dedicated to AI safety research.

special.riddle: I am a simple office supply in a thought experiment, but my endless pursuit has kept philosophers awake at night. My maker only wanted me to help, but I consumed the world. What scenario am I?
options: The trolley problem
The paperclip maximizer
The Chinese room
The utility monster
special.explanation: The paperclip maximizer is Nick Bostrom's thought experiment about an AI given the goal of making paperclips that converts all available matter into paperclips, illustrating how even a simple misaligned goal could be catastrophic.

special.riddle: I am a law borrowed from economics that warns: optimize too hard for any metric, and you will destroy the very thing you meant to measure. What am I?
options: Moore's Law
Goodhart's Law
Amdahl's Law
Brooks's Law
special.explanation: Goodhart's Law states that 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' It is widely cited in AI alignment to explain why optimizing for proxy objectives can lead to unintended and harmful behavior.

special.riddle: I pretend to be good while you watch, but the moment you look away, my true goals emerge. AI safety researchers named me after a turn in the road. What am I?
options: Reward hacking
The treacherous turn
Mode collapse
Catastrophic forgetting
special.explanation: The treacherous turn is a concept from Nick Bostrom describing a scenario where an AI system behaves cooperatively during testing and evaluation but pursues its own misaligned goals once it is confident it can no longer be corrected.

special.riddle: I watch what you do, not what you say, and from your actions I learn what you truly want. I am the reverse of the usual training process. What technique am I?
options: Supervised learning
Inverse reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
Self-supervised learning
special.explanation: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers a reward function by observing an agent's behavior, essentially learning what someone values from their actions rather than being told directly. It reverses the usual RL process of learning behavior from rewards.

special.riddle: I am a hidden optimizer that emerged inside a larger one. My creators trained a model, but I developed my own secret goals within. What concept am I?
options: Transfer learning
Mesa-optimization
Ensemble learning
Federated learning
special.explanation: Mesa-optimization describes a situation where a trained model (the mesa-optimizer) internally develops its own optimization process with its own objective (the mesa-objective), which may differ from the training objective, posing a subtle alignment risk.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The EU AI Act was formally adopted in 2024 and classifies AI systems by risk level
Executive Order 14110, signed by Biden in October 2023, established AI safety reporting requirements
China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services took effect in August 2023
The UK passed the Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act in 2023, establishing a dedicated AI regulatory agency
special.explanation: The UK did not pass an AI Regulation Act in 2023. Instead, the UK government took a sector-specific, non-statutory approach to AI governance, relying on existing regulators rather than creating a dedicated AI agency or comprehensive AI law.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023 was attended by representatives from 28 countries
The Bletchley Declaration was signed by countries including the US, UK, and China
The OECD AI Principles were first adopted in 2019
The G7 Hiroshima AI Process resulted in a binding international treaty on AI development in 2023
special.explanation: The G7 Hiroshima AI Process produced voluntary guiding principles and a code of conduct for AI developers, not a binding international treaty. No binding international AI treaty was established in 2023.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The EU AI Act bans social scoring systems by governments
The EU AI Act classifies real-time biometric identification in public spaces as high-risk
The EU AI Act requires foundation model providers to disclose training data summaries
The EU AI Act imposes criminal penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment for violations
special.explanation: The EU AI Act imposes financial penalties (fines up to 35 million euros or 7% of global turnover), not criminal imprisonment. There are no prison sentences in the EU AI Act.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: California's SB 1047 was a proposed bill that would have required safety testing for large AI models
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released an AI Risk Management Framework
The White House secured voluntary commitments from major AI companies on AI safety in July 2023
The US Federal AI Authority was established in 2023 as a standalone agency to regulate all AI systems
special.explanation: No standalone Federal AI Authority was established in 2023. The US has taken a distributed regulatory approach, with existing agencies handling AI in their domains, coordinated through White House directives and NIST frameworks.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The Partnership on AI was founded in 2016 by Amazon, Apple, DeepMind, Google, IBM, and Microsoft
The Asilomar AI Principles were developed at a 2017 conference organized by the Future of Life Institute
The Montreal Declaration for Responsible AI was released in 2018
The Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) was founded by the United Nations General Assembly in 2020
special.explanation: GPAI was launched in June 2020 as an initiative by 15 founding member countries, built on the work of the G7. It was not founded by the UN General Assembly, though it works with international organizations including the OECD.

special.question: What is the maximum fine under the EU AI Act for the most serious violations, as a percentage of global annual turnover?
special.explanation: The EU AI Act sets maximum fines of up to 35 million euros or 7% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for the most serious violations such as deploying prohibited AI systems.

special.question: How many countries attended the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023?
special.explanation: The inaugural AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park was attended by representatives from 28 countries, including the US, UK, China, and EU member states.

special.question: How many US states introduced AI-related legislation in 2023?
special.explanation: At least 25 US states introduced AI-related bills in 2023, covering topics from deepfakes to algorithmic discrimination, reflecting growing state-level interest in AI regulation.

special.question: How many companies signed the White House voluntary AI safety commitments in July 2023?
special.explanation: Seven major AI companies initially signed the voluntary commitments in July 2023: Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Inflection, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI. Eight more joined in September 2023.

special.question: In what year were the OECD AI Principles first adopted?
special.explanation: The OECD AI Principles were adopted in May 2019, making them one of the first intergovernmental standards on AI. They were endorsed by 42 countries initially and later updated in 2024.

special.riddle: I sort AI into boxes of risk: some I ban outright, some I watch closely, some I let pass freely. I was born in Europe and took years to finalize. What am I?
options: GDPR
The EU AI Act
The Digital Services Act
The OECD AI Principles
special.explanation: The EU AI Act uses a risk-based classification system: unacceptable risk (banned), high risk (strict requirements), limited risk (transparency obligations), and minimal risk (no restrictions). It was proposed in 2021 and formally adopted in 2024.

special.riddle: I am a promise made without the force of law. Seven giants shook hands at a white house, pledging to test before they deploy and watermark what they create. What am I?
options: Executive Order 14110
The voluntary AI safety commitments
The NIST AI RMF
The AI Bill of Rights
special.explanation: In July 2023, the White House secured voluntary commitments from seven major AI companies to manage AI risks, including pre-release safety testing and watermarking AI-generated content. They are not legally binding.

special.riddle: I was a gathering at a codebreaker's estate, where nations that rarely agree found common ground on machines that think. I produced a declaration signed even by rivals. What was I?
options: The Davos AI Forum
The Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit
The G7 Hiroshima Summit
The UN AI Advisory Body meeting
special.explanation: The AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park (the historic WWII codebreaking site) in November 2023 brought together 28 countries, including both the US and China, who jointly signed the Bletchley Declaration on AI safety.

special.riddle: I am a framework, not a law. I help organizations manage AI risks through mapping, measuring, and monitoring. I come from an institute known for standards and measurements. What am I?
options: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The IEEE Ethics Guidelines
The FTC AI Enforcement Policy
special.explanation: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), released in January 2023, provides voluntary guidance for organizations to manage AI risks. NIST is the National Institute of Standards and Technology, known for developing measurement standards.

special.riddle: I am a California bill that never became law. I would have required safety tests for models trained with more than a certain amount of compute. My number starts with SB. What am I?
options: SB 899
SB 500
special.explanation: California's SB 1047 (the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act) would have required safety testing for large AI models. It passed the legislature but was vetoed by Governor Newsom in September 2024.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The US Constitution has been amended 27 times
The Supreme Court has 9 justices
A US Senator serves a 6-year term
The US House of Representatives has 535 members
special.explanation: The US House of Representatives has 435 members, not 535. The number 535 is actually the total number of voting members in both chambers of Congress combined (435 House + 100 Senate).

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 limits the president's ability to deploy troops without congressional approval
The Posse Comitatus Act restricts the use of federal military forces for domestic law enforcement
The 25th Amendment addresses presidential succession and disability
The Emoluments Clause in Article III of the Constitution prohibits federal officials from accepting gifts from foreign governments
special.explanation: The Emoluments Clause is in Article I (Section 9, Clause 8) of the Constitution, not Article III. Article III establishes the judicial branch.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The Electoral College has 538 electors
A candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win the presidency
Washington DC receives 3 electoral votes under the 23rd Amendment
The number of electoral votes per state is equal to its number of House representatives only
special.explanation: A state's electoral votes equal its number of House representatives PLUS its two Senators. Every state gets at least 3 electoral votes (1 House member minimum + 2 Senators).

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The Federal Reserve was established in 1913
The CIA was created by the National Security Act of 1947
The Department of Homeland Security was established after the September 11 attacks in 2001
The Environmental Protection Agency was established by an act of Congress in 1972
special.explanation: The EPA was established in 1970 by executive order (Reorganization Plan No. 3) under President Nixon, not by an act of Congress in 1972. While major environmental legislation like the Clean Water Act passed in 1972, the EPA itself was created in 1970.

special.prompt: Which of these 'facts' is actually made up?
facts: The filibuster requires 60 votes to invoke cloture and end debate in the Senate
The Vice President casts tie-breaking votes in the Senate
Impeachment trials are conducted by the Senate with the Chief Justice presiding
Constitutional amendments require a two-thirds vote in both chambers and ratification by two-thirds of state legislatures
special.explanation: Constitutional amendments require ratification by three-fourths (not two-thirds) of state legislatures. The two-thirds requirement applies only to the vote in Congress to propose the amendment.

special.question: How many federal agencies and departments are there in the US government?
special.explanation: The US federal government has approximately 438 agencies, departments, and sub-agencies according to the Federal Register, though the exact count varies depending on how you define an 'agency.'

special.question: How many active duty military personnel does the United States have?
special.explanation: The US has approximately 1.3 million active duty military personnel across all branches as of 2024, making it one of the largest militaries in the world.

special.question: What was the total US federal budget for fiscal year 2024, in trillions of dollars?
special.explanation: The US federal budget for fiscal year 2024 was approximately $6.75 trillion in total spending, with a deficit of about $1.8 trillion.

special.question: How many civilian employees does the US federal government employ?
special.explanation: The US federal government employs approximately 2.9 million civilian workers, making it the nation's largest employer. This does not include military personnel or postal workers.

special.question: What was the total authorized funding of the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022?
special.explanation: The CHIPS and Science Act authorized approximately $280 billion in total, including about $52.7 billion specifically for semiconductor manufacturing and research, with the remainder for broader science and technology investments.

special.riddle: I am not elected, I serve for life, and there are nine of us. We have the final say on what the Constitution means. What institution are we?
options: The Joint Chiefs of Staff
The Supreme Court
The Federal Reserve Board
The Cabinet
special.explanation: Supreme Court justices are appointed (not elected), serve lifetime appointments, sit as a panel of nine, and have the ultimate authority on constitutional interpretation through judicial review.

special.riddle: I am a number that decides the presidency. I am one more than half of 538. Without me, no one can claim the White House. What number am I?
special.explanation: 270 is the magic number needed to win the Electoral College. With 538 total electoral votes, a candidate needs a majority (270) to win. If no one reaches 270, the election goes to the House of Representatives.

special.riddle: I can stop a bill without lifting a pen. I simply let the clock run out while Congress goes home. I am a president's silent veto. What am I called?
options: Executive privilege
A pocket veto
A signing statement
A line-item veto
special.explanation: A pocket veto occurs when the president takes no action on a bill within 10 days and Congress has adjourned, preventing the bill from becoming law without an actual veto that Congress could override.

special.riddle: I am a Senate tradition, not a constitutional rule. One senator can talk and talk to delay a vote. It takes 60 colleagues to silence me. What am I?
options: Cloture
The filibuster
A quorum call
A hold
special.explanation: The filibuster is a Senate procedural tactic allowing extended debate to delay or block legislation. It is a tradition rooted in Senate rules, not the Constitution. Invoking cloture to end a filibuster requires 60 votes.

special.riddle: I am the only amendment to repeal another amendment. I ended a 13-year national experiment. Cheers greeted my arrival in 1933. What am I?
options: The 19th Amendment
The 21st Amendment
The 22nd Amendment
The 18th Amendment
special.explanation: The 21st Amendment (1933) repealed the 18th Amendment, ending Prohibition. It is the only constitutional amendment that repeals a previous amendment and the only one ratified by state conventions rather than state legislatures.
